Software Design and Architecture [Week01 & 2 – Introduction]
Extra: Story as an introduction for Chapter1

The house analogy: a building can look finished and still crack later if the foundation is weak. In software the “cracks” are bugs, crashes and code that is painful to change. The foundation of software is its architecture (the big structure) and the design principles used inside it. The whole course is about building that foundation on purpose instead of by accident. Software engineering was named in 1968 because large projects of the 1960s kept running late, over budget or failing outright. The answer was to build software with the planned, measured methods of traditional engineering. Extra: Story as an introduction for Chapter1 Building software is like building a house.If the foundation is weak, cracks will appear over time, no matter how beautiful it looks. In software, the foundation is good architecture and design principles. Without them, you’ll face bugs, crashes, and hard-to-maintain code. This course will teach you how to build strong, scalable, and maintainable software that lasts—just like a well-built house. In the 1960s, software projects became too complex and often failed. In 1968, software engineeringwas introduced as a structured way to build reliable software, using methods similar to traditional engineering.
Lecture Outlines

The lecture moves from the general to the specific: what software engineering is, then design viewed as problem solving , then what design is and why we study it. Next come the challenges that make design hard and the process (the activities designers carry out). It ends with the fundamentals : principles, strategies and considerations. These are the tools you will apply in every later chapter, so they get the most slides. Software Engineering (revised)

Software is the set of instructions that lets a user make the hardware do useful work: operating systems, word processors and browsers are all software. Engineering is a systematic process: designers generate and evaluate designs whose functions meet the clients’ objectives and the users’ needs while respecting constraints (cost, time, laws, hardware). The bridge example makes the point: you plan for weight and weather before you build, and software needs the same planning. Keep user and client apart. The user is whoever actually works with the software; the client is whoever pays for it. A hospital buys a system (client) that nurses use every day (users), and the two may want different things. The IEEE definition is the one to memorise word for word: software engineering is the application of a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software, in short, applying engineering principles to software. Software Engineering (revised)

Systematic means the work is organised as a coherent body of ideas and is methodical: there is a plan and a procedure, not improvisation. Disciplined means a set of rules governs the work, and the team actually follows them (coding standards, review steps, approval rules). Quantifiable means you can measure the deliverables: how many requirements are done, how many defects were found, how long a response takes. If you can’t measure it, you can’t tell whether it is improving. The Extra example: agile methods run in short iterations with regular checks, which is one practical way to be systematic, disciplined and measurable at the same time. “To determine, express, or measure the quantity of deliverables” defines which word in the IEEE definition? Software Engineering (revised)

Requirements : find out what is needed, then analyse, specify and validate it. Everything later depends on this being right. Design turns the requirements specification into a software design, which has two levels: the architecture (major parts and how they connect) and the detailed design (the inside of each part). This course lives in this phase. Implementation writes the code, using the requirements, the architecture and the detailed design together. Maintenance changes the software after delivery: fixing faults, improving performance, or adapting it to a new environment. It is usually the longest and most expensive phase, which is why designs are judged by how easy they are to change. In which phase is the requirements specification used to create the software architecture and detailed design? Design gives a team a shared plan: who builds which part and how the parts fit. That is how it lets teams work in a disciplined way and keeps the product aligned with its specification. Engineering Problem-solving

Problem solving in design passes through three states . Knowing which state you are in tells you what activity is appropriate. Initial state : the problem is formulated and interpreted. Often the hardest part is understanding the problem itself (what exactly does the client need?). Operational state : once the problem is understood, you think about it and possible solutions appear. This is where creativity and alternatives matter, and where functional fixedness (slide 11) does the most damage. Goal state : a solution has been identified, evaluated and validated. Problem solving ends here. In which problem-solving state is the problem formulated and interpreted? Initial state Operational state Goal state Final state Engineering Problem-solving In general, problem-solving during design occurs in three different states: Initial State ⮚ Problems are formulated and interpreted ✔ In some cases, understanding the problem is a problem itself. ✔ Operational State ⮚ Once problem is understood, operational state begins ✔ Thinking about the problem and viable solutions come to light ✔ Goal State ⮚ Once an appropriate solution is identified, evaluated, and validated, goal state is reached ✔ Final solution found, marking the end of the problem-solving process. ✔

The classic nine-dot puzzle: connect all nine dots with four straight lines without lifting the pencil or retracing a line. Most students assumed each line must begin and end on a dot. The requirements never said so; it was an assumption they brought with them. Functional fixedness : you only see an object (or a component, or a technique) in the role you are used to, so solutions that use it differently never occur to you. It is a limit of the designer’s thinking, not a property of the software. The remedy is deliberate: attempt the problem several times, from different viewpoints and unusual angles (“think outside the box”). The possible solution on the right only works because its lines leave the square. It matters most in the operational state , the state where alternative solutions are generated (slide 9). In the context of engineering problem-solving, what is “functional fixedness”? A state where a solution is successfully validated and the goal is reached. A design strategy that focuses strictly on functional requirements. A cognitive bias that limits the ability to find solutions because objects are only seen in their usual function. Software Engineering Design

The formal definition has two halves. (1) Design is a process : identifying and evaluating the architectural and detailed models needed to build software that meets its functional and non-functional requirements. (2) Design is also the product of that process: the design diagrams and documents it produces. When someone says “show me the design”, they mean the product; when they say “we are in design”, they mean the process. True or false: in software engineering, “design” refers only to the diagrams produced, not to the activity. Software Engineering Design Formally, software engineering design is defined as: ⮚ (1) The process of identifying, and evaluating the architectural, and ✔ detailed models required to build software that meets its intended functional and non-functional requirements; and, (2) the product (output or the result)of such process. (i.e. the ✔ produced design diagrams or documents)
Software Engineering Design

Because the word covers both meanings, industry uses “design” for the process and the product interchangeably. Exam questions often ask which perspective a statement belongs to. Process perspective : the activities and tasks needed to model the software’s structure and behaviour before construction. This is mostly a project-management concern: the management team plans, organises and assigns the design tasks and lines up schedule and resources. Software Engineering Design In the software industry, the term design is used ⮚ interchangeably to describe both the process and product resulting from such process. From the process perspective, it describes the phase ✔ activities and tasks required to model software’s structure and behavior before construction.(This is concerned mostly with the project management’s aspect of development.) Extra: The project management’s team will plan, organize, and assign tasks; ensure schedule and resources are aligned before construction. From the product perspective, it describes artifacts ✔ resulting from design activities, e.g., class diagram. (This is concerned mostly with the technical aspects of development.) Extra: The Technical team will create the actual design artifacts (e.g., class diagrams, sequence diagrams) that define the software’s structure and behavior.
Why Study Software Engineering Design?
Section divider. The next two slides answer the question from both perspectives introduced on slide 15: project management (process) and technical (product). Why Study Software Engineering Design??
Possible reasons

Good design minimises the effect of requirements volatility . In a modular design a new feature, such as multi-language support, is added to one module without disturbing the others. It makes human resource allocation efficient: once components are defined and documented, the manager can give each one to a developer with the right skills. It protects the project from depending on “ one guy ” who owns the whole system in his head. If the design is written down, the project survives that person leaving. From a project management perspective, why is studying software design important? It ensures that only one person owns the entire system. It helps minimize the negative effects of requirements volatility. It focuses purely on technical artifacts like class diagrams. It eliminates the need for testing and maintenance phases. Possible reasons 1- From the project management’s perspective ”process perspective”, studying software ⮚ design is important, mainly because: • Good software design help minimize effects of requirements’ volatility Extra Example : If a new feature (e.g., multi-language support) is requested, a modular design allows for easier integration without disrupting existing components. • Increases efficiency in human resource allocation. Extra Example:Clear design documentation helps project managers allocate specific tasks to developers with relevant expertise, optimizing team productivity. • Shields the project from having “one guy” owning the whole system. • Overall, design helps improve project management: planning, organization, staffing, and tracking.
Possible reasons

Second reason set: the technical (product-development) perspective. The online-store example runs through all six points. Design gives a way to evaluate quality attributes (usability, efficiency…) before code exists, such as checking how many steps checkout takes. Major Software Design Challenges

Requirements volatility : the requirements change while you build. A banking app that started simple must suddenly add advanced login security late in development. Inconsistent development processes : teams don’t follow the same design process. One team uses Agile, another Waterfall, and integration gets delayed. Fast, ever-changing technology : platforms and libraries change constantly; new iOS and Android versions force quick updates just to keep the app working. Managing design influences : stakeholders pull in different directions; executives want profit features while the security team wants stronger protection. Requirements volatility is growth or change in the requirements during the project’s development life cycle. Some change is normal; the challenge is designing so it does not wreck the project. Software Design Challenge #4 Managing Design influences

A project has many stakeholders (users, clients, managers, security, operations), and each has needs that pull the design their way: one wants performance, another usability, another security. Some of those needs conflict , and each stakeholder is convinced they are right. Stronger security can make the system slower or harder to use, for instance. The designer has to make trade-offs that satisfy each stakeholder as far as possible, without the decision harming the project as a whole. This is especially difficult in large-scale systems , where there are more stakeholders and every decision touches more parts. Software Design Process

The design process has two major activities: software architecture and detailed design . These two are the heart of the course (architecture in chapters 2–4, detailed design in 5–7). Software Design Process

Software architecture is the macro-design approach: it creates models that show the quality and the function of the whole system, at the level of big parts rather than code. Its models are black boxes : each component is described by what it does and how it connects, not by its insides. That is enough to evaluate the system’s projected quality and functions early. It is designed from multiple perspectives (views), so stakeholders with different backgrounds can each check that their concerns are addressed. Chapter 2’s 4+1 views come from this idea. It focuses on the quality aspects (performance, security, availability…) before detailed design or construction begins, because quality is hard to add later. An initializeSystem() method opens database connections, loads configuration and logs the start time. Which cohesion is this? Temporal Functional Communicational Procedural Extra: ️℔ Functional ⮚ Cohesion Definition: All parts work together to do one single task. Example: A calculateTotal() method that sums prices of items in a cart. ᳀ Procedural(Sequential) ⮚ Cohesion Definition: Tasks are done in a specific sequence, where output of one step is input to the next. Example: A processOrder() method that:Validatesorder →Calculates cost →Processes payment. ᲼ Temporal ⮚ Cohesion Definition: Tasks happen at the same time or in the same phase. Example: An initializeSystem() method that sets up database connections, loads configuration, and logs startup time —all at program start. Შ Communication ⮚ Cohesion Definition: Tasks work on the same data. Example: A generateStudentReport() method that calculates GPA, lists enrolled courses, and prints grades —all using the same student record.
Extra: Good vs. Bad Design

Bad design: CartManager mixes addItemToCart() , sendEmailToUser() and connectToDatabase() , three unrelated jobs, so cohesion is low . It also creates the Database and EmailService objects itself, so coupling is tight : changing either service means editing CartManager. A CartManager class adds items to the cart, sends emails to users and connects to the database, and creates its own Database object. Identify the cohesion and coupling problems and suggest a fix. Extra: ✅ Good Design (Low coupling + High cohesion) • ShoppingCart class: o Methods: addItem(), removeItem(), calculateTotal(). o All methods are related to cart management → high cohesion. • The cart doesn’t talk directly to Database or PaymentService, but only through an interface → low coupling. o If tomorrow you change from SQLite to Firebase, ShoppingCart doesn’t break. ❌ Bad Design (High coupling + Low cohesion) • Utility class called CartManager: o Methods: addItemToCart(), sendEmailToUser(), connectToDatabase(). o These methods do completely different jobs → low cohesion. • CartManager directly creates Database and EmailService objects → tight coupling. o If you change the database or email service, you must edit CartManager.
Software Design Fundamentals (Principles)

It is not the same as encapsulation. Encapsulation hides the implementation details; this principle separates them, so the interface exists on its own. The payoff: different implementations of the same interface can be provided and swapped (a PaymentGateway interface with Visa and PayPal implementations) without affecting the code that uses the interface. How does separation of interface and implementation differ from encapsulation? Software Design Fundamentals (Principles) Design Principle #6: Separation of Interface and Implementation ⮚ Deals with creating modules in such way that a stable ✔ interface is identified and separated from its implementation. Not the same thing as encapsulation! ✔ While encapsulation dictates hiding the details ✔ of implementation, this principle dictates their separation, so that different implementations of the same interface can be provided Extra: Encapsulation Prevent direct access to an object’s internal dataandhideitsimplementationdetails. SegregationofInterfaceandImplementation •Meaning:Keep the what(interface) separate from the how (implementation) and allows changing the implementation withoutaffecting the interface users.
Software Design Fundamentals (Principles)

Completeness measures whether a design unit provides all the services it needs to achieve its intent: no less. Example: a communication class is complete only if it can establish and terminate a connection and send and receive messages. Missing any one makes it incomplete. Sufficiency measures whether the unit provides only the services sufficient for its intent: no more. Completeness asks “is anything missing?”, sufficiency asks “is anything extra?”. Example of insufficiency in the opposite sense: a messaging module that also manages user profiles has taken on a service outside its purpose. The banking example on the slide shows completeness: the transfer and history requirements must both appear in the design. Which design principle measures how well a unit provides only the services necessary for its intent, ensuring no extra, unnecessary features are included? Completeness. Sufficiency. Cohesion. Modularization. Software Design Fundamentals (Principles) Design Principle #7: Completeness ⮚ Measures how well design units provide the required services to a achieve their intent (no less) Example: in detailed design, a communication class is considered complete if it provides all required services establishing /terminating a connection, sending/receiving messages. If any of these service in missing the class is considered as incomplete Design Principle #8: Sufficiency ⮚ Measures how well design units are providing only the services that are sufficient for achieving their intent (no more) Extra: •Completeness= WHAT → all requirements are addressed. •Example:If the requirement says “the banking system must allow users to transfer money and view transaction history,”the design must include both features(transfer + history). •Sufficiency= HOW → the design solves them effectively, efficiently, and adequately and nothing extra is there. •Example:A messaging module should not also manage user profiles —that’s outside its purpose.
So …. To Wrap-up

Coupling = dependency between modules; cohesion = how related the tasks in a module are. Separation of interface and implementation = one interface, possibly several implementations. Completeness = every required service is there; sufficiency = only the services needed. A one-line definition of each is a likely short question. Match each principle to its one-line meaning: modularization, abstraction, encapsulation, coupling, cohesion, completeness. So …. To Wrap-up Design Principles ⮚ Modularization� Decompose into separate modules Abstraction� Separate the (what) from the (how) Encapsulation � Information hiding Coupling� Dependency between modules Cohesion � Tasks in a module Separation of Interface and Implementation � An interface … with different implementations All required units for achieving intent Completeness� Sufficiency � Sufficient units for achieving intent
Software Design Fundamentals (Strategies)

Every object has a unique identity (a name), a state (its attribute values) and well-defined behaviour (its operations). It supports inheritance and polymorphism and suits object-oriented languages such as Java. Chapters 5–7 use this strategy throughout. Software Design Fundamentals (Strategies) Object-oriented design strategy ⮚ Design strategy in which a system or ✔ component is expressed in terms of objects and connections between those objects. Focuses on object decomposition. ✔ ▪ Objects have unique identity (name) ▪ Objects have state (attributes) ▪ Objects have well-defined behavior Supports inheritance and polymorphism ✔ Appropriate for use with Object-oriented ✔ Languages
Software Design Fundamentals

The structured (functional) strategy decomposes a system into single-purpose, independent modules using an iterative top-down approach: start with the whole function and keep breaking it down. It is inappropriate for object-oriented languages because it is centred on functions, not objects. It fits procedural languages such as C. Compare the object-oriented and structured design strategies. Software Design Fundamentals (Strategies) Structured (or Functional) design strategy ⮚ Design strategy in which a system or ✔ component is decomposed into single-purpose, independent modules, using an iterative top- down approach. Focuses on ✔ Extra: ▪ The functions that the system needs to provide, Structured (Functional) Design Strategy: ▪ The decomposition of these functions, and - Meaning: Breaks the system into independent, single- ▪ The creation of modules that incorporate these purpose modules using a top-down approach. functions. - Focuses on: 1-The functions the system must perform. Inappropriate for use with object-oriented 2-Breaking functions into smaller ones. ✔ 3-Creating modules that implement these functions. programming languages. - Limitation: Not suitable for object-oriented programming since it centers on functions, not objects.
Software Design Fundamentals (Considerations)

When two design options compete and both meet the requirements, choose the one that is less complex (fewer parts, fewer dependencies). Design for change : software will change, so design with extension in mind. Several techniques (modularity, interfaces, the principles of chapter 5) help achieve this. Fill in the blank: When two designs satisfy the same requirements, the design with fewer unnecessary dependencies is generally preferred because software design should minimize ___. Software Design Fundamentals (Considerations) Design for minimizing complexity ⮚ Design is about minimizing complexity. ✔ Every decision that is made during design must take into account reducing complexity. ✔ When faced with competing design option, always choose the one that minimizes ✔ complexity Design for change ⮚ Software will change, design with extension in mind. ✔ A variety of techniques can be employed through the design phase to achieve this. ✔

n: Slide 1

Week 3, first architecture lecture. Chapter 1 named architecture as the first major design activity; this lecture defines it formally and lists what an architect actually does. Software Design and Architecture [Software Architecture] – Week 03, L01
Lecture Outlines

First half: the fundamentals, meaning what architecture is and why it matters. Second half: the key tasks, from identifying stakeholder concerns to keeping the implementation in sync with the design. Final 252 asked you to list five of them. It closes by applying Chapter 1’s problem-solving framework to architecture. Lecture Outlines Fundamentals of software architecture ⮚ What is software architecture? ✔ Why is it important? ✔ Key tasks in software architecture ⮚ Stakeholders concerns ✔ Identify architectural views, styles, and patterns ✔ Identify major component’s and interfaces ✔ Evaluating and validating the Architecture ✔ Introducing policies for design synchronicity ✔ Problem-solving in architecture ⮚ What’s next… ⮚ Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 2 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Architecture is first a communication tool: it gives every stakeholder (developers, managers, clients, operators) one shared picture of the system to discuss and decide on. Its two questions are what parts exist and how they fit together : the major components and the connections between them. It is not about development details, algorithms or data structures . Those belong to detailed and construction design. A diagram that shows sorting logic is no longer an architecture diagram. Software architecture is NOT about: Communication High-level structure Algorithms Nonfunctional requirements Fundamentals of Software Architecture Architecture is: ⮚ All about communication. ✔ What ‘parts’ are there? ✔ How do the ‘parts’ fit together? ✔ Architecture is not: ⮚ About development. ✔ About algorithms. ✔ About data structures. ✔ Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 3 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

“Architecture” has three meanings at once: the high-level structures of a system, the discipline of creating them, and the documentation that records them. It captures three dimensions: structure (the parts), communication or behaviour (how the parts interact at run time), and non-functional requirements (the qualities the system must have: performance, security, availability…). It focuses on the decisions that would be difficult to change once the system is built : the choice of components, how they talk, where data lives. That is why these decisions are made first and with care. Which is NOT one of the three primary dimensions captured by software architecture? Coding style Structure Communication (behavior) Nonfunctional requirements Fundamentals of Software Architecture What is Architecture ? Refers to the high level structures of a software system, the discipline of ⮚ creating such structures, and the documentation of these structures. Architecture captures three primary dimensions: ⮚ Structure ✔ Communication (behavior) ✔ Nonfunctional requirements ✔ Focuses on those aspects of a system that would be difficult to change ⮚ once the system is built. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 4 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

The formal definition, part (1): architecture is the foundational software design activity . It comes first and everything else is built on it. All of this exists to support detailed design and construction : it is an input to the next phases, not an end in itself. Part (2): architecture is also the product of that activity, the high-level diagrams and component models (the same process/product split as Chapter 1). Define the formal software architecture and then pick any three major parts of the definition and explain them. Fundamentals of Software Architecture Let’s get straight to the point, formally, we define software architecture as ⮚ (1)The foundational software design activitythat evaluates and translates software requirements ⮚ (both functional and non-functional) into a collection of design elements that specify structuraland behavioral aspects of the major components of the system, together with their provided qualityand interrelationships required to support the detailed design and constructionof software systems. • (2) and the productresulting from such activity. Extra: Software architecture (big-picture ) 1-Process is deciding how the major componentsof the system (frontend, backend, database, etc.) will be structured and interact. 2-Product is the high-level diagrams, component models. • Example • Imagine you are building an e-commerce website(like Amazon). ➢ Architecture activity (process): You decide the system needs: • A frontend(user interface) where customers browse and order. • A backend(server logic) to process orders. • A databaseto store products and users. • A payment serviceto handle credit cards. ➢ Architecture product (blueprint): A diagram showing these components (Frontend → Backend → Database → Payment Service) and how they talk to each other. 5 Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides
Extra: Architecture vs. Detailed Design

Extra: Comparison between Software Architecture and Detailed Design Software Architecture (big picture) • Process: Deciding how the major components of the system (frontend, backend, database, etc.) will be structured and interact. • Product:The blueprint (high-level diagrams, component models). • Example: For an online shopping app → deciding that you need a frontend (website/app), backend (server logic), payment service, and database. Software Design (detailed picture) • Process:Working out the details inside those components —the classes, functions, data structures, algorithms, and how they solve the requirements. • Product:The design diagrams/documents (class diagrams, sequence diagrams, flowcharts, etc.). • Example:For the same online shopping app → designing how the “ShoppingCart” class works, what methods it has (addItem(), removeItem(), checkout()), and how it communicates with the Payment class.
Extra: Architecture = high-level interaction

At this level we deliberately don’t care how each part works inside . Only which parts exist and how they talk. Extra: Comparison between Software Architecture and Detailed Design • 1. Architecture = High-level Interaction (Big Picture) • Focus: Which components exist and how they connect. • Shows: Subsystems or major modules, not individual classes. • Interaction = component-to-component. • Example (Online Shopping App, Architecture): Frontend Backend Database Payment Gateway. The diagram would show arrows like: “Frontend sends requests to Backend,” “Backend stores data in Database,” “Backend calls Payment Gateway.” • So here, we don’t care how each part works internally — only which components exist and how they talk.
Extra: Design = low-level interaction

Zooming into the backend: a ShoppingCart class ( addItem() , removeItem() , checkout() ) and a Payment class ( processCreditCard() , confirmTransaction() ). At checkout, ShoppingCart calls Payment.processCreditCard() . Here method names, data flow and logic matter. You can use the same diagram types in both phases (a sequence diagram, for instance). The difference is the level: in architecture they show subsystems, actors and major flows; in design they go down to classes, methods and attributes. Give one example of an architecture-level interaction and one of a detailed-design interaction for an online shop. Extra: Continue 2. Design = Low-level Interaction (Detailed Picture) Focus: How components are implemented internally. Shows: Classes, methods, data structures, algorithms. Interaction = object-to-object / class-to-class. Extra: you can use the same diagram types across both phases Example (Online Shopping App, Design): In Architecture and Detailed design but: In the Backend, you zoom in and design: •In Architecture, they are high-level(just showing subsystems, • ShoppingCartclass(methods: addItem(), actors, or major flows). removeItem(), checkout()) •In Design, they are detailed(down to classes, methods, • Payment class(methods: processCreditCard(), attributes, exact interactions). confirmTransaction()) • So, the ShoppingCartcalls Payment.processCreditCard()when user checkout. • So here, we do care about method names, data flow, and logic.
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Slide 15: architecture supports (is an input to) detailed design and construction. These five phrases are exactly what Final 252 Q2-1 asked you to explain (any three). Fundamentals of Software Architecture From this definition, a few things are of interest and need further ⮚ explanation: Foundational design ✔ Transforming requirements (from textual base into a graphical base) ✔ Collection of design elements (diagrams) ✔ Major system components together with their provided quality ✔ Support (an input to) detailed design and construction ✔ Let’s take a more detailed look at these… ⮚ Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 9 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Foundational means architecture provides the groundwork for meeting the requirements, both functional and non-functional. Without it, there is nothing for the rest of the design to stand on. It should be forward engineering : done first, leading to the implementation. The opposite, reverse engineering , analyses a system after it has been built to recover its architecture. That is useful for old systems, but it is not how a new one should be designed. Because it is foundational, architecture is where designing for quality begins . Ignoring quality attributes here is a grave mistake: performance or security that the structure doesn’t support is very hard to add later. Which statement best explains why software architecture is considered a foundational design activity? It focuses on low-level coding decisions It documents completed systems It establishes the groundwork for satisfying functional and non-functional requirements It replaces detailed design activities Fundamentals of Software Architecture On “ … foundational software design…” ⮚ Software architecture provides the groundwork ”basic” essential for meeting ✔ requirements (functional + non-functional) This suggest that architecture is not an optional activity, it is a major activity. ✔ • New development efforts should approach software architecture as a forward engineering activity that leads to the implementation of systems and Extra :not as a reverse engineering analyzing the system after the system has been built and implemented. As foundational design, it is where designing for quality begins ✔ Not considering quality attributes of the system during the software ✔ architecture activity can be a grave mistake! Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 10 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Architecture provides abstractions of the requirements in the design domain: each requirement is mapped to design elements (components, connectors) that will satisfy it. That mapping turns requirements from text into diagrams , and it makes requirements traceable : for any requirement you can point to the components that implement it, and follow it through to code and tests. The mapping assumes the requirements are understood, which is often not the case . Architects therefore need to be good at requirements engineering : gathering, analysing and clarifying what the system must do. Chapter 2 Lecture 2 covers this. Fundamentals of Software Architecture On “…translates software requirements…” ⮚ Software architecture provides abstractions for software requirements in the design domain ✔ Design elements (diagrams) need to be created so that there is a mapping between ✔ requirements and design element. − When we do this, we transform requirements from textual form into a graphical form − This allows us to provide easy means for tracing requirements through the development life- cycle. To create design elements from requirements, it is assumed that requirements are understood, ✔ however, this is not always the case − This suggest that architects must be proficient in activities related to requirements engineering. • Extra: This statement means that before architects can create design elements based on requirements, they need to fully understand those requirements. However, understanding the requirements isn't always straightforward. Therefore, architects need to be skilled in requirements engineering, which involves gathering, analyzing, and clarifying what the system needs to do. This ensures that the design aligns with what is actually needed. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 11 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

No single structure or diagram can describe a whole architecture. Try judging both usability and performance from one picture: a screen-flow diagram says nothing about load, a deployment diagram says nothing about ease of use. The second reason is communication: architecture serves stakeholders with different backgrounds and questions, so different diagrams are needed for different stakeholders . Why are multiple architectural views required in complex systems? To reduce documentation effort Because no single view can represent all system aspects for all stakeholders To replace requirements engineering To simplify coding Fundamentals of Software Architecture On “…collection of design elements…” ⮚ No one structure or diagram can fully describe the software architecture. ✔ − Think about this: can you evaluate a system’s usability and performance with one diagram? This suggest that architectures are composed of multiple structures (or diagrams). ✔ This is also because architecture design aims for communicating the system structure with different ✔ stakeholders. Therefore, different diagrams are required for different stakeholders. Extra: Why one diagram is not enough in Software architecture? ❖ A single diagram cannot show everything (usability, performance, security, data flow, deployment). ❖ Different stakeholders (developers, testers, managers, customers) care about different views of the system. ❖ That’s why multiple diagrams (structures) are used in software architecture. Example: Online Shopping App • Component Diagram –shows major parts (frontend, backend, database, payment) and their interactions (for architects). • Class/Sequence Diagrams –show detailed logic and method calls (for developers). ❖ In short: Software architecture = collection of diagrams. Each one highlights a different aspect of the system so the right people can understand what they need. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 12 slides
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Architecture records three things about each major component: the component itself, the services (functionality) it provides to others, and the quality properties of those services. Example A (left): component B provides an algorithm, but nothing is said about its quality. The client just assumes it is “good enough”, and may discover too late that it is too slow or can’t be reused. Example B (right): the same component tagged with its qualities, e.g. performance O(n²) (slow for large inputs) and low reusability. Now the client knows the limits and can decide whether to use it. Quality tags make components transparent and choices informed. Fundamentals of Software Architecture On “…major components of the system, together with their provided quality…” ⮚ This means that architectural work focuses on the major components, the quality properties, ✔ and services (functionality) that these components exhibit and provide to other components. Extraabout the Figure: software architecture, it’s not enough to say “this component provides a service” —you also need to describe the quality of that service. Example A (Left Side) • Component B provides an algorithm. • But no quality info is given. • The client just assumes it’s “good enough.” • Risk: The component might be too slow or not reusable. Example B (Right Side) • Same component B, but now tagged with quality properties. • Example: • Performance: O(n²) (slow for large inputs). • Reusability: Low. • Now the client knows the limitations and may decide not to use it. Extra: When we design software architecture, we don’t just list the big parts (components). Why this matters Architecture is not just about structure, but also We also describe: about qualities (performance, scalability, security, reliability). Major components–the building blocks (e.g., Frontend, Backend, Database). Adding quality tags makes components transparent → clients can Quality properties–how they behave in terms of performance, security, make enlightened choices. scalability, etc. 13 Services (functionality)–what they actually provide to other components.
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Fundamentals of Software Architecture More on “…major components of the system, together with their ⮚ provided quality…” Expected quality requirements identified during architecture trickles down all the ✔ way to the implementation of components. Extra: 1. Assign quality to components • In the architecture, each component is tagged with expected qualities. • Example: Component B must be fast (performance), reliable, and secure. 2. Design & Coding phase • Programmers take these components into detailed design and coding. • The quality tags act like requirements guiding how the code should be written. 3. Output (code) • The produced code should meet the quality requirements (as specified in the architecture). • Example: If performance was required, the code should use efficient algorithms. 4. Important note • The same approach applies not only to quality requirements (e.g., performance, security) but also to functional requirements (what the system should do). 14
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

Architecture focuses on quality, but it must also produce a design that supports efficient detailed design and construction . A structure that is elegant on paper but awkward to implement fails this test. That is why architects benefit from knowing programming and design concepts well: they must foresee how their components will be built. And architecture alone cannot guarantee quality . Example: the architect requires security, a programmer skips it for lack of time, and the final code meets every quality except security. Qualities must be carried through into the code. True or false: a well-designed architecture guarantees the quality of the final system. Fundamentals of Software Architecture ⮚ On “…support detailed design and construction…” Although architecturefocuses on the quality properties of the system, it must also result in a design that supports efficient ✔ detaileddesign and constructionof the system. − Architects benefit greatly from having proficiency in general programming design concepts. This suggests that architecture alone cannot guarantee the quality of the system! ✔ •Extra: •Architect defines quality requirements(e.g., security). •Programmer ignores some (e.g., “no time for security”). •Final code meets most qualitiesbut misses security. •Result:Architecture alone ≠ guarantee → qualities must be implemented in code. 15
Fundamentals of Software Architecture

It often runs in parallel with some specification activities: sketching an architecture helps discover and check requirements. Fundamentals of Software Architecture To wrap up … ⮚ Architectural design should be an early stage of the system design ✔ process Represents the link between specification and design processes ✔ Often carried out in parallel with some specification activities ✔ It involves identifying major system components and their ✔ communications with required quality attributes Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 16 slides
Key Tasks in Architectural Design

Identify stakeholders’ concerns : the requirements and quality attributes each stakeholder cares about (slides 18–23). Identify architectural styles and patterns . A style is a general template for organising a system (e.g. distributed system); a pattern is a more specific reusable solution to a recurring problem (client–server, pipes and filters). Identify the influences of architectural decisions in organisations : their effect on budget, schedule and resources. Establish policies for design synchronicity , so every part follows the same design rules. Example: if the rule is “one database system, MySQL”, no team quietly uses MongoDB in its module (slide 28). List five of the key tasks in Architectural Design (the order is not important). Which FOUR of the following are key tasks performed during the Software Architecture Design effort? (Options included designing algorithms, unit testing, installing software, writing source code, budgeting and debugging.) Which task is part of architectural design? Writing source code Identifying stakeholders’ concerns Debugging Unit testing Key Tasks in Architectural Design Formally, key tasks that need to be performed during the software ⮚ Extra: architecture design effort include: 1. Architectural Views ▪ Identifying stakeholdersconcern (requirements & quality •Definition:Different perspectives to describe the attributes) system for different stakeholders. ▪ Identifying appropriate architectural views •Purpose:Communicate structure and behavior clearly ▪ Identifying architectural stylesand patterns to users, developers, testers, managers, etc. ▪ Identifying influencesof architectural decisions in Example: organizations Physical (deployment) view:servers, nodes, ▪ Identifying the system’s major componentsand interfaces network. ▪ Evaluatingand validating the architecture 2. Architectural Styles ▪ Establishing policies for ensuring architectural design Definition:A general template/approachfor synchronicity. organizing system structure. ▪ Extra: synchronicity means It means making sure all parts Purpose:Provides a high-level solution shape. of the system follow the same design rulesso everything Example: Distributed System. fits together. 3. Architectural Patterns ▪ Example: If the rule is “use one database system (MySQL)”, Definition:Reusable solutionsto recurring and then all teams must use MySQL, not mix MySQL in one repeated architectural problems (more specific than module and MongoDB in another. styles). Purpose:Guide detailed design decisions inside the style. Examples: 17 Client –Server, Filters and pipes
Key Tasks in Architectural Design

A stakeholder is any person, group or organisation with a direct or indirect stake in the system: systems, software and hardware engineers, project management, customers, testers, QA and configuration management, among others. A stakeholder’s concern is high-level information about a characteristic they want the system to have (“it must never lose a payment”, “it must be easy to learn”). The architect must make sure the design addresses the concerns of all stakeholders. Concerns are the driving force behind architectural decisions : the components and styles are chosen to satisfy them. The slide marks this as important. Key Tasks in Architectural Design Identifying stakeholders concerns ⮚ Stakeholders are persons, groups, or organizations that have a director indirect ✔ stake or interest in the system. − They include systems engineers, software engineers, hardware engineers, project management, customers, testing teams, quality assurance teams, members of the configurationmanagement team,etc. A stakeholder’s concernprovides high-level information about desired ✔ characteristicsof the software system. • The software architect must ensure that the software to be developed addresses the concerns of all stakeholders.”it considers the needs and interests of everyone involved.” − Stakeholders’ concerns serve as driving force behind architectural decisions (important) Extra: 18
Key Tasks in Architectural Design

The architect must find out how each group of stakeholders influences the system, and those concerns must be elicited before any design begins . Designing first and asking later produces the wrong system. University app example: students want to see schedules and grades easily, professors need to upload grades and message students, administrators need to manage courses and records. Their concerns differ in kind, not just in features: students care about a user-friendly interface (usability), administrators about security and data management. Each concern points the architecture in a different direction. Key Tasks in Architectural Design Identifying stakeholders concerns (cont.) ⮚ The software architect must identify and understand the different ways ✔ stakeholders influence the system. − These need to be elicited before any design effort can begin. • Extra: Imagine you're designing a new mobile app for a university. The stakeholders include students, professors, and administrators. • Studentswant an easy way to view their schedules and grades. • Professorsneed a tool to upload grades and communicate with students. • Administratorsrequire features to manage courses and student records. • Before you start designing the app, you need to talk to each group to understand their specific needs and concerns. • For example: Students might want a user-friendly interface, while Administrators are more concerned with security and data management. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and 19 slides
Key Tasks in Architectural Design

Quality attributes stakeholders worry about, read as “the degree of complexity involved” or “the system’s ability”. Usability : how hard it is to learn or use. Modifiability : how hard it is to change. Security : protecting information. Performance : useful work under time and resource limits. Reliability : the failure rate. High synchronicity is the goal, but it is easy to deviate from the design, especially in multi-year projects where people, priorities and deadlines change. n: Slide 1

Week 3, second lecture. Lecture 1 listed what an architect does; this one gives the order in which it is done, and then studies the first step, understanding the requirements, in detail. Software Design and Architecture [Software Architecture] – Week 03, L02
Lecture Outlines

Part 1 is the five-step architecture process (slide 3). Part 2 is requirements engineering , the discipline behind step 1, with its four activities: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation. Lecture Outlines ➢Software Architecture Process ✓ Understand and Evaluate Requirements ✓ Design the Architecture ✓ Evaluate the Architecture ✓ Document the Architecture ✓ Monitor and control implementation ➢ Requirements Engineering ✓ Elicitation ✓ Analysis ✓ Specification ✓ Validation ➢ What’s next..
Software Architecture Process

Understand and evaluate requirements : find the architectural drivers, meaning the requirements, quality attributes and constraints that will shape the structure. Design the architecture : define the major structures (components, connectors) and the design decisions behind them. Evaluate the architecture : check whether it satisfies the important requirements and stakeholder concerns before building on it. Document the architecture : communicate the structures and decisions to everyone who needs them (chapter 9). Monitor and control implementation : check that the code stays consistent with the architecture. This is design synchronicity from Lecture 1, and it is why architecture work doesn’t end when coding starts. Match each architecture process activity with its main purpose: understand and evaluate requirements; design architecture; document architecture; evaluate architecture; monitor and control implementation. Fill in the blank: After designing an architecture, the activity used to determine whether it satisfies important requirements and stakeholder concerns is architecture ___. Software Architecture Process ➢On a larger scale, the process for creating software architectures can be executed using the following tasks: ✓ Understand and evaluate requirements ✓ Design the architecture ✓ Evaluate the architecture ✓ Document the architecture ✓ Monitor and control implementation
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

Requirements engineering is the part of software engineering concerned with a systematic approach to requirements: getting them, understanding them and writing them down properly. It has four activities, explained on the next slides: elicitation (discover), analysis (clean up), specification (document) and validation (confirm). Architects spend a lot of time here. Even after requirements are specified they keep going back and forth between requirements and design, because designing exposes gaps and conflicts. On some projects they are completely immersed in the requirements phase and help write the specification. List the four activities of requirements engineering in order. Understand and Evaluate Requirements ➢ Requirements engineering ✓ The discipline within software engineering that is concerned with the systematic approach to requirements specification, mainly through the following activities: − Elicitation − Analysis − Specification − Validation ➢Software architects spend a great deal of time working with software requirements. ✓ Even after requirements are specified, software architects find themselves going back and forth between requirements and design. ✓ In some cases, architects are completely immersed(Deep and involved) in the requirements phase, playing a keyrole in the specification of requirements.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Elicitation)

Elicitation is the discovery activity: identify the stakeholders, uncover what the customer needs and wants, and determine the non-functional requirements (which customers rarely state unprompted). It starts by listing every source of information that can produce requirements, before collecting a single requirement. Sources may have similar but different visions of the system: two departments can describe “the same” workflow differently. Spotting that early prevents conflicts later. Common sources: stakeholders ; goals (the business objectives the system serves); domain knowledge (how banking, medicine or education works); and the operational and organisational environment (existing systems, policies, hardware the new system must live with). Fill in the blank: The requirements activity in which stakeholder needs are discovered using techniques such as interviews and observation is called ___. Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Elicitation) ➢ Elicitation ✓ Activity that deals with identifying stakeholders, uncovering what the customer needs and wants, and with determining the non-functional requirements. ✓ Begins by identifying all sources of information that can be used to generate requirements. ✓ Different sources can have similar but different visions for the system. ▪ Common sources of requirementsinclude: – Stakeholders – Goals – Domainknowledge – Operational and organizationalenvironment
Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Elicitation)

Interviews : ask stakeholders directly, one at a time or in small groups. Good for detail; limited by what people remember to say. Facilitated meetings (workshops): bring stakeholder groups together with a facilitator so conflicting views surface and get discussed in one place. Observation : watch users do their current work. It reveals steps and workarounds that people never mention in interviews because they take them for granted. Scenarios : walk through concrete stories of use (“a student registers for a full course…”) to discover what the system must do and how it should respond. An architect interviews end users, observes their current work, and runs a facilitated workshop to discover system needs. Which requirements activity is being performed? Negotiation Architecture documentation Elicitation Classification Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Elicitation) ➢ Common Elicitation Techniques ✓ Interviews ✓ Facilitatedmeetings ✓ Observation ✓ Scenarios
Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis)

Analysis takes requirements in their raw form and fixes the ones that are contradictory, incomplete, vague or simply wrong . Contradiction example: one requirement says the system runs 24/7, another needs daily maintenance downtime. Both can’t be true as written, so someone must decide. Analysis lets architects clear the air about what really needs to be done before they invest in detailed designs. Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis) ➢Analysis ✓Requirements are analyzed in their raw form to address and solve issues such as requirements that are contradicting, incomplete, vague, or just wrong. ✓Extra: For example, if one requirement states the system must operate 24/7, but another says it needs daily maintenance downtime, these are contradictory and need to be resolved. ✓Allows architects to clear the air in regard to what needs to be done before devising more detailed designs. ✓The following tasks can be performed during analysis: −Requirement classification −Requirement prioritization −Requirement negotiation −Conceptual modeling
Extra: Banking App requirements analysis

R1 Secure login is vague : “secure” could mean a password, two-factor authentication or a fingerprint. Resolution: clarify the exact login method with the stakeholders. R2 Fast & seamless experience may conflict with R1, since strong security slows things down. Resolution: a design that balances the two (efficient encryption, smart caching). R3 Multiple payment methods is incomplete : which methods (card, PayPal, crypto)? Resolution: define them explicitly. R4 24/7 availability contradicts the need for maintenance downtime. Resolution: rolling updates or redundant servers, so updates happen without the service going down. Each row is one of slide 7’s problem types. For each banking-app requirement, name the problem analysis would find: (a) “secure login”, (b) “multiple payment methods”, (c) “24/7 availability” alongside planned maintenance downtime.
