Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis)

Classification identifies the nature of each requirement, along three independent axes. Functional vs. non-functional : functional says what the system does (“users can log in”); non-functional says how well it behaves (“the page loads within 2 seconds”). Imposed vs. derived : an imposed requirement comes straight from stakeholders (“the app runs on iOS and Android”); a derived one is worked out by the team to meet a higher goal (“to support both platforms, use Flutter”). Classify “The app must be developed using the Agile methodology” on the product/process axis, and “To support both platforms we will use Flutter” on the imposed/derived axis. “The system must load within 2 seconds” is a: Non-functional requirement Functional requirement Process requirement Derived requirement Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis) ➢Requirement classification Extra: ✓Performed for identifying the nature of each 1. Functional vs. Non-Functional requirement • Functional → What the system does. −Functional vs. non-functional Example: “The system must allow users to log in”. • Non-Functional → How the system behaves. −Product vs. process Example: “The system must load within 2 seconds.” −Imposed vs. Derived 2. Product vs. Process • Product requirement → what the delivered software must have or do. Example: “The app must support online payments.” • Process requirement the way of developing that product (the steps, methods, or standards used). Example: “The app must be developed using Agile methodology.” 3. Imposed vs. Derived • Imposed → Given directly by stakeholders. Example: “The app must run on iOS and Android.” • Derived → Identified by the development team to meet higher goals. Example: “To support both platforms, the app should use Flutter framework.”
Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis)

Done well, it refines the schedule by deciding which requirements are handled first : payment and security early, less urgent features later. It also defines the builds (releases): Release 1 has the core features, Release 2 adds the chatbot and extras. Two stakeholder groups request requirements that cannot both be fully satisfied. Which activity is most directly used to resolve this conflict? Requirements classification Code inspection Requirements negotiation Requirements elicitation Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis) ➢ Requirement prioritization and negotiation ✓ Helps identify the most important functions of the softwaresystem. ✓ When done properly, it can help refine the projected schedule by determining which requirements need to be processedfirst. ✓ Can be used to determine different builds of thesoftware ✓ Can help during negotiation when conflicts between requirements are identified. Extra: 1. Identify key functions → e.g., login security is more important than adding a theme color. 2. Refine schedule → do critical features first (payment, security) → less urgent features later. 3. Plan builds/versions → Release 1: core features, Release 2: chatbot + extras. 4. Support negotiation → if conflict → focus on security now, move chatbot to future update.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis)

Boundaries decide what is inside and outside the system. Online banking: login, balance and transfers are inside ; ATM hardware and cash withdrawal are outside . Getting this wrong means designing (or forgetting) whole subsystems. This is often where architectural design begins , because building a good conceptual model already requires decomposing the system into parts. The slide marks this as important. Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Analysis) ➢ Conceptualmodeling ✓ Conceptual models are created to further identify the requirements by understanding their context, discovering the bounds of the software system, and conceptualizing how the system interacts with itsenvironment. ✓ In many projects, this is where architectural design begins, sincesystem decomposition is essential to developing effective conceptualmodels.(important) ➢Extra: Conceptual Modeling ➢Purpose: Understand requirements, system context, and boundaries. ➢Boundaries: Decide what the system will include and exclude. ✓ Inside:login, account balance, money transfer. ✓ Outside:ATM hardware, cash withdrawal. ➢Shows: How the system interacts with users and its environment. ➢Example: Online banking system → users log in, check balance, transfer money (but ATMs are not part of this system).
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

Validation : stakeholders review the documented requirements to confirm they are accurate, complete and feasible, i.e. that they really represent their needs. Each requirement must have six characteristics: specific, correct, complete, consistent, attainable, verifiable . Slides 13–18 take them one at a time. Fill in the blank: Checking whether documented requirements correctly represent stakeholder needs is called requirements ___. List the six characteristics a well-specified requirement should have. Understand and Evaluate Requirements (Specification & validation) ➢ Specification and validation ✓ Activity where the results of elicitation an analysis are formally captured and documented in an appropriate format for the use and review of all stakeholders. Extra: Stakeholders review the classified requirements to ensure accuracy, completeness, and feasibility. ✓ When specifying requirements, it is important that each requirement exhibit certain characteristics desired for designing successful systems. Requirements mustbe: Specific Consistent Correct Attainable= ”Achievable”, Possible” Complete Verifiable
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

Specific has three parts: the requirement is clear, concise and exclusive. Clear : not open to interpretation. Ambiguity leads to wrong designs, wrong code, and deceptive validation : a test can “pass” against one reading of the requirement while the stakeholder meant another. Exclusive : each requirement states one and only one thing, which makes it easy to verify; a requirement that bundles two things can be half met. Understand and Evaluate Requirements ➢ On being specific, ✓ Requirements need to be specified in a clear, concise” short and brief,” and exclusivemanner. ✓ Clearrequirements are not open to interpretation; unclear or ambiguous requirements lead to incorrect designs, incorrect implementations, and deceptive validation duringtest. ✓ Conciserequirements are briefand to the point and are therefore easier to understand. ✓ Exclusiverequirements specify one, and only one thing, making them easier to verify. Example of specific and nonspecificrequirements:
Extra: Specific vs. non-specific requirements

Specific examples: searching by product ID , authenticating with user ID and password , acknowledging within ½ second . Each says exactly what, how, or how much. “The software shall be secure” is not specific: security covers encryption, authentication, access control… which one is required? “Secure and fast” fails twice: two vague qualities in one sentence (not exclusive), with no measurable meaning for either. Rewrite “The software shall be secure and fast” as specific requirements. ➢Extra: Specific Requirements Non-Specific Requirements: 1. “The software shall search for a product using the product ID.” ✓ Specific: Yes, because it clearly states what needs to be searched (product) and how (using product ID). 2. “The software shall authenticate users with user ID and password.” ✓ Specific: Yes, as it specifies the authentication mechanism (user ID and password). 3. “Server acknowledgment message shall be sent within 1/2 second from the time a request is received.” ✓ Specific: Yes, it provides a measurable performance requirement (response time within 1/2 second). 4. “The software shall search the database.” ✓ specific: No,Thisis vague because it doesn’t specify what to search for in the database. It lacks context and detail about the search criteria or the expected outcome. 5. “The software shall be secure.” ✓ specific: No, Security is a broad concept. This requirement doesn’t specify what aspects of security are important, such as whether it refers to data encryption, secure user authentication, or another security measure. 6. “The software shall be secure and fast.” ✓ specific: No, This requirement combines two qualitative attributes—security and speed—without detailing what "secure" or "fast" means in measurable terms.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

A requirement is correct when it accurately describes a function the stakeholders actually want. A wrong requirement, implemented perfectly, still gives wrong or undesired behaviour. The cartoon is an incorrect requirement in action. The specification said each user ID + password combination must be unique , so registering as user123/pwd123 is rejected with “you must use a unique combination”. But that error tells the new user that someone else already has exactly that username and password: the system has just given away another person’s login. The code did what the requirement said; the requirement was wrong. (Usernames should be unique; passwords should never be compared across users.) Explain why “each username and password combination must be unique” is an incorrect requirement. Understand and Evaluate Requirements ➢ On beingcorrect, ✓ Requirements need to be correct in the sense that they must accurately describe a desired system function. ✓ Incorrect requirements can lead to incorrect or undesired behavior. ➢The diagram you're describing seems to illustrate a sequence of interactions around user registration and login for a software system, highlighting an error handling scenario where a username and password combination is not unique. Here’s a detailed breakdown based on the described elements: Extra: Scenario Overview: 1. Attempt to Register: A user tries to register with a username and password via a registration form. 2. Error Display: The system checks if the username and password combination is unique. Since the combination is already taken, the system generates an error message stating, "Error! You must use a unique combinationof user ID and password!" 3. User's Reaction: This prompts the user to either choose a different username or password to ensure uniqueness.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

Complete applies at two levels. Individually, each requirement is specified thoroughly enough to describe fully the function it asks for. Collectively, the whole set in the SRS (software requirements specification) must cover all the required functionality: nothing missing, everything specified. A perfect login requirement doesn’t make the SRS complete if account recovery was never written down. Understand and Evaluate Requirements ➢On being complete, ✓ Requirements must be complete both individuallyand as collectiveset. − This means that each requirement should be specifiedthoroughly so that it absolutely describesthe functions required to meet some need. − Collectively, requirements need to provide complete specification of the software’s required functionality in the software requirements specification (SRS). ❑ Extra: ▪ Individually → each requirement should be fully detailed and clear. ▪ Collectively → together, they should describe the entire functionality in the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). In short: Complete requirements = nothing missing, everything specified. ✓ Incomplete requirements lead to incomplete designs, which in turn leads to incomplete construction of the software system.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements: consistent and attainable

Attainable : unattainable requirements serve no purpose. A requirement is attainable if it can realistically be achieved within the project’s constraints of time, technology, budget and resources, and this applies to both product and process requirements. Understand and Evaluate Requirements ➢ On beingconsistent, Extra: ✓ Requirements are consistent when they Consistent do not preclude “prevent” the design or construction of other requirements. •No conflicts between requirements. • Example: “System must support online payments” ➢ On beingattainable, & “System must support credit card payments” (work ✓ Requirements that are unattainable together). serve nopurpose. • Conflict: “System must be offline only” & “System ✓ Attainability can be determined for both must support online payments.” product andprocess. Attainable ✓ Requirements are attainable if they •Realistic within time, budget, technology, resources. can realistically be achieved within • Example: “App must handle 1,000 users at once.” the project constraints, which • Not attainable: “App must handle 1 billion users include time, technology, budget, on a $500 budget.” and resources. Tip: Good requirements = clear, non-conflicting, and realistic.
Understand and Evaluate Requirements

A requirement that can’t be verified can’t be claimed as met, and being unable to verify a requirement points to a serious flaw early in development: nobody knows what “done” means. “The system shall maximise speed” is not verifiable (maximise compared with what?). “The system’s data rate shall be at least 1 Mbps” is. Rule of thumb: use numbers, limits or conditions. The requirement “The system should respond quickly” is sufficiently specific and verifiable for architectural evaluation. Understand and Evaluate Requirements Extra: A requirement is verifiable if there is a suitable way to measure or test it to confirm that the requirement has been met. This could be through tests, demonstrations •Extra: ➢ On being verifiable, ➢ Verifiable Requirements ✓ Perhaps the most obvious desirable ➢Good requirement= measurable, testable, characteristic of requirements. clear. ✓ Requirements that cannot be verified cannot be claimed as met. ➢Bad requirement = vague, not testable. ✓ Inability to verify requirements ➢Examples: point to a serious flaw early on in ➢ Not verifiable:“The system shall the developmentprocess maximize speed.” ➢ Verifiable:“The system’s data rate shall be at least 1 Mbps.” ➢ Tip:Always make requirements measurable → use numbers, limits, or conditions.
Summary

This lecture gave the basics of requirements engineering, enough to write good requirements: elicit, analyse, specify and validate, then check each requirement against the six characteristics. Next: designing the architecture with the 4+1 view model : logical, development, process and physical views, plus the user (scenario) view that ties them together. Summary ➢In this session, we presented fundamentals concepts of requirements engineering, and provided enough information to successfully create good requirements. ➢ In the next session, we’ll discuss how to design the software architecture using the popular 4+1 View Model, which includes: ✓ Logical view ✓ Development View ✓ Process View ✓ Physical View ✓ User View

decks.t: Designing the Architecture with the 4+1 View Model
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 2 · Lecture 3: Designing the Architecture with the 4+1 View Model
n: Slide 1

Third architecture lecture. Lecture 1 said an architecture needs several views; this one names the standard set of views and shows each on one example system, an ATM. Software Design and Architecture [Software Architecture] – Chapter 02, L03
Lecture Outlines

The “+1” is the user view, also called the scenario view. It is not a fifth independent description but the use cases that connect and check the other four. Lecture Outlines ➢Designing the Architecture with the 4+1view model ✓The logical view ✓The process view ✓The development view ✓The physical view ✓Plus … The user view Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Designing the Architecture

No single view can present every aspect of a system. A class diagram says nothing about servers; a deployment diagram says nothing about classes. Each view is a partial representation aimed at specific stakeholders (users, analysts, developers…), so every group gets the view that answers its own concerns. The best-known way to organise those views is the 4+1 view model . Why are multiple architectural views required in complex systems? To reduce documentation effort Because no single view can represent all system aspects for all stakeholders To replace requirements engineering To simplify coding Designing the Architecture ➢When designing the architecture of a software system, there is no single view that can present all system aspects ➢Instead, software designers can organize the description of their architectural decisions using a collection of different views (why?) ➢Specific views can provide partial representation of the software architecture to a specific stakeholder (e.g. system users, analysts, developers, etc.) Extra: • In software architecture, multiple views are used because no single view can capture all aspects of a complex system. • This approach helps manage complexity by breaking the system into understandable perspectives. • It ensures that different stakeholders’ concerns (e.g., developers, users, managers) are addressed. • This makes it easier to develop, analyze, and maintain the software effectively. • Each view targets a different area (e.g., functional, structural, behavioral). A popular model is usually used for designing different architectural views is the 4+1 view model Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
The 4+1 View Model

It has four essential views : logical, process, physical and development. Each one has its own stakeholders, concerns and diagrams. To keep the four consistent with one another, the user’s perspective is captured in use cases that form the user view. Running a use case through every view checks that they all describe the same system. Who introduced the 4+1 view model, and what is the role of the “+1” view? The 4+1 View Model ➢The 4+1 view model was originally introduced by Philippe Kruchten in 1995. ➢The model provides four essential views: the logical view, the process view, the physical view, and the development view. ➢To ensure consistency among all 4 views, the user’s perspective is captured through several use cases, as part of the user view Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
The logical View

It is an abstraction of the functional requirements : it shows what the system does, in terms of the things it is made of. Diagrams: static ones (class and object diagrams) for structure, and dynamic ones (interaction overview, sequence, communication, state and activity diagrams) for how those objects behave together. Fill in the blank: The 4+1 view that emphasizes the major functional elements of the system and their relationships is the ___ view. The logical View ➢The logical view specifies system decomposition into conceptual entities (such as objects or classes) and the connection between these entities ➢The view basically is an abstraction of the system's functional requirements ➢The logical view is usually modeled using: −Static diagrams such as: class/object diagram −Dynamic diagrams such as: interaction overall diagram, sequence diagram, communication diagram, state diagram, and activity diagram ➢The usual stakeholders of the logical view are the end-users, analysts, and designers. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
ATM Example Logical View

A class diagram shows the classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them. For the ATM: Bank, ATM Info, Customer, Debit Card, Account and ATM Transaction, each box listing attributes ( +code , +address ) and operations ( +manages() ). Directionality : the arrow from ATM Transaction to Account (“Modifies”) means the transaction acts on the account, and not the other way round. A bidirectional association has two arrowheads or none. Inheritance : the lines ending in a hollow triangle point from subclass to superclass. Current Account and Saving Account are kinds of Account; Withdrawal, Query, Transfer and PIN-validation transactions are kinds of ATM Transaction. Association names describe the relationship in words: Bank Maintains ATM Info, Customer Owns Account, Debit Card Provides Access to Account. Multiplicities give how many objects take part: 1 means exactly one, 1..* one or more. One Bank maintains one or more ATMs. In the ATM class diagram, what do the hollow triangles from Current Account and Saving Account to Account mean, and how is “1..*” read? *ATM Example – Logical View (Class Diagram) Class diagrams : show the classes of the system, their inter-relationships, and the operations and attributes of the classes. •Extra: •Directionality: The arrow points from ATM Transaction to Account, showing that the action originates with the ATM Transaction. •Impact: The ATM Transaction directly affects the Account, unlike a bidirectional association where both classes might equally influence each other. In UML diagrams, bidirectional associations can havetwo arrows”Bidirectional Relationship” orno arrows: Arrow from Subclass to Superclass: •These are inheritance relationships shown with a line ending in a triangular arrowhead, pointing from the subclass to the superclass. They indicate that the subclass is a specialized form of the superclass. For example: • Account (superclass) to Current Account and Saving Account (subclasses). Names above arrows (e.g., Maintains, Modifies, Provides Access to) describe the nature of the relationship from one class to another. For example: •"Maintains" on the arrow from Bank to ATM Info implies that each Bank maintains one or more ATMs. Multiplicities (the numbers near the lines) indicate the number of instances of one class that can be associated with another class. For example, "1..*" means "one to many" and "1" means "exactly one. 6
ATM Example Logical View

The communication (collaboration) diagram shows the objects that cooperate in one scenario (Bank Client, ATM Machine, Account, Checking Account) as boxes joined by links. Messages are written along the links with a number that gives their order. Reading the withdrawal scenario: 1–4 The ATM asks for the transaction kind and amount; the client enters them. 5–8 The ATM asks Account to process the transaction; Account withdraws from the Checking Account and reports success. 9–14 The ATM dispenses cash, the client takes it, the ATM asks whether to continue, the session ends and a receipt is printed. It focuses on who talks to whom . The same messages appear on the next slide as a sequence diagram, which focuses on when . How does a communication (collaboration) diagram differ from a sequence diagram? *ATM Example – Logical View (Collaboration Diagram) Extra: Explanation of the previous communication Diagram • Bank Client: Represents the user of the ATM. • ATM Machine: Handles transactions and connects client with accounts. • Account: General representation of a bank account. • Checking Account: a specialized account object participating in the ATM transaction scenario Bank Client inserts card. 1. ATM Machine requests PIN. 2. Bank Client enters PIN. 3. ATM Machine requests the amount to be withdrawn or deposited. 4. Bank Client enters the amount. 5. ATM Machine Process transaction with Account/Checking Account. 6. ATM Machine requests to take cash (for withdrawals). 7. Withdraw successfully: The banking system confirmed your money is deducted. 8. Validates transaction(Successful) 9. Dispense cash: The ATM machine hardware actually pushes the cash out. 10.Request take cash 11.Take cash: You physically grab it. 12.Requests continuation 13.Terminates session 14.print receipt Collaboration diagram: is more focused on showing the communication between main entities 7
* ATM Example Logical View

How to read it: Boxes along the top The participants: C : customer , A : ATM , Accnt : Account , and later CKA : Checking Account (object name : class). Dashed vertical lines Lifelines. Time runs downward. Thin rectangles Activations: the period when that object is busy handling a message. Numbered arrows Messages in order: 1 insert card, 2 request PIN, 3 PIN entered, 4 verify PIN, 5 PIN OK … 11 withdraw from checking, 13 transaction successful, 14 dispense cash … 19 print receipt. The class diagram (slide 6) gives the structure ; the sequence diagram gives the behaviour over time for one use case, making clear who does what and in which order. Which logical-view diagram should you use to show the time order of the messages exchanged during an ATM withdrawal? Sequence diagram Class diagram Deployment diagram Package diagram *ATM Example – Logical View (Sequence Diagram) Sequence diagram: used to model interactions between design units together with the messages exchanges and the time-order of the messages Extra: •Class Diagram (Structure) → shows the structure of the system (objects and relationships). •Sequence Diagram (Behavior)→ shows the behavior over time (order of interactions) So it: ✓ Show the order of interactions between objects. ✓ Explain system behavior step by step. ✓ Clarify who does what in a use case. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8 * Example taken from: http://www.programsformca.com/2012/03/uml-diagrams-library-mgmt-system.html
The Process View

It contributes to non-functional requirements such as scalability and performance , which depend on how work is spread across processes. Stakeholders: developers and integrators , who put the running pieces together. Which architectural view mainly contributes to evaluating scalability and performance? Logical view Development view Process view User view Which 4+1 view should an architect emphasize when analyzing concurrent execution, communication among running processes, and synchronization? Development view Scenario view Logical view Process view The Process View ➢The process view focuses on the dynamic aspects of the system, i.e., its execution time behavior. ➢This view is an abstraction of processes or threads Extra: •Concurrency: Looks at how tasks that run at the same time ➢Shows process synchronization and concurrency. interact and coordinate. •Synchronization: Manages how processes or tasks share ➢It presents how all execution units are organized at run-time resources or data without interfering with each other. ➢It contributes to non-functional requirements and quality attributes such as scalability and performance requirements. ➢The UML activity diagram and interaction overview diagram support this view. ➢The stakeholders of this view are usually the developers and integrators Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
ATM Example Process View

An activity diagram describes the flow of the system: its operations and processes, in order, with decisions and parallel paths. Reading the ATM diagram (three swimlanes: customer, ATM machine, bank): Filled circle Start. The customer inserts the card and the ATM validates it. Diamonds Decisions: an invalid card is ejected; the PIN is authorised (valid/invalid); the balance is checked against the amount. Thick bars Fork and join: “take money from slot” and “debit account” happen in parallel, then join. This parallelism is exactly what the process view is about. Circle with ring End, after the balance is shown and the card is ejected and taken. *ATM Example – Process View (Activity Diagram) Activity diagram: helps to describe the flow the system, and explore operations and processes Note: click on the diagram to view an online larger size diagram Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10 * Example taken from: http://www.programsformca.com/2012/03/uml-diagrams-library-mgmt-system.html
The development View

It lets you analyse how logical components map onto physical files and directories , which matters for builds, reuse and team ownership. Fill in the blank: The 4+1 view that focuses on the organization of source-code modules, packages, and development units is the ___ view. The development View ➢The development view describes the software static organization of the system modules. (from implementation point of view) ➢Modules such as class library, sub-system, or packages (building blocks that group classes) ➢UML diagrams such as package diagrams and component diagrams are often used to support this view. ➢This view can be used to analyze the system from the perspective of how logical components map to physical files and directories. ➢The stakeholders of this view can be programmers and software project manager Extra: The development View means how source code is organized into modules, packages, subsystems, and libraries. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
ATM Example Development View

Reading the banking system: Rectangles with two small tabs Components: ATM Machine, Customer Console, Card Reader, Bank Database, Web Page, Client Desktop, Employee Console. Dashed arrows into Bank Database Dependencies: the ATM, card reader, web page and client desktop all depend on the database. Small circles (lollipops) Provided interfaces, e.g. ATM Transaction, Account Information, Online Transaction, Web Merchant Transaction. Reading tip: a circle attached to a component is an interface it provides . In the development view these components are units of code that teams build and package separately. *ATM Example – Development View (Component Diagram) Component diagram: shows components of a system and required interfaces, ports, and relationships between them Full banking system Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12 * Example taken from: http://www.programsformca.com/2012/03/uml-diagrams-library-mgmt-system.html
The Physical View

It is the right view to evaluate availability (redundant nodes), performance and scalability (processor speed, bandwidth) and security (firewalls), because all of these depend on the hardware layout. A deployment engineer wants to know which software elements run on which servers and hardware nodes. Which 4+1 view is most useful? Process view Development view Logical view Physical view The Physical View ➢ The physical view represents the deployment aspects of software systems (from configuration and installation point of view) ➢ The physical view can be modeled in UML using: ✓ Deployment diagrams ➢ The physical view is appropriate to evaluate the system’s: ✓ Availability: for example, specifying the need for redundant nodes to increase the system’s availability ✓ Performance and scalability: for example, required processor speed, bandwidth, etc. to meet performance requirements. ✓ Security: for example, required firewalls ➢ The stakeholders of this view are system installers, system administrators, and system engineers Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
ATM Example Physical View

The 3-D boxes are nodes (hardware or execution environments): ATM_Machine, Customer Console, Card_Reader, Bank_Database, Web_Page, Client_Desktop, Employee_Console. The lines are communication paths. Most nodes connect to Bank_Database, so it is the node whose failure takes everything down, which is where you would add redundancy for availability. *ATM Example – Physical View (Deployment Diagram) Deployment diagram: A diagram used to model the physical structure of a software system Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14 * Example taken from: http://www.programsformca.com/2012/03/uml-diagrams-library-mgmt-system.html
The User View (or Scenario view)

It provides the foundation for the other four views and lets them work together logically: every view has to support the same use cases. It is used twice: to discover architectural elements during design (what does this scenario need?) and to validate the design afterwards (walk the scenario through each view). The “+1” view represents the database structure of the system. The User View (or Scenario view) ➢The scenario view describes the functionality of the system, i.e., how user will use the system and how the system provides services to the users. ➢This view provides a foundation for other 4 views and allow them to work together seamlessly and logically. ➢ It helps designers discover architectural elements during design and helps to validate the architectural design afterward. ➢So, the scenario view helps to make the software architecture consistent and validated against functional and non-functional requirements. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
ATM Example User View

The stick figure is the actor, Bank Client . The ovals are use cases: Bank ATM Transaction, Checking Tran, Saving Transaction History, Deposit Amount, Withdrawal Amount, Approval process, Invalid pin. «uses» (include): Bank ATM Transaction always uses the Approval process. «extends» : optional or special-case behaviour added to a base use case, e.g. Deposit and Withdrawal extend the transaction, and Invalid pin extends the approval process. *ATM Example – User View (Use case diagram) Use case diagram: Behavioral diagram used to capture, specify, and visualize required system behavior Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 16 * Example taken from: http://www.programsformca.com/2012/03/uml-diagrams-library-mgmt-system.html
Extra: The 4+1 views at a glance

Extra: In the 4+1 View Model 1. Logical View (what the system should do) 3. Considers row. Logical: functional requirements. Process: non-functional requirements. Development: software module organisation (reuse, tool constraints). Physical: non-functional requirements tied to the hardware. Scenario: system consistency and validity. decks.t: Quality Attributes: Scenarios, Tactics and Design Decisions
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 3 · Lecture 1: Quality Attributes: Scenarios, Tactics and Design Decisions
n: Slide 1

Chapter 3 is about quality attributes , the non-functional requirements that architecture exists to satisfy. Lecture 1 gives the tools (scenarios, tactics, design decisions); Lecture 2 applies them to six major qualities. Software Design and Architecture [Quality Attributes] – Chapter 03, L01
Lecture Outlines

First, how functional and quality requirements relate to architecture. Then how qualities are specified precisely (scenarios) and achieved (tactics). The six major quality attributes themselves come in Lecture 2. Lecture Outlines ➢Architecture and Requirements ➢Quality Attribute Considerations ➢Quality Design Decisions ➢Major Quality Attributes Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Architecture and Requirements

Non-functional requirements , also called quality attributes (QA) , are criteria for judging how the system operates as a whole , not a specific behaviour: speed, reliability, security… The plan for implementing them is detailed in the architecture . That split (functions → detailed design, qualities → architecture) is the reason architecture spends so much effort on quality. Software architecture is concerned only with functional structure and does not need to consider non-functional requirements. Architecture and Requirements ➢System requirements can be categorized as: ✓Functional requirements: −State what the system must do, usually in the form of “system shall do <requirements>”. −Functional requirements define specific behavior or function −The plan for implementing functional requirements is produced in the system detailed design. ✓Non-functional requirements or Quality attributes (QA)): −Specify criteria that can be used to judge the operation of the system as a whole rather than specific behavior −The plan for implementing non-functional requirements is detailed in the system architecture Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Architecture and Requirements

Quality has to be considered in every phase : design, implementation and deployment. A fast architecture can still be ruined by slow code or a badly configured server. Architecture cannot achieve qualities on its own . It provides the foundation , but the foundation is useless if the details in later phases are ignored (the same point as Chapter 2: architecture alone cannot guarantee quality). Architecture and Requirements ➢ Achieving quality attributes must be considered throughout design, implementation, and deployment. ➢Architecture, by itself, is unable to achieve qualities. It provides the foundation for achieving quality, but this foundation will be to no use if attention is not paid to the details in later phases of software development. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Architecture and Requirements

Each has their own opinion about which quality matters most, so the architect has to weigh them against each other. The development team cares about maintainability (easy to change) more than the customer does; the QA team cares about testability . The end user (the slide’s question) mostly cares about qualities they can feel: usability, performance and availability. Which quality attribute is the QA (testing) team most likely to prioritise, and which the development team? Architecture and Requirements ➢Architectural documents are used by a variety of system stakeholders: ✓E.g. Developers, managers, sales, testers, support, maintenance, and customers ➢Each stakeholder will have their own opinion about what non-functional requirement matters the most: ✓e.g. The development team will care about maintainability more than the customer ✓e.g. Quality assurance team will be more interested in the testability of the application ✓What will the end user be interested in??? Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Quality Attribute Considerations

Take one functional requirement: “when the user presses the green button, the Options dialog appears”. The function is the same in every case below; only the quality constraint changes. For the requirement “when the user presses the green button the Options dialog appears”, write one performance and one usability quality requirement. Quality Attribute Considerations ➢Quality attributes are constraints on the manner in which the system implements and delivers its functionality (how the system achieves its functionality). ➢Extra: Quality attributes are used as criteria for evaluating the performance and effectiveness of the system during and after development. ✓i.e. Efficiency, availability, scalability, adaptability, security, dependability, etc. … ➢Example: assume the following functional requirement “when the user presses the green button the Options dialog appears”: ✓A performance QA might describe how quickly the dialog will appear ✓An availability QA might describe how often this function will fail ✓A usability QA might describe how easy it is to learn this function. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
Quality Attribute Considerations Scenarios

Quality attribute words have unstable definitions and overlapping concerns : people mean different things by “reliable” or “secure”. The DoS example shows the overlap: a denial-of-service attack makes the system down (availability), very slow (performance), is an attack (security) and stops users reaching the service (usability). Which quality does it “belong” to? Real example: if the payment server crashes during a transaction (stimulus), the system switches to a backup within 2 seconds (response), keeping 99.99% uptime (measure). That is clear, testable and no longer overlaps with other qualities. Quality Attribute Considerations – Scenarios ➢ Quality attributes can have unstable definition or an overlapping concerns, Example: Is a system failure due to a denial of service attack an aspect of availability, performance, security, or usability? ➢ Extra: A Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack: ✓ Availability → system is down. ✓ Performance → system becomes very slow. ✓ Security → the attack is a security breach. ✓ Usability → users can’t access the service. ➢ Here, the same problem “overlaps” multiple attributes. ➢ A solution for this is (unstable definitions and overlapping concerns) is to use quality attribute scenarios as a means of characterizing quality attributes. Extra: Solution: Quality Attribute Scenarios • Instead of vague terms, define concrete scenarios that describe: ▪ Stimulus (what happens), ▪ Response (what the system should do), ▪ Measure (how success is judged). Real Example • Attribute: Availability ▪ Scenario: If the payment server crashes during a transaction (stimulus), ▪ The system should automatically switch to a backup server within 2 seconds (response), ▪ With 99.99% uptime guaranteed (measure). • This way, the attribute is clear, testable, and not overlapping. 7
A quality attribute scenario has the

Source of stimulus : the entity that generates it: a human, another computer system, an internal component. Environment : the conditions the system is in when the stimulus occurs: normal operation, overload, start-up, maintenance. Response : the activity the system undertakes after the stimulus arrives: process it, log it, fail over, deny access. Response measure : the response must be measurable , so the requirement can be tested: response time under 2 seconds, 99% uptime, repair within 30 minutes. A scenario without a measure is not testable. Match each quality attribute scenario element with its meaning: source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, response measure. Quality Attribute Considerations – Scenarios Extra: 6 Steps for Using Quality Attribute Scenarios ➢A quality attribute scenario has the 1. Source → Who triggers the action (e.g., user, attacker, system). following parts: 2. Stimulus → The action or event that happens 1. Stimulus – a condition that needs to be (e.g., request, failure, attack). considered 3. Environment → The situation in which it happens (e.g., under load, during maintenance). 2. Source of stimulus - (e.g., human, computer 4. Artifact → The part of the system affected (e.g., system, etc.) database, server, UI). 3. Environment - what are the conditions 5. Response → How the system reacts (e.g., log error, retry, deny access). when the stimulus occurs? 6. Response Measure → How success is judged 4. Artifact – what elements of the system are (e.g., response time < 2 sec, 99% uptime). stimulated. 5. Response – the activity undertaken after arrival of the stimulus 6. Response measure – when the response occurs it should be measurable so that the requirement can be tested. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
A Quality Attribute Scenario Template

The one-sentence template: some source generates some event ( stimulus ) that arrives at some artifact under some conditions ( environment ) and must be dealt with ( response ) in a satisfactory way ( response measure ). Write any scenario by filling these six slots in this order. Source : who or what generates the stimulus. Stimulus : the event or condition that arrives. Environment : the conditions the system is in when it arrives. Artifact : the part of the system that is stimulated. Response : what the system does. Response measure : how the response is measured, so the requirement can be tested. Online Voting System: “During an election, thousands of eligible voters access the Online Voting System to submit their votes. While the system is operating under heavy election-day traffic, a voter submits a vote for a selected candidate. The system must validate the voter, securely record the vote, prevent duplicate voting, and display a confirmation message. The complete voting transaction must be processed within 4 seconds for at least 95% of voting requests.” Identify the six elements of the quality attribute scenario. Performance scenario: “During peak registration time, an enrolled student submits a course search request to the university registration system. The system processes the request and displays matching course sections. The search results must be displayed within 2 seconds for at least 95% of requests.” Match the six elements. A Quality Attribute Scenario Template ➢A template for writing a quality attribute scenario which is commonly used is: Some (source) generates some events (stimulis) that arrives at some artefact under some conditions (environment) and must be dealt with (response) in a satisfactory way (response measure) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
Quality Attribute Scenarios: a performance example

A performance scenario drawn as a picture. Read it left to right, like the template on slide 9. Source : users. Stimulus : they initiate transactions (the handwritten note gives “orders” as an example). Artifact : the system. Environment : under normal operations. Response : the transactions are processed. Response measure : with an average latency of two seconds. The measure is what turns “the system should be fast” into a requirement you can test. In the performance scenario on this slide, which part is “with average latency of two seconds”? Response measure Response Environment Stimulus Quality Attribute Considerations – Scenarios A Performance Scenario Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
Quality Attribute Scenarios: a maintainability example

A maintainability (modifiability) scenario. Here the “stimulus” is not a failure or a request but a wish to change the system. Source : a developer. Stimulus : wishes to change the UI. Artifact : the code. Environment : at design time (not while the system runs). Response : the modification is made with no side effects. Response measure : in three hours. If the UI is well separated from the rest of the code, the change stays small and the measure is met. Write a modifiability scenario in which a developer must add a new payment method. Quality Attribute Considerations – Scenarios A maintainability Scenario Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
Quality Attribute Considerations Scenario

A general scenario lists the possible values of each part for one quality (here availability). A concrete scenario then picks one value per part. Stimulus (the fault): crash (sudden failure), omission (no response when one was expected), timing (response at the wrong time), no response, or an incorrect response. The rest of the picture: Artifact The system’s processors, communication channels or persistent storage. Environment Normal operation, start-up, shutdown, repair mode, degraded (fail-safe) mode, overloaded operation. Response Prevent the failure, log it, notify users or operators, disable the source of the failure, or be temporarily unavailable. Measure Time interval available, availability %, detection time, repair time, degraded-mode time interval, unavailability time. The handwritten notes show one concrete pick: hardware failure → primary server crash → normal operation → switch to a backup server → restored in 30 seconds. Construct one quality attribute general scenario for availability. Availability scenario: “A monitoring service detects that the primary application server has stopped responding during normal operation. The system redirects requests to a standby server and restores service within 30 seconds with no more than 0.1% failed requests.” Match the six elements. Quality Attribute Considerations – Scenario Example: General Availability Scenario Extra: •Source •Internal to System: Problems or events that occur within the system itself, like a software bug or a memory leak. •External to System: Issues that come from outside the system, such as a power outage or a hacking attempt. •Stimulus: The event that triggers the system's response. This can include: •Crash: Sudden failure of the system. •Omission: Failure to respond when expected. •Timing: Response at the wrong time. •No Response: Complete lack of a response. •Incorrect Response: The system responds, but the response is wrong. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
Quality Attribute Considerations Tactics

These architectural design primitives are called tactics . A tactic targets one quality response (Chapter 2: a tactic is a design decision that controls a quality attribute response). Like design patterns, tactics are proven techniques experienced architects have used for years; we capture them and apply them. Lecture 2 lists tactics for each major quality. Quality Attribute Considerations – Tactics ➢There are a collection of primitive design techniques that an architect can use to achieve a quality attribute response. ➢We call these architectural design primitives tactics. ➢Tactics, like design patterns, are techniques that architects have been used for years by experienced architects that we can simply capture and apply in our designs. ➢We will show examples of tactics later in the following lecture. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
Extra Examples of Tactics

Redundancy (availability): run multiple instances of critical components so that if one fails another takes over. Stimulus: hardware failure or network outage. Response: automatic failover to the backup. Caching (performance): keep frequently accessed data in fast temporary storage. Stimulus: many read requests. Response: serve from the cache instead of fetching from primary storage, which cuts response time and load. Keeping several instances of a critical component so that another takes over when one fails is a tactic for: Availability Usability Testability Modifiability Extra Examples of Tactics ➢1. Redundancy • Purpose: To prevent system failure in case of a component failure. • Tactic: Implement multiple instances of critical components so that if one fails, others can take over. • Stimulus: Hardware failure, network outage. • Response: Automatic failover to backup systems. ➢2. Caching • Purpose: To improve response time and reduce load on the system. • Tactic: Store frequently accessed data in a temporary storage area to make it quickly accessible. • Stimulus: High number of read requests. • Response: Serve data from cache rather than re-fetching it from the primary storage. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
Quality Design Decisions

Architecture design is a systematic way of making design decisions, and every quality is achieved through them. They fall into seven categories. The first three are about the system’s parts: allocation of responsibilities (which element does which function), the coordination model (how elements interact) and the data model (data abstractions, their operations and properties). The last four: management of resources , binding time (how and when elements are bound), choice of technology , and mapping among elements (modules to run-time elements). Slides 16–17 give an example of each. List the seven categories of quality design decisions. Quality Design Decisions ➢Architecture design is a systematic approach to making design decisions. These decisions can be categorized into: 1. Allocation of system responsibilities (responsibilities of system functions) 2. Coordination model (coordination between system elements) 3. Data model (identify data abstractions, their operations and properties) 4. Management of resources 5. Binding time decisions (Determine how and when architectural elements are bounded) 6. Choice of technology 7. Mapping among architectural elements (mapping of modules and runtime elements ) 15
Extra: Quality Design Decisions explained

Coordination model : how the parts communicate and work together, e.g. how the payment system tells the inventory system an item was bought (direct call? event? message queue?). Extra: Quality Design Decisions Explanation 1. Allocation of System Responsibilities: ✓ This is about deciding which parts of the system will handle specific tasks. ✓ For example, in a shopping app, one part handles user logins, another manages the shopping cart, and other processes payments. 2. Coordination Model: ✓ This involves figuring out how different parts of the system will communicate and work together. ✓ For example, how the payment system informs the inventory system when an item has been purchased. 3. Data Model: ✓ This decision revolves around the types of data the system will use, how it's organized, and how it's accessed. ✓ For example, deciding to use a customer object that includes name, address, and order history. 16
Extra: Quality Design Decisions explained (cont.)

Management of resources : how memory, CPU time and network bandwidth are used and allocated, e.g. making sure there is enough server capacity during peak traffic (a performance decision). Binding time : when something is fixed: at compile time, installation, start-up or run time. Example: is the user’s language chosen at installation or switchable at run time? Later binding gives flexibility (modifiability) at some cost (performance, complexity). Deciding whether a user’s language is set at installation or can change at run time is which kind of design decision? Binding time decision Coordination model Data model Management of resources 4. Management of Resources: ✓This is about deciding how the system's resources like memory, processor time, and network bandwidth are used and allocated. ✓ For example, ensuring there are enough server resources during a high traffic period on a website. 5. Mapping among Architectural Elements ✓This involves planning out how different parts of the system (like code modules) correspond to runtime elements (like processes or tasks). ✓For example, mapping a user interface module to specific services that run when the application is used. 6. Binding Time Decisions: ✓These decisions determine when parts of the system are set or chosen, such as when certain modules are loaded or when specific configurations are applied. ✓For instance, choosing whether a user's language preference is set at installation or at runtime. 7. Choice of Technology: ✓This is about selecting the technologies the system will use, like programming languages, databases, or hardware platforms. ✓ For example, deciding to use Python for server-side logic, PostgreSQL for the database, and AWS for cloud hosting. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Summary

Practise writing one six-part scenario for each. Second quality lecture. Lecture 1 gave the tools (scenarios and tactics); this one applies them to each major quality attribute in turn. Software Design and Architecture [Quality Attributes] – Chapter 03, L02
Lecture Outlines and quality definitions

The table repeats Chapter 2’s one-line descriptions: usability (complexity of learning or using), modifiability (complexity of changing), security (protecting information), performance (useful work under time and resource limits), reliability (failure rate), portability, testability, availability (uptime), interoperability. Quality Description Usability The degree of complexity involved when learning or using the system. Lecture Outlines Modifiability The degree of complexity involved when changing the system to fit current or future needs. ➢ Major Quality Attributes Security The system’s ability to protect and defend its information or information system. − Definition Performance The system’s capacity to accomplish useful work under time and resource constraints. − Example with scenario Reliability The system’s failure rate. Portability The degree of complexity involved when adapting the system − Tactics to other software or hardware environments. Testability The degree of complexity involved when verifying and validating the system’s required functions. Availability The system’s uptime. Interoperability The system’s ability to collaborate with other software or hardware systems. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Major Quality Attributes

Testability is how easily the software can be made to demonstrate its faults . To be testable, a system must let testers control its inputs and observe its outputs. List and define three of the major quality attributes of software architecture. Which quality attribute is about the cost of change in time and money? Modifiability Performance Availability Usability Major Quality Attributes ➢Availability: is concerned with system failure and duration of system failures. (System failure means, when the system does not provide the service for which it was intended) ➢Modifiability: is about the cost of change, both in time and money. ➢Performance: is about timeliness. Events occur and the system must respond in a timely fashion. ➢Security: is the ability of the system to prevent or resist unauthorized access while providing access to legitimate users. An attack is an attempt to breach security. ➢Testability: refers to the ease with which the software can be made to demonstrate its faults. To be testable the system must control inputs and be able to observe outputs. ➢Usability: is how easy it is for the user to accomplish tasks and what support the system provides for the user to accomplish this. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Availability: general scenario

The general availability scenario lists every possible value of each part. Pick one value per column to write a concrete scenario. Source : internal or external to the system. Stimulus (the fault): crash, omission, timing, no response, incorrect response. Artifact : processors, communication channels, persistent storage. Environment : normal operation, start-up, shutdown, repair mode, degraded (fail-safe) mode, overloaded. Response : prevent the failure, log it, notify users or operators, disable the source, or be temporarily unavailable. Trip planning system (blackboard design): write an availability quality attribute scenario. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Availability Scenario Example

A concrete availability response : if a server becomes unresponsive, switch to a backup server, reallocate resources, or take other corrective action to keep the service running. The response measure judges how well the response worked, focusing on its effect on the whole system: the time taken to restore service, or whether the system kept operating with no downtime. The right-hand box repeats the six parts with examples: source (user, attacker, system), stimulus (request, failure, attack), environment (under load, during maintenance), artifact (database, server, UI), response (log, retry, deny access), measure (under 2 s, 99% uptime). Availability – Scenario Example Extra: Response: • Example on the response: If a server becomes unresponsive, the response might involve: • Switching to a backup server. • Reallocating resources. • Or other corrective actions to ensure continued service. •Response Measure: It is the criteria used to evaluate the effectiveness of the response. Also, we need it to determine how well the response addressed the problem, focusing on the outcome and impact on Extra: 6 Steps for Using Quality Attribute Scenarios the system’s overall operation. 1. Source → Who triggers the action (e.g., user, attacker, system). • Example on the response measure: For the server 2. Stimulus → The action or event that happens (e.g., request, failure, attack). unresponsiveness issue, a response measure could 3. Environment → The situation in which it happens (e.g., under load, during be: maintenance). • The time taken to restore service. 4. Artifact → The part of the system affected (e.g., database, server, UI). 5. Response Measure → How success is judged (e.g., response time < 2 sec, 99% uptime). 6
Availability – tactics

Fault detection : ping/echo (send a ping, expect an echo), heartbeat (a component sends a regular “I’m alive” signal; a missing beat means a fault), exceptions (catch the error when it happens). The goal is to find faults quickly. Recovery – preparation and repair : voting (several components compute the result and the majority wins), active redundancy (a duplicate runs in parallel, ready to take over instantly), passive redundancy (the backup starts only when the primary fails), spare (a standby that must be configured before use). Recovery – reintroduction brings a repaired part back: shadow (run it alongside the active one, or keep a shadow copy of the state, e.g. a database shadow page to fall back to), state resynchronisation (bring its data up to date with the others, e.g. sessions and caches after a server restarts), rollback (restore a previous good state). Prevention stops faults recurring: removal from service (take a failing component out, e.g. switch off a payment gateway that keeps failing and route customers to another), transactions (all-or-nothing updates), process monitor (watch processes and restart them). The diagram: a fault enters, tactics act, and the fault is masked or repaired. Heartbeat is a performance tactic used to reduce response time. What is the difference between active and passive redundancy? Extra: 1.Fault Detection: 1. Tactics: Ping/Echo, Heartbeat, Exception 2. Purpose: These tactics are designed to identify faults promptly. For example, the Heartbeat monitors the pulse of the system to detect any abnormal behavior or failures. 2.Recovery-Preparation and Repair: 1. Tactics: Voting, Active Redundancy, Passive Redundancy, Spare 2. Purpose: These strategies prepare the system for a quick recovery. Active redundancy involves having a duplicate system running in parallel, ready to take over immediately, while passive redundancy kicks in only when the primary system fails. 3.Recovery Reintroduction: 1. Tactics: Shadow State, Resynchronization, Rollback 2. Purpose: Once the immediate fault is managed, these tactics help in bringing the system back to its normal state. As Shadow means the system keeps a parallel copy (a “shadow”) of its current state while it is making changes. Example: A database keeps a shadow page (copy of the data page) when updating records. If the update fails, the system can roll back to the shadow copy without losing integrity. And Resynchronization means ensures that the restarted part has the latest valid data and is aligned with other running components. Example: In a distributed system, if one server crashes and comes back online, it resynchronizes its state (e.g., user sessions, cache, logs) with the other servers to ensure everyone has the same data. And Rollback, for instance, undoes any errors by restoring previous data states. 4.Prevention: 1. Tactics: Removal from Service, Transactions, Process Monitor 2. Purpose: These are long-term strategies aimed at preventing faults from reoccurring or minimizing their impact. Or Removing faulty components from service and monitoring ongoing processes help maintain system health and integrity. Example: If a payment gateway keeps failing, it is turned off and customers are sent to another working gateway. 7
Extra: Modifiability – Scenario Example

Three modifiability scenarios, differing by who wants the change. End user : cannot change the code, so they request changes (“I want dark mode”, “it’s too slow with 500 users”). Environment: run time. Artifact: interfaces, resources, configuration. Response: developers or admins implement and redeploy. Measure: cost in money, time, downtime and user satisfaction. •Extra: Modifiability – Scenario Example 1. Source: End User 2. Stimulus: Requests new functionality or changes in capacity/quality (e.g., faster login, dark mode, more users supported). cannot directly modify code or capacity. Instead, the end user requests new features, enhancements, or more capacity. Example: “I want a dark mode” or “The system is too slow when 500 users log in.” 3. Stimulus: Adds/modifies/deletes functionality or quality attributes (e.g., refactoring code, improving security, optimizing performance). 3. Environment: Design time, compile time, build time. 4. Artifact: Code, components, data. 5. Response: Implement change → test → integrate. 6. Measure: Effort in coding/testing, complexity of changed artifacts. 1. Source :System Administrator 2. Stimulus: Modifies capacity or technology (e.g., scaling servers, upgrading database, adjusting configuration). 3. Environment: Initialization time or runtime. 4. Artifact: Configurations, resources, deployment environments. 5. Response: Apply configuration/upgrade → redeploy system → test stability. 6. Measure: Cost in downtime, effort, risk of errors, affected system resources. 9
Extra: three modifiability scenarios

End user version: a user requests a feature or reports a bug that affects the UI or a function; feedback is handled during updates at run time; the team updates the UI or function; success = user satisfaction and fewer complaints. Developer version: a developer wants to enhance the UI; the change affects the UI code; it is made at design time; the developer updates and tests it; success = done and tested within three hours (the classic sample scenario on slide 9). Administrator version: the system faces more load or needs stronger security; scripts, network setup and security settings change during live operation or planned downtime; success = better reliability, faster responses, improved security.
