Modifiability Scenario Example

The textbook’s sample modifiability scenario : source developer; stimulus wishes to change the UI; artifact code; environment design time; response change made and unit tested; response measure in three hours. Memorise this one as the model answer shape for a modifiability scenario. Modifiability – Scenario Example More information about general and sample Modifiability scenarios can be found in: http://www.ece.ubc.ca/~matei/EEC E417/BASS/ch04lev1sec4.html Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
Modifiability tactics

Localise changes : assign responsibilities so a likely change touches as few modules as possible. Tactics: semantic coherence (keep related responsibilities together), anticipate expected changes, generalise the module, limit possible options, abstract common services. Changing the UI should only touch UI components. Prevent ripple effects : stop a change in one module from forcing changes in others. Tactics: hide information, maintain existing interfaces, restrict communication paths, use an intermediary. Updating a banking app’s UI must not affect how account data is processed. Defer binding time : postpone decisions as late as possible, ideally to run time, so changes need no recompile. Tactics: runtime registration, configuration files, polymorphism, component replacement, adherence to defined protocols. Example: a UI theme read from a config file at run time instead of hard-coded; a language the user can switch while the app runs. The response measures for modifiability are costs: time, effort and complexity of implementing the change. The diagram’s output: changes made, tested and deployed within time and budget. Name the three categories of modifiability tactics and give one tactic for each. •. Modifiability – tactics •Extra: • Localize Changes: When developers wish to change the UI, employing a strategy like "Generalize Module" or "Semantic Coherence" ensures that the change does not impact other parts of the software, focusing the change only on relevant components. • Prevention of Ripple Effect: Example: You are updating the UI of a banking app to make it more user-friendly. any changes to the UI, like adding new visual elements or changing layouts, do not directly impact how account data is processed or retrieved. • Defer Binding Time = delaying a decision as late as possible. Usually at runtime, not at design or compile time. Why we do it Easier to change No need to recompile or rebuild More flexibility examples •Response Measures in Context: UI Theme Hard binding: theme written in code Measures of cost in including time, Deferred binding: theme read from a config file at runtime Language setting effort, and complexity of implementing Chosen at compile time changes are important for User selects language while app is running understanding efficiency. summary Deferred binding time means postponing decisions to runtime so the system stays flexible and easy to modify. 12
Performance – Scenario Example

Environment for performance: normal mode, overload (beyond usual capacity), reduced capacity (maintenance or partial failure), emergency (high-priority work first), peak (highest expected demand). The same system may meet its target in one mode and fail in another. Stimulus = how events arrive: periodic (regular, e.g. daily backups), sporadic (occasional and unpredictable, e.g. a sudden large upload), bursty (sudden spikes, e.g. everyone logging in at once), stochastic (random with a probability distribution, e.g. network traffic). Source: internal (a process) or external (users, other systems). Artifact: the component whose performance matters (server, database, network). Response: process the events, or change the level of service (degrade non-essential services to protect core ones). Measures : latency (delay before work starts, e.g. 2 s before a video plays), deadline (latest finish time, e.g. payment confirmed within 5 s), throughput (work per unit time, e.g. 1,000 requests/minute), jitter (variation in response time), miss rate (share of deadlines missed, e.g. 2 of 100 frames = 2%), data loss (data that never arrives). Define latency, throughput and jitter as performance response measures. Performance – 4. Environment: - - Normal Mode: Standard operating conditions. - Overload Mode: When the system is operating beyond its usual capacity. Scenario Example - Reduced Capacity Mode: When the system is operating under resource constraints, possibly due to maintenance or partial failure. - Emergency Mode: High-priority operations taking precedence during a crisis. Extra: - Peak Mode: Highest expected operational demand. 1. Source: it is the entity that generates the need for a 5. Response: response or action by the system. - Process Events: Handling the incoming tasks or requests. - Change Level of Service: Adjusting the performance levels, possibly by degrading non-essential - Internal to the System: Such as a process within the system services to maintain core functionality. that requests resources. - External to the System: Such as a user interaction or an 6. Measure: external system's demand. • Latency: Delay before data starts moving. o Example: Waiting 2 seconds before a video starts playing. 2. Stimulus: • Deadline: Latest time a task must finish. o Example: A payment transaction must confirm within 5 seconds. - Periodic Events: Regularly occurring events, e.g., daily data • Throughput: How much work/data is done per second. backups. o Example: A server handles 1,000 requests per minute. - Sporadic Events: Occasional, unpredictable events, e.g., a • Jitter: Inconsistency in response times. user starting a large data upload unexpectedly. o Example: Sometimes a message arrives in 1s, other times in 4s. - Bursty Events: Sudden changes in activity, e.g., many users • Miss Rate: How often deadlines or tasks are missed. logging in simultaneously. o Example: out of 100 frames, 2 frames did not meet the speed requirement → Miss Rate = 2%. - Stochastic Events: Random events that have probabilistic • Data Loss: Data that never arrives. distributions, e.g., incoming network traffic. o Example: 5 out of 100 packets lost in a video call. 3. Artifact: - System Component: Any part of the system where the performance is measured or impacted, such as a server, database, or network component. 14
Performance Scenario Example

The sample performance scenario : source users; stimulus initiate transactions; artifact system; environment normal operation; response transactions are processed; response measure average latency of two seconds. The same scenario as Lecture 1, slide 10. Performance – Scenario Example More information about general and sample Performance scenarios can be found in: http://www.ece.ubc.ca/~matei/EEC E417/BASS/ch04lev1sec4.html Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
Performance tactics

Resource demand : reduce the work that reaches the system. Tactics: increase computational efficiency (better algorithms), reduce computational overhead, manage the event rate, control the frequency of sampling. Resource management : make better use of the resources you have. Tactics: introduce concurrency (process requests in parallel), maintain multiple copies (of data or computations, e.g. caches and replicas), increase available resources (faster CPU, more memory). Resource arbitration : decide which task gets a contended resource first, through a scheduling policy (FIFO, priority, deadline-first). Events arrive, the tactics act, and the response is generated within time constraints. Choosing which waiting request gets the CPU first is which category of performance tactic? Resource arbitration Resource demand Resource management Fault detection Performance – tactics •Extra: •Resource Demand: This can mean making the software run faster using less processing power and managing how often it checks or updates data. •Resource Management: Using resources like memory and processing power more effectively. •Resource Arbitration: Deciding how to prioritize different tasks that need resources Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 16
Security Scenario Example

The general security scenario . Read the first three columns: source an identified user, an unknown user, or a hacker from outside or inside the organisation. Careful: the Environment, Response and Measure columns on this slide (normal/overload/peak mode; process events; latency, throughput, jitter) are the performance scenario’s values, copied by mistake. For security, the textbook uses: environment online/offline, connected or not, behind a firewall or not; response authenticate, block access, encrypt, log and notify; measure time or effort to break in, probability of detecting the attack, how much data was exposed, time to restore. Use those in an exam. Give a correct environment, response and response measure for a security scenario (the slide’s columns belong to performance). Security – Scenario Example 18
Extra: Security – Scenario Example

A concrete security scenario. Source : a dissatisfied person (e.g. an employee) working from a remote location. Stimulus : the attempt to modify pay-rate data. Response : the system maintains an audit trail , a record of who did what and when, so the change can be traced. Response measure : how quickly the correct data is restored and whether the source of tampering is identified (the textbook version: correct data restored within a day, source identified). Security scenario: “While the system is connected to the public Internet, an unauthorized external user repeatedly attempts to log in using incorrect credentials to an administrative account. The authentication service rejects the attempts, records the activity, and temporarily locks the account after repeated failures. The system must block the account after 5 failed attempts within 10 minutes and generate an audit record for every attempt.” Match the six elements. Extra: Security – Scenario Example Source: A (Dissatisfied person) attempting to modify payroll data from a remote location. Stimulus: The attempt to modify the pay rate data. Artifact: The specific data targeted by the attack within the system. Environment: The system operates under normal conditions when the attack occurs. Response: The system's response includes maintaining an audit trail, which helps in tracking and recording the sequence of activities. Response Measure: The effectiveness of the response is measured by how quickly the correct data is restored and the identification of the source of tampering. 19
Security – tactics

Resisting attacks (keep them out): authenticate users (who are you?), authorise users (what may you do?), maintain data confidentiality (encryption), maintain integrity (checksums, hashes), limit exposure (fewer entry points), limit access (firewalls, need-to-know). Detecting attacks : intrusion detection, comparing traffic and behaviour against known attack patterns. Recovering from an attack : restoration (uses the availability tactics, “see availability” in the tree) and identification of the attacker through an audit trail . The output: the system detects, resists or recovers from attacks. Authenticating and authorising users belong to which category of security tactics? Resisting attacks Detecting attacks Recovering from attacks Resource arbitration Extra Security – tactics Resisting Attacks: Methods to prevent unauthorized access or modifications. This includes authenticating and authorizing users, maintaining data confidentiality and integrity, and limiting access and exposure. Detecting Attacks: Techniques to identify when an attack is occurring, by intrusion detection systems. Recovering from an Attack: Steps to restore system functionality and data integrity after an attack. This involves restoration, identification of the threat source, and maintaining an audit trail. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
Testability Scenario Example

Response : execute the test suite and capture results, capture the cause of a fault, control and monitor the system’s state. Measures : effort to find a fault, effort to reach a coverage %, probability that the next test reveals a fault, time to perform tests, effort to detect faults. Testability – Scenario Example 21
Testability Scenario

Response measure : 85% path coverage within three hours . Coverage plus a time limit makes the testability goal checkable. Testability scenario: “During pre-release system testing, a QA engineer initiates an automated test suite to verify the order-processing component. The system exposes the required interfaces, records internal test results, and reports failed test cases. The complete test suite must finish within 15 minutes and identify the failing component in at least 95% of injected faults.” Match the six elements. Testability – Scenario Example •Extra: •Source: The Unit Tester is the individual responsible for testing. •Stimulus: The completion of a code unit, prompting the test. •Artifact: The specific code unit that has been completed and is being tested. •Environment: Development environment where testing typically occurs. •Response: Results of the testing are captured. •Response Measure: Evaluates the effectiveness of the testing with metrics such as 85% path coverage within three hours. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 22
Testability tactics

Manage input/output : control what goes in and observe what comes out. Tactics: record/playback (capture real inputs and replay them to reproduce a failure), separate interface from implementation (swap in test doubles behind the interface), specialised access routines/interfaces (test-only hooks into a component). Internal monitoring : built-in monitors that expose the component’s internal state (counters, logs, performance data) during testing. The diagram: an increment is completed, the tactics act, and faults are detected. Give two testability tactics. Testability – tactics Extra This diagram outlines general strategies that enhance the testability of a system: •Manage Input/Output: Includes techniques like record/playback and separating interface from implementation, which simplify testing by allowing testers to manage how data enters and exits the system. •Internal Monitoring: Involves built-in monitors that help in observing the system’s internal state, providing valuable data during testing. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 23
Usability Scenario Example

Artifact : the system, or the part the user is interacting with. Environment : run time or configuration time. Response : provide the features needed and anticipate the user’s needs. Usability – Scenario Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 24
Usability Scenario Example

Response measure : the user is productive within two minutes of starting the app. That number is what makes “easy to learn” testable. Usability scenario: “A first-time student user uses the university Learning Management System during normal operation and attempts to submit an assignment for the first time. The system provides clear instructions, guides the student through selecting and uploading the file, and displays a confirmation message after successful submission. The student should complete the task within 2 minutes, without external help, and with no more than one input error.” Match the six elements. Usability – Scenario Example Extra: This diagram represents a usability scenario where a user downloads and begins using a new application. The key elements are: 1.Source: Users who initiate the test by downloading the app. 2.Stimulus: The action of downloading and starting the app. 3.Artifact: The overall system that supports and runs the app. 4.Environment: Occurs in real-time during application use. 5.Response: The user is able to use the app effectively almost immediately. 6.Response Measure: Success is measured by the user achieving productivity within two minutes of starting the app, indicating high usability. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 25
Usability – tactics

Separate the user interface from the system’s operations, so the UI can change on its own. Example: a blog platform’s visual editor changes the design without touching the code (MVC in Chapter 4 does exactly this). Support user initiative : give users tools to manage their own actions: cancel (remove items before checkout), undo (revert an edit), aggregate (combine many items into one, e.g. a weekly activity summary). Support system initiative : the system anticipates the user using models: a user model (recommendations from viewing history), a system model (sync the most important emails first), a task model (deadline reminders from the project timeline). An “Undo” button supports which usability tactic? Support user initiative Support system initiative Separate the user interface Resource arbitration Extra: 1. Separate User Interface Usability – tactics Explanation: Keeping the user interface distinct from system operations. Example: A blog platform lets you customize your blog’s design through a visual editor without needing to touch the underlying code. 2. Support User Initiative Explanation: Tools that help users manage their actions. • Cancel: In an online shopping cart, users can remove items before checkout. • Undo: In a document editor, users can revert changes by clicking the "undo" button. • Aggregate: A fitness app compiles weekly activity into a summary report for easy review. 3. Support System Initiative Explanation: The system anticipates and reacts to user needs based on user behavior and tasks. • User Model: A streaming service recommends movies based on your viewing history. • System Model: An email client automatically syncs your most important emails first. • Task Model: A task management app sends reminders for deadlines based on project timelines. 26
Summary

For each major quality you should be able to give the definition, write a general and a sample scenario, and name its tactics. Next chapter: architecture patterns, ready-made structures that bundle several of these tactics (e.g. MVC separates the UI, a broker hides locations). Summary ➢Major Quality Attributes − Definition − General and sample scenario examples − Tactics ➢ Next … Architecture Design Patterns ➢https://www.youtube.com/watch?time_continue=85&v=rKwSIih_U74&embeds_referring _euri=https%3A%2F%2Fchatgpt.com%2F&source_ve_path=MjM4NTE Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 27
Extra: Question – one tactic per quality

The exercise: give one tactic per quality attribute. Name the tactic, not the quality again. Model answers from the slide: security resisting or detecting attacks, authenticate users; testability separate interface from implementation; modifiability localise changes, encapsulation, hide information; performance concurrency, increase available resources. Add availability : heartbeat or redundancy, and usability : undo or cancel. List one design tactic for each of: security, testability, modifiability, performance, availability, usability. Extra: Question List one design tactic that you can use to achieve each of the following quality attributes: Quality Attribute Tactics Resisting Attacks, Security Detecting Attacks, Authenticate users Separate interface from implementation Testability Localize changes, Modifiability Encapsulation, Hide information Concurrency, Performance Increase available resources. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 28

decks.t: Architecture Patterns: Overview, History and Classification
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 4 · Lecture 1: Architecture Patterns: Overview, History and Classification
n: Slide 1

Chapter 4 is about architecture patterns : ready-made system structures. This first lecture is the overview and classification; the patterns themselves come in Lectures 2 and 3. Homework on the title slide: research serverless architecture (applications built from cloud functions that the provider runs on demand, with no server you manage). Software Design and Architecture [Architecture Patterns] – Chapter 04, L01 HW: Serverless architecture
Lecture Outlines

The classification at the end uses five system types: data-centered, data flow, distributed, interactive and hierarchical. Lecture Outlines ➢ Overview of Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢ History of Architectural Styles and Patterns ✓ Origin of styles and patterns Extra: ➢ Architectural Style: A high-level template that defines the overall structure of the system (like Layered ). ➢ Architectural Pattern: A specific, reusable solution to a common problem inside that structure (like MVC within a Layered style). ➢ In short: Styles set the big picture, patterns provide the detailed recipe. ➢ Classification of Architectural Styles and Patterns ✓ Data-Centered ✓ Data flow ✓ Distributed ✓ Interactive ✓ Hierarchical Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Extra: Calculating the average, a reusable recipe

An analogy for reuse: once you know the three steps for an average (list the numbers, total them, divide), you reuse them for students’ scores, weekly temperatures, anything. Seen as a pattern , each step is a filter that transforms the data and passes it to the next one: pipes and filters. Because each step is independent, the same pipeline is reused for different averages. Extra: Example: Calculating the Average • Step 1: Define the list of numbers. • Step 2: Find the total. • Step 3: Calculate the average. Applying to Different Problems 1. Students’ Average Score: Calculate average scores of students in a session. 2. Weekly Temperature Average: Calculate average temperature over a week. Connection to Software Engineering Concepts Architectural Style: Architectural Pattern Data flows Style: Pipes-and-Filters: Each step in the process (input, processing, output) can Each step (define list → find total → calculate be viewed as a stage in the flow of data. average) acts as a filter, transforming the data and For example, input (list of numbers), processing passing it to the next stage. (sum), output (average). This allows scalability and reuse for different average 3 calculations.
Overview

Good logical architectures come from past experience : strategies that already worked in other systems. Overview ➢Software systems need to be carefully architected and evaluated from different perspectives. ✓This is necessary to address multiple concerns that shape the quality of the system from different stakeholders with different backgrounds. ➢In this chapter, we pay special attention (mostly) on decomposing the software system into logical components that represent the structural integrity that supports functional and non-functional (quality) requirements. ➢When designing logical architectures, it is important to use past experience to discover overall strategies that have been used successfully in the development of software systems. ✓To this end, the concepts of architectural styles and architectural patterns have emerged as mainstream approach for achieving reuse at the architectural level. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Overview: the caveman and today’s architect

The caveman has to invent the structure of a house from scratch, which is slow and risky. Today’s architect reuses years of documented experience. The boxed point is the lesson: it is more efficient to build systems from successfully employed designs than to design from scratch. Overview Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Overview: reusing documented patterns

The software version of the same story: the customer asks for “an interactive system that displays data from storage in multiple displays and formats”, and the architect recognises the requirement as the Model-View-Controller pattern. Once a pattern is identified, the architect looks it up in a pattern catalogue for its documented structure (the MVC class and sequence diagrams on the right) and knows the quality properties a system built that way will have. Overview Similar to the previous example, today’s software architects can benefit from numerous documented styles and patterns for software architecture. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
Overview

Styles and patterns are generic, reusable solutions that are easy to understand and apply to new problems with similar needs. Benefits of that reuse: improved quality (they encode refined best practice), consistency (the same structure across an application or across projects, so it is easier to understand and maintain), and efficiency (well-understood, tested designs speed up design and implementation). Decisions based on them benefit from years of documented experience describing the solution, its benefits, and the consequences (trade-offs) of using it. Knowing the consequences in advance is the real value. What is the benefit of reusing architectural styles and patterns? Overview ➢Architectural styles and patterns provide generic, reusable solutions that can be easily understood. ✓These can be easily applied to new problems requiring similar architectural features. ✓What is the benefit of this reuse???? (discuss) •Extra: 1. Improved Quality: Patterns are based on best practices that have been refined over time, leading to more robust and reliable software. 2. Consistency: Ensures uniformity in architecture across different parts of an application or different projects within an organization, making the system easier to understand and maintain. 3. Increased Efficiency: Using well-understood and tested patterns speeds up the design and implementation phases. ➢Decisions based on architectural styles and patterns benefit from years of documented experience that highlights ✓The solution approach to a given problem. ✓The benefits of these approaches. ✓The consequences of employing these approaches. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 7
History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns

In 1977 Christopher Alexander , a building architect, published a pattern language to help people design good buildings and towns of any size. It became a catalogue of 253 patterns , each documented with a picture, its context, the problem it solves, evidence that it works, and related patterns. That documentation format is the ancestor of every software pattern catalogue. History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢In 1977, Christopher Alexander presented a language intended to help individuals, or teams, design quality structures of different sizes, shapes, and complexities. (i.e. this was for buildings) ➢ Alexander’s work resulted in a catalogue of 253 patterns, each describing in detail the essential information required for documenting the patterns, including: ✓ Picture of the pattern ✓ Context of the pattern ✓ Problem that the pattern attempts to solve ✓ Evidence for its validity ✓ Related patterns Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns

In the 1990s software engineers began cataloguing recurring high-level solutions (elements and their relationships) and called them architectural styles . Their focus was the solution. History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢ In the 1990s, the software engineering community began researching and finding recurring high- level problem solutions in terms of specific elements and their relationships; these were originally referred to as architectural styles. ✓ Similar to Alexander’s work, Architectural Styles provided the means for software architects to reuse design solutions in different projects; that is, to use a “solution a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.” (its focus: solution) Extra: 1. Alexander’s example: windows placement in buildings. ✓ Example: He described a pattern like “Light on Two Sides of Every Room” → if you design a room, give it windows on two sides for better natural light. ✓ Focus: documenting patterns for reusing good design ideas in physical buildings. 2. Software’s example: Pattern idea: Client–Server → clients send requests, server responds. ✓ Reuse: Many projects use this idea. ✓ Adapt differently: − In Gmail, the client is a browser; the server handles emails. − In a Banking App, the client is a mobile app; the server handles transactions. ✓ Same pattern reused, but each project implements it in its own way. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns

Inspired by Alexander, they called them design patterns : a catalogue of 23 patterns, each described in a fixed specification format. Chapters 6–7 study several of them (Singleton, Builder, Composite, Observer…). The Gang of Four (1994) catalogued how many design patterns, at what level? 23 detailed-design (object-oriented) patterns 253 building patterns 23 architectural styles 5 system types History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢ In 1994, Gamma, Helm, Johnson, and Vlissides—better known as the Gang of Four (GoF)—published their influential work that focused on a finer- grained set of object-oriented detailed design solutions that could be used in different problems “a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.” ✓ Influenced by Alexander’s work, they called these Design Patterns. ✓ Their work resulted in the creation of a catalogue of 23 (detailed design) patterns. ✓ Each pattern was described in detail, using a specific pattern specification format. Extra: In other words, These patterns allow developers to apply similar solutions in various situations without repeating the same code, inspired by Alexander’s architectural design principles. Each pattern is thoroughly described in a specific format to make them easy to understand and implement. 10
History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns

In 1996 Buschmann et al. combined the two lines of work: well-known architectural styles written in a pattern format (context – problem – solution). They called these architectural patterns . Design patterns are medium-scale : applying one has no effect on the fundamental structure of the system, though it may strongly shape one subsystem. That sentence is the clearest way to tell the two apart. How do architectural patterns differ from design patterns (Buschmann et al.)? History of Software Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢ In 1996, the work of Buschmann, Meunier, Rohnert, Sommerland, and Stal, integrated the work of architectural styles and design patterns by providing a set of well-known architectural styles using a pattern-like approach. ✓ They referred to these as Architectural Patterns. (its focus: context-problem-solution) ➢ In their work, Buschmann et al. provided their views about architectural patterns vs. design patterns: ✓ “Architectural patterns … specify the system-wide structural properties of an application. They specify the system-wide structural properties of an application, and have an impact on the architecture of its subsystems.” ✓ “Design patterns are medium-scale patterns.” ✓ “The application of a design pattern has no effect on the fundamental structure of a software system, but may have a strong influence on the architecture of a subsystem.” 11
Extra: Architectural patterns vs. design patterns

Architectural patterns define the overall structure of the whole system and how all subsystems are organised and interact: client–server, layers, pipes and filters. The diagram groups them by system type (data-centered: blackboard, repository; data flow: pipes and filters; distributed: client-server, broker; interactive and hierarchical). Design patterns are solutions at the subsystem or component level that do not change the overall structure: Observer, Factory, Strategy. The lower diagram groups them as creational, structural, concurrency and behavioural. 12
Extra: Timeline of styles and patterns

Put in order and match: Gang of Four, Buschmann et al., Alexander, architectural styles. Extra 1977 – Christopher Alexander • What he did: Created a catalogue of 253 patterns (originally for buildings). • Focus: Documenting patterns → described problems + solutions + context. • Key Idea: Gave the world the language of patterns. ________________________________________ 1990s – Software Engineering Community • What they did: Introduced Architectural Styles. • Focus: Solution reuse at a high level (whole system structures). • Key Idea: Reuse big system structures (e.g., client–server, layered). ________________________________________ 1994 – Gang of Four (GoF) • What they did: Published the Design Patterns book (23 OO patterns). • Focus: Problem–solution reuse at a smaller scale (classes, objects). • Key Idea: Standardized and popularized design patterns. ________________________________________ 1996 – Buschmann et al. • What they did: Combined Architectural Styles + Design Patterns. • Focus: Context–problem–solution at system level. • Key Idea: Introduced Architectural Patterns (system-wide) vs Design Patterns (subsystem-level). ________________________________________ In short: 1. Alexander (1977): First to document many patterns → gave the language. 2. SE Community (1990s): Added architectural styles → reuse at system level. 3. GoF (1994): Focused on design patterns → reuse at class/object level. 4. Buschmann et al. (1996): Unified everything → introduced architectural patterns (big) vs design patterns (smaller). 13
Architecture Patterns Classification

Which pattern to apply depends on the type of system, its requirements and the desired quality attributes . These, not the pattern’s popularity, decide between patterns. Large systems often combine patterns : a client–server system whose server is internally layered, for example. Patterns are classified by the type of system they suit (next slide). Architecture Patterns Classification ➢The choice of applying architectural patterns depend on the type of system, requirements, and desired quality attributes. ✓These characteristics help guide the choice of selecting one particular pattern over another. ➢In some cases, more than one architectural pattern can be used in combination to collectively provide the appropriate architectural solution. (specially for large systems) ➢Architectural patterns can be classified depending on the type of system. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
Architecture Patterns Classification

The table: Data-centered A centralised repository of data that clients access and work on → blackboard, repository. Data flow Built around transporting and transforming a stream of data → pipes and filters. Distributed Independent processing units interacting over a network → client–server, broker. Interactive User-centric systems → MVC. Hierarchical Components arranged in levels of abstraction and responsibility → layered (main program and subroutine). Match each scenario with the most suitable architectural style (each used once): (1) payroll app whose UI, salary rules and data storage must evolve independently; (2) security-log app where separate units extract fields, normalise timestamps, remove sensitive values and summarise; (3) hospital app talking to lab equipment from different vendors through one request format; (4) speech-understanding app whose components repeatedly add and reconsider partial interpretations; (5) museum ticketing shown differently on desktop and kiosks, updated by user actions; (6) classroom response app with one authoritative session for hundreds of phones; (7) emergency messaging between nearby phones with no Internet and no central node. Pipes and filters belongs to which system type? Data flow Data-centered Distributed Hierarchical Architecture Patterns Classification ➢Major types of systems: Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
Data Centered Systems

The diagram: many client software components around one data store (repository or blackboard). Clients don’t talk to each other, only to the store. Sharing data is easy; the store can become a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Data Centered Systems ➢Systems that serve as a centralized repository for data, while allowing clients to access and perform work on the data ➢Used in DBMS, library information system, the interface repository in CORBA, compilers and CASE tools, speech recognition, image recognition, security system, and business resource management systems 16
Extra: Data Centered Systems

They do not communicate directly with each other; the repository is the intermediary. In a repository the store is passive; in a blackboard, components react to changes on the shared data (Lecture 2). Extra: Data Centered Systems ➢Patterns: ➢Blackboard, Repository ➢Example: ➢Central data repository systems where different components interact primarily through a central data store. ➢Explanation: In such systems, the core component is a central database or repository where data is stored and managed. Components of the system interact with this central repository to retrieve, add, or modify data. They do not communicate directly with each other but rather use the repository as an intermediary. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Data Flow Systems

Example: video streaming. The picture shows data entering from a source, passing through processing nodes (which may branch and rejoin), and leaving to the cloud: each node transforms the stream and hands it on. Data Flow Systems ➢ Systems oriented around the transport and (or) transformation of a stream of data (Example: video streaming) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 18
Extra: Data Flow Systems

Typical uses: signal processing and data streaming, compilers (lexer → parser → code generator), image and video processing. Extra: Data Flow Systems • Pattern: Pipes-and-Filters • Example: • Data processing systems where data passes through a chain of components, each transforming the data. • Explanation: • This pattern involves a series of processing elements called filters, connected by pipes which transmit data from one filter to the next. Each filter processes the input data and produces output data, often transforming the data in some way. This setup is commonly used in signal processing or data streaming applications. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 19
Distributed Systems

The diagram: four computers, each with its own local OS, running applications A, B (spread over two machines) and C, joined by a middleware layer that hides the network so the applications can talk as if local. Network delays and partial failures are the price of distribution. Distributed Systems ➢ Systems primarily involved in interaction between several independent processing units connected via a network ➢ Example: network applications like the world wide web (web applications) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
Extra: Distributed Systems

Extra: Distributed Systems Patterns:Client-Server, Broker Example: Systems distributed across multiple networked components, managing communication and data exchange. -Explanation: - Client-Server: This is a decentralized pattern where multiple clients (users' machines) request resources and services from a central server. The server processes these requests and returns the responses. This model is fundamental in web interactions. Such as, in web applications where a web server handles requests from web browsers (clients) to serve web pages - Broker: In this pattern, a broker component is responsible for coordinating communication between components, often in different processes or across networks. The broker routes requests, translates messages, and often ensures security and scalability. such as in service-oriented architectures (SOA) where multiple services interact through a messaging system. 21
Interactive Systems

The Extra rule: an app that works offline only (calculator, offline dictionary, offline game) is interactive; an app that needs a server (WhatsApp, Gmail, banking) is distributed. Many real apps are both: interactive on the phone, distributed overall. Interactive Systems ➢Systems that serve users (user-centric systems) and require heavy interaction between the user and the system. ➢Example: mobile applications Extra: - If the mobile app works offline only (e.g., calculator, offline dictionary, offline game) → Interactive System. - If the mobile app requires server communication (e.g., WhatsApp, Gmail, banking app) → Distributed System. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 22
Extra: Interactive Systems

Example: a desktop calculator. The flow is user interface (handles interaction) → application logic (processes commands) → data management → local database. This separation of interface from logic is what MVC formalises. Extra: Interactive Systems Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 23
Extra: Interactive vs. Distributed Systems

Is an offline dictionary app interactive or distributed? Is WhatsApp? Extra Interactive vs Distributed Systems (Simplified) •Interactive (Local) • Runs fully on one machine. • Example: Calculator, offline dictionary. • Works offline, single user. •Distributed (Networked) • Split across multiple machines (client + server). • Example: Gmail, banking app. • Needs internet, supports many users. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 24
Hierarchal Systems

Example: control systems in manufacturing, robotics and vehicles. In the diagram the top-level node sends tasks and goals down; lower nodes pass sensations and results up; sensors and actuators at the bottom touch the controlled process. Hierarchal Systems ➢ System where components can be structured as a hierarchy (vertically and horizontally) to reflect different levels of abstraction and responsibility ➢Example: control systems in manufacturing, robotics and vehicles Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 25
Extra: Hierarchal Systems

Example: an operating system , from hardware interaction at the lowest layer to user-interface management at the top. Each layer uses only the services of the layer below it. The pattern is layered (and main program and subroutine). Extra: Hierarchal Systems •Description: These systems are structured in layers, each layer having a specific role or responsibility, allowing for the separation of concerns across a vertical (layered) or horizontal (module) scale. •Example: •Operating systems where different layers handle tasks ranging from hardware interaction at the lowest level to user interface management at the highest level. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 26
Extra: Question – pick the pattern

The exercise: pick the pattern for each requirement. 1. Video processing in a fixed sequence (decode, filter, encode) Pipe-and-filter : a chain of transformations. 2. Online banking used through web, mobile and desktop Client-server : many clients, one central service. 3. Financial analysis where collaborating modules contribute expertise to one evolving solution Blackboard : independent knowledge sources refine shared data. A DBMS can be seen two ways: as a repository (data-centered: all applications share one database) or as part of a client–server system (distributed: clients send SQL queries, the server processes them). The classification depends on the viewpoint. Extra: Question Extra: A DBMS can be viewed in two ways: •As a Repository (Data-Centered Style) → all apps use one central shared database. 27 •As part of a Client-Server system (Distributed Style) → clients send SQL queries, server processes them.
Summary

Summary ➢Overview of Architecture Styles and Patterns ➢ History of Architectural Styles and Patterns ✓ Origin of styles and patterns ➢ Classification of Architectural Styles and Patterns ✓ Data-Centered ✓ Data flow ✓ Distributed ✓ Interactive ✓ Hierarchical ➢Next …, we will discuss two types of systems: Data-centered and Data Flow, together with essential architectural patterns for these systems, including: Blackboard and Pipes-and-Filters Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 28

decks.t: Data-Centered, Data-Flow and Distributed Patterns: Blackboard, Pipes-and-Filters, Client-Server, Broker
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 4 · Lecture 2: Data-Centered, Data-Flow and Distributed Patterns: Blackboard, Pipes-and-Filters, Client-Server, Broker
n: Slide 1

Second patterns lecture: the patterns for the first three system types of Lecture 1. For each one learn its components (the roles you will be asked to name), how they communicate, and its quality properties. Software Design and Architecture [Architecture Patterns] Ð Chapter 04, L02
Lecture Outlines- Architecture Patterns Ð Chapter 04

Distributed → client–server and broker. Interactive and hierarchical systems come in Lecture 3. Lecture Outlines- Architecture Patterns Ð Chapter 04 ➢ Data-Centered Systems ➢ Distributed Systems ¥ Overview ¥ Overview ¥ Patterns: ¥ Patterns: − Blackboard − Client Server ➢ Data Flow Systems − Broker ¥ Overview ¥ Patterns: − Pipes-and-Filters Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview

Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview ➢ Data-centered systems are systems primarily decomposed around a main central repository of data. These include: ¥ Data management componeLnt:o thae dingÉ data management component controls, provides, and manages access to the systemÕs data. ¥ Worker components: worker components execute operations and perform work based on the data. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview

Communication is one-to-one and two-way between each worker and the data manager (the “two way communication” arrows). Workers do not interact with each other directly; everything goes through the data management component. That keeps workers independent, but makes the data manager critical: if it is slow or down, everyone is. Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview ➢ Communication in data-centered systems is characterized by a one-to- one bidirectional communication between a worker component and the data management component. ➢ Worker components do not interact with each other directly; all communication goes through the data management component. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview

Because everything depends on shared data, these systems must handle data integrity : data stays complete, accurate and consistent across operations, even when several workers update it (the diagram adds transactions and recovery, and security, at the data manager). They must also define the communication protocols (and security) between the workers and the data manager. The Extra box repeats Lecture 1: a DBMS can be seen as a repository or as the server in client–server. Data-Centered Systems Ð Overview ➢Because of the architecture of these systems, they must consider issues with: ¥ Data integrity −Extra: Integrity means that LoadingÉ data is complete, accurate, and consistent across various databases, systems, or during any operation (like transfer, Extra: A DBMS can be viewed in two ways: ¥As a sRteoproasgiteo,r yo (rD raetat-rCieevntaelr)e.d Style) → all apps use one central shared database. ¥As part of a Client-Server system (Distributed Style) → clients send SQL queries + server processes them+ ¥ Communication protocols Database → stores data. between worker and data Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5 management
Blackboard Architectural Pattern

The components work independently , each providing a partial solution , in an opportunistic way: whoever can contribute something useful given the current state does so. There is no predetermined sequence of operations that leads to the answer. That is the key difference from pipes and filters, whose order is fixed. Best Flight Itinerary system (Midterm 252): a Passenger App sends a trip request to the Trip Planning Service, which creates an empty itinerary draft in the Draft Itinerary Record. The Route Builder lists possible routes, the Constraint Checker filters out routes that break the passenger’s or airline’s rules, and the Best Option Selector picks the best one; each step retrieves the current draft, improves it and saves it back, until the draft is stable and the service returns it to the app. Write the name of the most suitable architectural pattern for this system. Blackboard Architectural Pattern ➢ Blackboard decomposes systems into components that work around a central data component to provide solutions to complex problems. ¥ These components work independently from each other to provide partial solutions to problems using an opportunistic problem-solving approach. ¥ That is, there are no predetermined, or correct, sequences of operations for reaching the problemÕs solution. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
Blackboard Architectural Pattern

The pattern copies how a group of scientists would attack a hard problem together at one blackboard. A mediator (controller) controls access to the board. When it hands control to a scientist, that scientist looks at the current state and, if possible, advances the solution before releasing the board. With the new knowledge on the board, control goes to the next scientist who can improve it, and so on until no more progress can be made. There is no fixed order: each contributes when the current state makes their expertise useful. This is how expert systems work (AI that applies knowledge and inference rules like a human expert, in medicine or finance), so the blackboard pattern is a good fit for their logical architecture. Blackboard Architectural Pattern ➢ The Blackboard architectural pattern resembles the approach a group of scientists would employ to solve a complex problem. ¥ Consider a group of scientists at one location using a blackboard (chalkboard, whiteboard, or electronic blackboard) to solve a complex problem. ¥ Assume that to manage the problem-solving process, a mediator controls access to the blackboard. ¥ Once the mediator (or controller) assigns control to the blackboard, a scientist evaluates the current state of the problem and if possible, advances its solution before releasing control of the blackboard. ¥ With new knowledge obtained from the previous solution attempt, control is assigned to the next scientist who can further improve the problemsÕ state. ¥ This process continues until no more progress can be made, at which point the blackboard system reaches a solution. ¥ Extra note: − There is no strict order in which team members must contribute. They jump in as needed, making decisions on the spot about the best way to add to the solution based on the current information available. ➢ This behavior is famous in expert systems; therefore, the Blackboard architectural pattern is a good choice for depicting the logical architecture of expert systems. − Extra Note: 7 − An expert system is a type of AI that uses knowledge and inference rules to solve complex problems typically handled by human experts. It mimics human decision-making to provide solutions in fields like medicine, finance, and customer service.
