A piece of software works out who a person is automatically with a pipe-and-filter architecture: it accesses videos (with audio) from YouTube, detects faces, recognizes faces, and predicts the identity. (1) Place the lifelines of the sequence diagram from left to right in the order the data flows. (2) Which statements about the correct diagram are true? Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2 ¥ Consider software that houses algorithms for automatically determining the identity of an individual: ¥ The software access videos (with audio) from YouTube ¥ The software detects faces of individuals in the video (Face detection is used to determine if a face is in the video) ¥ The software recognizes faces from the video (Face recognition is used to determine the identity of the person from the detected face). ¥ Based on detection and recognition, the software predicts the identity of individuals in the video ¥ Using the pipes and filters architecture, the logical structure of the system can be modeled as shown in the next slide Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 32
Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2

The box-and-line view: a big video file enters the YouTube Manager , which prepares it. Identity manager produces the final output, such as an identity report (“Wanted: Joe Developer”). The callout asks the design question: if a better recognition algorithm appears, only that one filter changes. Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2 ¥Extra Explanation: ¥Big Video File: A large video file serves as the input source. ¥YouTube Manager: This component processes the video file to prepare it for further analysis. ¥Face Detection: This stage identifies and isolates faces within the video data. It transforms the video data into specific information related only to the detected faces. ¥Face Recognition: This process analyzes the detected faces to identify individuals by matching features with known faces. ¥Identity Manager: Produces a final output based on the face recognition results, such as identity reports, which could be used for verification or security purposes. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 33
Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2

A UML component diagram (next slide) makes the transport explicit. Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2 ¥ In the previous example, the box-and-line diagram was useful for visualizing the components in the system, however, it conveyed nothing about how data is transported from one Filter to the next, (i.e., the Pipes). ¥ Consider the following UML component for the same system to understand how the data is transported between the different filters (components) in the system Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 34
Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2

Here the pipe is the file system : a FileSystemManager component (built on .NET’s FileSystemWatcher) monitors directories and fires an event when a new file appears. The pipeline components (VideoManager, FaceDetection, FaceRecognition, IdentityManager) each require the IFileSystemPipe interface the manager provides. A filter writes its output as a file; the manager detects it and triggers the next filter. The warning notes this is not the typical pipes-and-filters example but shows how flexible the pattern is. Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Example2 ¥Extra: ¥The system uses .NET's FileSystemWatcher : to monitor directories for new video files, triggering the data processing pipeline when new files are detected. ¥Processing Pipeline: Consists of several components: ¥Video Manager: Handles initial video file management. ¥Face Detection: Detects faces in the videos. ¥Face Recognition: Identifies the detected faces. ¥Identity Manager: Manages identity data from recognized faces. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 35
Pipes-and-Filters – Example 2 sequence diagram

FileSystemManager : the coordinator. Its onFileDetected(file) notifies the registered filter whenever a new or processed file appears, which is what moves data along the pipeline. Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern Ð Extra Explanation: Example2 1. VideoManager ¥put(file) → Puts new video file into the system. 2. FaceDetection ¥register() → Registers with FileSystemManager. ¥process() → Processes video data for face features. ¥put(file) → Passes processed file to next stage. 3. FaceRecognition ¥register() → Registers with FileSystemManager. ¥process() → Identifies and recognizes faces. ¥put(file) → Passes recognized face data forward. 4. IdentityManager ¥ register() → Registers with FileSystemManager ¥process() → Determines identity of individuals from recognition data. 5. FileSystemManager it works like a central coordinator ¥onFileDetected(file) → Detects new/processed files and triggers notifications. 36
Pipes-and-Filters

Extensibility : add new filters easily (a spam filter). Efficiency : filters can run in parallel. Reusability : filters are reused across systems. Modifiability : add, remove or change filters independently. Security : security filters can be inserted anywhere in the chain. Maintainability : independent filters make updates simple. Trade-off: every boundary needs agreed data formats, and the pattern suits batch-like flows, not interactive ones where the user steers the work midway. List three quality properties of the pipes-and-filters pattern. Pipes-and-Filters Architectural Pattern ➢ Quality properties of the Pipes-and- Extra: Filters architectural pattern include the 1. Extensibility Ð Easy to add new filters (e.g., ones specified below. spam filter). 2. Efficiency Ð Filters can run in parallel for faster processing. 3. Reusability Ð Filters can be reused across systems. 4. Modifiability Ð Easy to add/remove/modify filters. 5. Security Ð Security filters can be integrated anywhere. 6. Maintainability Ð Independent filters make updates simple. 37
Distributed Systems

Peer-to-peer : peer nodes with similar capabilities collaborate as equals, e.g. music-sharing applications. The pictures contrast a mesh of peers with a star around one server. Distributed Systems ➢ Distributed systems are decomposed into multiple processes that (typically) collaborate through the network. ¥ In some distributed systems, one or more distributed processes perform work on behalf of client users and provide a bridge to some server computer, typically located remotely and performing work delegated to it by the client part of the system. (client-server) ¥ Other distributed systems may be composed of peer nodes, each with similar capabilities and collaborating together to provide enhanced services, such as music-sharing distributed applications. (peer-to-peer) Peer-to-peer client-server Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 38
Distributed Systems

With multi-core processors , distributed architecture also applies inside a single machine: work is spread across cores instead of computers. Distributed Systems ➢ The previous types of distributed systems are easy to spot, since their deployment architecture entails multiple physical nodes. ➢ However, with the advent of multi-core processors, distributed architectures are also relevant to software that executes on a single node with multiprocessor capability. Extra: Distribution can be across many computers or across many cores(CPUs) in one computer. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 39
Distributed Systems

How does peer-to-peer differ from client–server? Distributed Systems ¥ Some examples of distributed systems include: ¥ Internet systems ¥ Web services ¥ File-or music-sharing systems ¥ High-performance systems, etc. ¥ Common architectural patterns for distributed systems include: ¥ Client-Server Pattern Extra: ¥ Broker Pattern ¥ ClientÐServer: The system has two roles. Clients request services, and a central server (or servers) provides them. Example: a web browser (client) requesting pages from a web server. ¥ Peer-to-Peer (P2P): All nodes act as both clients and servers. They share resources and collaborate without relying on a single central server. Example: music/file-sharing apps like BitTorrent. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 40
Client-Server Pattern

Clients communicate with the server over HTTP ; the server responds with processed data. The box-and-line diagram above shows the same thing as request/response arrows. Client-Server Pattern Server: a computer program or a device that provides functionality for other programs or devices, called "clients". Client: is a piece of computer hardware or software that accesses a service made available by a ÒserverÓ. (Note that multiple clients will communicate with the server. These clients are independent and do not communicate with each other) Extra: 1. Bottom part (UML Deployment Diagram): 1. A deployment diagram shows how software components (artifacts) are deployed on hardware nodes. 2. PC Node runs pc_browser.exe (client application). 3. Mobile Phone Node runs mp_browser.exe (mobile client app). 4. Server Node runs web_server.exe (server app) and pc_browser.exe (server-side browser process). 2. Communication: 1. Clients (PC or Mobile) communicate with the server through HTTP. 2. The server responds back with processed data. Summary: This figure shows a clientÐserver system: PC and mobile clients send requests via HTTP to a web server. The UML deployment diagram maps artifacts (programs) like browser.exe and web_server.exe onto nodes (PC, mobile, server), making it clear where software runs and how they communicate. 41
Client-Server Pattern

Modifiability : changes are made once at the server and reach all clients. A classroom response application allows hundreds of students to submit answers from their phones while an instructor watches the results on a dashboard. Scores and question status must come from one authoritative course session so that every participant sees consistent information. Which architectural style? Client-Server Pattern ➢ Quality properties of the client-Server architectural pattern include the ones specified below. ¥Extra: ¥Interoperability → Clients on different platforms can work with servers on different platforms. ¥Modifiability → Server changes are centralized and easily distributed to many clients. ¥Availability → Backup server nodes increase service and data availability. ¥Reusability → Server services/data can be reused in different applications. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 42
Client-Server Pattern

The main problem: clients are tightly coupled to servers , which becomes complex when services come from many servers in different places. What is the main drawback of client–server that the broker pattern fixes? Clients are tightly coupled to specific servers It cannot store data It needs a blackboard Clients talk to each other Client-Server Pattern ➢ Although Client-Server Pattern supports the quality attributed described in the previous slide it has the following problems: ¥ Clients are tightly coupled with servers. ¥ This leads to complexity for systems that need to provide services from multiple servers hosted at different locations. ¥ Extra: − Client tightly depends(tightly coupled ) on a specific server. − Must know serverÕs exact IP/URL/protocol. − Server changes → client code updates required. − Increases complexity with multiple servers. ¥ To overcome this issue the Broker pattern was introduced. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 43
Broker Pattern

A hospital application sends requests to several types of laboratory equipment supplied by different vendors. Equipment can be replaced or added over time, but the clinical application should continue using the same request format and should not need vendor-specific logic. Which architectural style? Broker Pattern ➢ The Broker architectural pattern provides mechanisms for achieving better flexibility between clients and servers in a distributed environment by acting as an mediator between the two components. ➢ The Broker pattern decreases coupling between client and servers by mediating between them so that one client can transparently access the services of multiple servers Extra: Client-Server versus Broker Client-Server 1. Direct communication between client and server. 2. Client must know serverÕs exact address and protocol. 3. Tightly coupled → server changes require client updates. 4. Simpler but less flexible for scaling or multiple servers. Broker 5. Communication goes through a broker (middleware). 6. Clients donÕt need to know server details, only the broker. 7. Loosely coupled → server changes donÕt affect clients. 8. More scalable, flexible, and supports multiple servers/services. In short: Client-Server = direct & tightly coupled, while Broker = indirect & loosely coupled via a broker. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 44
Broker Pattern

This makes systems more flexible and interoperable . In the diagram the client relies on Broker 1 for services from Server 1, and Broker 1 can talk to Broker 2 to reach Server 2’s services too. Broker Pattern ➢ The broker component is responsible for coordinating communication between a client and server(s), such as forwarding requests, as well as for transmitting results and exceptions. ¥ Leads to systems that are more flexible and interoperable. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 45
Broker Pattern components

Client : uses services of one or more servers. Provides nothing; requires the client proxy. Client proxy : makes remote components look local to the client (transparency). Provides a local service to the client; requires the broker. Server proxy : makes remote components look local on the server side. Provides a local service to the broker; requires the server. Bridge (optional): connects different brokers so they can interoperate. List the components of the broker pattern in the order a request passes through them. Broker Pattern Extra: ➢ The Broker architectural pattern ➢ includes the following components: ¥Extra: ¥ Client ➢ Provided Interface: None ➢ Required Interface: Services from ClientProxy ¥ ClientProxy ➢ Provided Interface: Local service to Client ➢ Required Interface: Broker ¥ Broker ➢ Provided Interface: Mediation service to ClientProxy ➢ Required Interface: ServerProxy ¥ ServerProxy ➢ Provided Interface: Local service to Broker ➢ Required Interface: Server ¥ Server ➢ Provided Interface: Real application services (exposed through Broker/ServerProxy to clients) ➢ Required Interface: Broker (if the server acts as a client to another service) 46 ¥ Bridge ➢ Provided Interface: Interoperability between different Brokers ➢ Required Interface: Other Brokers
Broker Pattern

The pattern separates communication functionality from application functionality : everything about networks and messages sits in the broker and proxies, so clients and servers contain only application logic. Reading the detailed class diagram: Client-side proxy packData() , unpackData() , sendRequest() , return() : marshals requests into messages and results back out. Broker registerService() , findServer() , findClient() , forwardRequest() , forwardResponse() : knows where services are and routes messages. Server-side proxy packData() , unpackData() , callService() , sendResponse() : calls the real service. Client / Server / Bridge The client calls callServer() via the broker API; the server registerService() s and runService() s; the bridge transmits messages between brokers. The client side proxy decides if the request can be resolved locally or to forward the request to the broker Broker Pattern ➢ Separates system communication functionality from the main application functionality by providing a broker that isolates communication-related concerns. Detailed Broker Pattern Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 47
Broker Pattern

Which is a quality property of the broker pattern? Interoperability across platforms Tighter client–server coupling No need for middleware Guaranteed fastest performance Broker Pattern ➢ Quality properties of the Broker architectural pattern include the ones specified below. Extra: ¥Interoperability → Clients can work with servers across different platforms and multiple servers. ¥Modifiability → Centralized server changes can be quickly distributed to many clients. ¥Portability → Broker can be ported to different platforms, making services easily accessible to new clients. ¥Reusability → Brokers handle system calls, enabling reuse of complex services in other applications. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 48
Summary

Summary ➢ Data-Centered Systems − Blackboard pattern ➢ Data Flow Systems − Pipes-and-Filters pattern ➢ Distributed Systems − Client Server pattern − Broker pattern ➢ WhatÕs nextÉ − Interactive Systems − Hierarchical Systems Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 50

decks.t: Interactive and Hierarchical Systems: Model-View-Controller and Layered
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 4 · Lecture 3: Interactive and Hierarchical Systems: Model-View-Controller and Layered
n: Slide 1

Final architecture-patterns lecture: the patterns for interactive systems (MVC) and hierarchical systems (layered). After this, the course moves from architecture to detailed design. Software Design and Architecture [Architecture Patterns] – Chapter 04, L03
Lecture Outlines

Lecture Outlines ➢Interactive Systems ✓Overview ✓Patterns: Model-View-Controller (MVC). ➢Hierarchical Systems ✓Overview ✓Patterns: −Layered Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Interactive Systems

Two quality attributes matter most: usability (the UI must be easy to use) and modifiability (UIs change often, so changing them must be cheap). The mainstream pattern for interactive systems is MVC , because it isolates the part that changes most (the UI) from the data and rules. Interactive Systems ➢Interactive systems support user interactions, typically through user interfaces. ✓ When designing these systems, two main quality attributes are of interest: − Usability − Modifiability ➢The mainstream architectural pattern employed in most interactive systems is the Model- View-Controller (MVC). Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Interactive Systems

MVC is for interactive applications that need flexible human-computer interfaces: the UI can be replaced or multiplied without touching the core. The three component types (the table): Model Represents the system’s core: its major processing capabilities and data. View The output representation of the system (graphical or console-based). Controller Associated with a view; handles user input. In MVC, which component handles user input? Controller Model View Broker Interactive Systems ➢The MVC pattern is used in interactive applications that require flexible incorporation of human-computer interfaces. With the MVC, systems are decomposed into three main types of components: Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Extra: MVC inside a mobile app

The same app is also part of a distributed system: the mobile client sends requests (login, messages, balance) through APIs to a server that applies business rules and uses a database. Summary: MVC inside the app, client–server outside it. Patterns combine at different levels. Extra: Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL

The motivating example: the same core data is shown in different formats (line chart, bar chart, pie chart, table). Each is a different representation of one data set. When the data changes, all views must update to reflect it. MVC achieves that by keeping one model and letting every view observe it, instead of each view keeping its own copy that could drift. Which pattern best fits an app that shows the same data in several synchronised views that the user can edit? MVC Pipes and filters Blackboard Broker MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN

Model : holds the core data and system functionality; when the data changes, it updates (notifies) the views. In the box-and-line diagram one model sits under all the views and controllers. Safari Explorer: a mobile app helps preschoolers (ages 3–5) learn about animals and their sounds. It must be highly responsive to touch and visually engaging. It has a Database with animal names, image file paths and audio clips, an Interactive Map (the graphical world map of animals), and a Selection Handler that detects a tap on a continent or animal and decides what to display next. Identify the architecture pattern that fits and draw its component diagram. MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN Extra: 1.Model Example Scenario: User Updates Their Profile Name 1. Holds core data and system functionality. 1.User action (input) 2. When data changes, it updates the Views. 1. The user types a new name and clicks Save. 2.View 2. This action goes to the Controller. 1. Displays information to the user. 2.Controller 2. Each View is linked with a Controller. 1. The Controller receives the input (new name). 3.Controller 2. It translates the input into a request to update the Model. 1. Receives user input. 3.Model 2. Translates input into service requests for the Model. 1. The Model updates the user’s name in its data. 4.Flow of interaction 2. After updating, the Model notifies the View that data has changed. 1. User interacts with Controller. 4.View 2. Controller updates the Model. 1. The View retrieves the updated data from the Model. 3. Model notifies and updates the View. 2. It refreshes the screen to display the new name. 4. View presents the updated information back to the user. Flow summary: In short: Controller handles input → Model updates data → View shows User → Controller → Model → View → User (cycle continues for next action 7 s). changes.
MVC for the real-estate system

MVC for a real-estate system with two very different interfaces (not a UML diagram). The model in the middle holds the real-estate data and the core functionality. Two controllers translate input into the same kind of service request, sendCommand(FIND, 5FH, 33803) : on the very large screen, a controller uses hand-gesture recognition ; on the small screen (no room for buttons), a controller uses speech recognition (“Find single family home in Lakeland, FL”). Each view is updated to display the results of the service request: two views of the same data. Adding a third interface would mean adding a view–controller pair, without touching the model. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
Extra: Explanation of the System

Extra: Explanation of the System: 1. User Large Screen: Uses hand gestures to navigate or control options. Small Screen: Uses voice commands due to limited space. 2. Controller Role: Connects View and Model. Task: Converts user input (gestures/voice) into actions like fetching or filtering property data. 3. Model Role: Stores real estate data (properties, prices, locations). Task: Provides data to the View and updates based on Controller requests. 4. View Role: Shows information to the user. Task: Updates display dynamically based on user actions (gestures/voice). In short: User → Controller → Model → View → User (with gestures/voice as inputs). Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN

In the real-estate MVC component diagram, why does the model provide IObservable while each view provides IObserver? MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN Extra: 1.RealEstateModel (Model) Central data component storing real estate information. Exposes IObservable for updates and IModel for data access. 2.Controllers SbController (SmartBoard Controller): Handles pen/gesture input via IPenController. SpeechController: Handles voice commands via ISpeechController. Both translate user input into actions on the RealEstateModel (through IModel). 3.Views SmartBoardView: Displays info for large-screen (gesture/pen-based). PCView: Displays info for smaller screen (voice-based). Both register as IObservers to the RealEstateModel, so they update automatically when the Model changes. Note:View requires the Model (to get the data). But the Model also requires View (to send updates). So, both provide and require exist at the same time because of the two-way dependency created by the Observer pattern. 4.Communication Flow User interacts → Controller (pen or speech). Controller updates the RealEstateModel. Model notifies Views via IObserver. Views refresh to display updated real estate data. In short: User input → Controller → RealEstateModel → Views (auto-updated via Observer pattern). Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
MVC: real-estate sequence diagram

RealEstateModel : processCommand() handles the FIND command, update() changes its internal state (and notifies views), getResults() is how views fetch the search results (messages 10–12). Application (set-up, messages 1–5): creates the model, the speech-customised view and the voice controller, and attach(aView) es the view to the model. User : onVoiceInput("find single family homes in Lakeland, FL") starts the interaction (message 7). Reading order: set-up, then input → controller → model → view. SpeechController Class Methods: • processSpeech()(called when voice input is received) • sendCommand(FIND_CMD, 5FH, 33803)(sends parsed command to model) RealEstateModel Class Methods: • processCommand()(processes the FIND command) • update()(updates internal state) • getResults()(retrieves search results) PCView Class Methods: •show()(called twice - displays the view) •Internally enables voice input mode(not a method call, but internal state change) Application Class Methods: •new Model()(constructor) •new SpeechCustomizedViewModel()(constructor) •new VoiceController()(constructor) •attach(aView)(attaches view) External/User: •onVoiceInput("find single family homes in Lakeland, FL")(this is the user/system calling the controller's input handler) 11
MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN

The quality properties table: modifiability (easy to exchange, enhance or add user interfaces), usability (because UIs are exchangeable, systems can be configured with different interfaces for different groups of users), reusability (with concerns separated, model, view and controller components can be reused in other systems). MVC has many variations : Microsoft’s 1990s Document-View architecture fused view and controller into one component; presentation-abstraction-control is a more extensive variant (the slide calls it “process-abstraction-controller”). Remember the three qualities as the payoff of separating the UI: change it, tailor it, reuse the parts. The cost is more objects and update paths, which isn’t worth it for a trivial static screen. True or false: MVC lets the user interface change without changing the model. MODEL-VIEW-CONTROLLER ARCHITECTURAL PATTERN ➢Quality properties of the MVC architectural pattern include the ones specified below. ➢There are many variations of the MVC architectural pattern. ✓One popular variation includes the fusion of views and controller components, as made famous in the 1990s by Microsoft’s Document-View architecture ✓Other more extensive variations include the process-abstraction-controller pattern. Extra: Modifiability- Easy to exchange or enhance user interfaces Usability- Configure different UIs for different customer needs Reusability- Model, View, and Controller components can be reused in other systems Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
Hierarchical Systems

Two common patterns: main program and subroutine (a main routine calls subroutines, which call lower ones) and layered . This lecture covers layered. Hierarchical Systems ➢Hierarchical systems can be decomposed and structured in hierarchical fashion. Two common architectural patterns for hierarchical systems are: ✓Main program and subroutine ✓Layered Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
Extra: Hierarchal Systems

The diagram: a top-level module (highest abstraction) uses intermediate modules (middle layer), which use low-level modules (base operations). Calls go downward; higher levels never need to know how lower ones work. Extra: Hierarchal Systems •Description: These systems are structured in layers, each layer having a specific role or responsibility, allowing for the separation of concerns across a vertical (layered) or horizontal (module) scale. •Example: •Operating systems where different layers handle tasks ranging from hardware interaction at the lowest level to user interface management at the highest level. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
Layered Pattern

Modifiability : dependencies stay local within a layer; components only reach others through a well-defined, unified interface, so a layer component can be swapped for an enhanced one. Portability : everything that touches the platform’s APIs is encapsulated in one layer; port that layer and the higher layers move to the new platform unchanged. Security : the controlled hierarchy makes it easy to insert security components, e.g. a layer that encrypts and decrypts all incoming and outgoing data. A payroll application must allow the user interface, salary-calculation rules, and data-storage technology to evolve with minimal impact on one another. For example, replacing the database should not require rewriting payroll policies, and interface code should not contain persistence logic. Which architectural style? Layered Pattern ➢Quality properties of the Layered architectural pattern include the ones specified below. Extra: Modifiability- Easy to swap layer components through defined interfaces Portability- Encapsulate platform APIs for easier cross-platform migration Security- Easy to add security components in controlled hierarchical structure Reusability- Compartmentalized layer services are easier to reuse Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
Layered Pattern

A layered remote-monitoring system, top to bottom. SatcomLayer handles satellite communication; it provides ISatcom to the outside. HardwareLayer controls the physical devices and sensors; it provides IHardware . In the UML diagram each layer requires exactly the interface of the layer below; the subsystem’s external ports (IMonitorPlan, INodeMonitor) are delegated to the top and bottom layers. Each extra layer adds a call, which is the pattern’s performance cost. In a strict layered architecture, which layers may a layer use, and what is the main drawback? Layered Pattern SatcomLayer Component •Purpose:Handles satellite communication functions •Interface:IJSatcom (provides satellite communication services to other layers) SecurityLayer Component •Purpose:Manages security and encryption functions •Interface:IJSecure (provides security services, requires application services) ApplicationLayer Component •Purpose:Contains main application logic and business rules •Interface:IApplication (provides application services, requires hardware access) HardwareLayer Component •Purpose:Controls physical hardware devices and sensors •Interface:IHardware (provides hardware access, requires monitoring services) Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 16
What’s next

This completes the architectural patterns: blackboard, pipes and filters, client–server, broker, MVC and layered . WHAT’S NEXT… ➢• In this session, we continued the discussion on distributed systems and presented fundamentals concepts of interactive and hierarchical systems, together with essential architectural patterns for these systems, including: ✓MVC ✓ Layered ➢This finalizes our coverage of architectural patterns. In the next module, we start the discussion on detailed design, which is the next activity in the design process. Detailed design begins once the architecture of the software is sufficiently complete. Dr. Banda Ramadan | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17

decks.t: Principles of Detailed Design I: What Detailed Design Is and Its Key Tasks
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 1: Principles of Detailed Design I: What Detailed Design Is and Its Key Tasks
n: Slide 1

Chapter 5 moves from architecture to detailed design , the second major design activity. Lecture 1 explains what it is and the tasks it involves; Lectures 2 and 3 cover the principles (SOLID) used to judge a detailed design. Software Design and Architecture [Principles of Detailed Design] – Chapter 05, L01
Lecture Outlines

First: what detailed design is and where it fits in the life cycle. Then its five key tasks, each on its own slide (7–13). Lecture Outlines ➢Overview of Detailed Design ✓What is detailed design? ✓Where does it fit? ➢Key Tasks in Detailed Design ✓Understanding architecture and requirements – (chapters 3 & 4) ✓Creating detailed designs ✓Evaluating detailed designs ✓Documenting detailed designs ✓Monitoring and controlling implementation 2 Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides
Where we are: from requirements to construction

Detailed design : break the architecture into smaller components and detailed functions, e.g. for login, specify password validation, authentication and session management. The diagram marks this “we are here”: design shifts from a macro approach to a micro one, decomposing components into fine-grained elements, functions and data. Lets think about, where we are … Extra: 1. Start (Requirements Phase): Gather and document what the system must do. Example: In a banking app, users must be able to check balances or transfer money. 2. Architecture (High-Level Design): Define the overall structure and interactions of the system. Example: Decide the system will use a client-server model with a database, app, and security layer. 3. Detailed Design (Refinement): Break down architecture into smaller components and detailed functions. Example: For login, specify password validation, authentication, and session management. 4. Goal (Construction Phase): Start coding based on the detailed design. Example: Implement login, account management, and transfer features. 3
What is Detailed Design?

Designers go deep into each component to define its internal structure and behaviour , so that construction becomes natural and efficient. Structure = how the component is built inside; behaviour = how it acts and reacts in different scenarios. Detailed design produces specifications, algorithms, database schemas, interface definitions and class diagrams, but no code yet . Login example: password rules (minimum length, special characters), hashing plus salting for authentication, session timeout and refresh tokens. It is the blueprint before building. What is the primary focus of “Detailed Design”? External properties of software components and non-functional requirements. The overall development process for both hardware and software. The internals of system components and their behavior to fulfill functional requirements. Project management tasks like staffing and tracking. What is Detailed Design? Extra: ➢ Detailed design is: 1. What is Detailed Design?

Detailed design sits between architecture and construction , so detailed designers need a full understanding of both the requirements and the architecture they are refining. Designers must also be proficient in design strategies (e.g. object-oriented), programming languages, and quality-control methods, because their output must be directly implementable. Detailed design provides the bridge between: Design and code Requirements and architecture Testing and deployment Users and managers What is Detailed Design? Detailed design is closely related to architecture and construction; therefore successful designers (during detailed design) are required to have or acquire full understanding of the system’s requirements and architecture. ✓Just as architecture provides the bridge between requirements and design, detailed design provides the bridge between design and code. ✓They must also be proficient in particular design strategies (e.g., object-oriented), programming languages, and methods and processes for software quality control. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Designer’s Mental Model During Detailed Design

Forward : given requirements and architecture, detailed designers must move the project all the way to code (the funnel: requirements/architecture → detailed design → code). Reverse engineering means analysing existing code to recover what the system does, how it is structured, and how it maps back to design and requirements (useful for legacy systems and maintenance). Designer’s Mental Model During Detailed design Extra: • Detailed design sits between requirements/architecture and code. •If you are given requirements + architecture, you must design details until you reach code. •If you are given code, you should be able to go backwards (reverse engineer) to recreate the detailed design and architecture. • So detailed designers need to think in both directions → from design to code, and from code back to design. • Tools (like UML modeling, code generators, compilers, and version control) are essential in this stage. • What is Reverse Engineering? Reverse engineering = analyzing existing code to figure out: • what the system does, • how it is structured, 6 • and how it maps back to design and requirements.
Key Tasks in Detailed Design

1. Understand the architecture and the requirements allocated to your components (slide 8). 2. Create the detailed designs: interfaces, GUI, internal structure and behaviour, data (slide 9). 3. Evaluate them, mainly through technical reviews (slide 10). 4. Document them, mainly in the SDD (slides 11–12). 5. Monitor and control implementation , keeping code and design in sync (slide 13). The tasks form a loop: a review or a coding discovery can send you back to an earlier task. List the five key tasks of detailed design.
