decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 2: Principles of Detailed Design II: Component Design, SRP, OCP and LSP
n: Software Design and Architecture: Principles of Detailed Design
This is the second lecture of Chapter 5. Lecture 1 described the detailed design process; this one is about the principles that make a detailed design good: easy to change, reuse and test.
Lecture Outlines

Internal structure means which classes and interfaces a component contains and how they relate. It is drawn with class diagrams. SOLID is five principles. Only the first three (S, O, L) are taught in this lecture; slide 39 moves I and D to the next one. Internal behavior (what the classes do at run time, drawn with sequence or state diagrams) is also left for the next lecture.
Overview of Component Design

Component design is the part of detailed design that opens each component up. Structure is what it is made of (classes, attributes, interfaces); behavior is how those parts act to deliver the component’s services. It does not invent new top-level components. It refines the ones the architect already chose, so every class you design belongs to one architectural component. In an object-oriented system each component’s inside is usually shown with one or more class diagrams. A large component may need several.
Overview of Component Design

How to read the top diagram (architecture view): ClientSystem, ServerSystem UML components: boxes with the small component icon. They are black boxes at this stage. Ball-and-socket on ServerInterface The circle (ball) is the interface ServerSystem provides ; the half-circle (socket) is what ClientSystem requires . Joined, they mean the client uses that service. The bottom diagram is the same two components after detailed design: they are opened up to show the classes inside. Client A class inside ClientSystem. «interface» ServerInterface The provided interface, now an actual interface type inside ServerSystem. The dashed arrow with an open arrowhead from Client to ServerInterface is a dependency : Client calls the interface and never names the concrete class. The dashed line with a hollow triangle from ConcreteServer to ServerInterface is realization : ConcreteServer implements the interface. Another class could replace it and Client would not change. The takeaway box says it in one line: in detailed design you stop thinking in components and start thinking in classes, interfaces and types.
Overview of Component Design

Four things are decided in component design. Data structures say how information is stored. Algorithms say how results are computed. Interface details are the exact method names, parameters and return types. Communication mechanisms say how components talk: direct calls, messages or events. That makes component design the place where functional correctness is won or lost. Architecture can be perfect, but if the algorithm or the data passed between classes is wrong, the system still gives wrong answers. In the payment example the three classes must agree on details like the order of operations (discount before tax?) and the number format. Only then is the total right for every valid input. Those agreements are exactly what component design writes down.
Overview of Component Design

Because component design fixes the actual logic, it is a major factor in whether the system does what users need. The four object-oriented ideas a component designer must be fluent in. Slides 7–14 refresh each one: Class / object A class is the blueprint; an object is one instance created from it at run time. Abstract class / interface Types that define a contract other classes must complete or implement. Inheritance A subclass reuses and specializes a parent (“is-a”). Polymorphism One call, such as animal.sound() , runs different code depending on the actual object.
What Is Abstract Class?

An abstract class is declared with the abstract keyword. It can mix abstract methods (a signature with no body) and concrete methods (normal methods with code). The slide’s definition requires at least one abstract method. Java itself also accepts an abstract class with none, but answer with the slide’s definition in the exam. Any concrete (non-abstract) subclass must give a body to every abstract method it inherits. If it doesn’t, it must be declared abstract too. “Cannot be instantiated” means new Animal() is a compile error when Animal is abstract. You can still declare a variable of that type: Animal a = new Cat(); . The four reasons all come down to sharing: common code lives once in the parent (default functionality, reuse), and the abstract methods fix a common set of operations every subclass must offer (template, common interface). Reading the small diagram: Top box «abstract» The abstract class. It holds an abstract method (italic) and + concreteMethod() , which has a body. Arrow to ConcreteClass ConcreteClass derives from it and supplies + abstractMethod() . The slide draws the arrow downward; standard UML points a hollow triangle from the subclass up to the parent. True or false: an abstract class can contain concrete methods, and it can be instantiated with new .
What is Interface?

An interface is a pure contract: it lists method signatures and no code. The slide says no concrete methods at all. Modern Java also allows default and static methods, but for this course an interface has only abstract methods. You cannot write new AnimalInterface() . You create an object of a class that implements it and refer to it through the interface type. Interfaces hold no instance variables (no per-object state). The only fields allowed are constants: public static final . Benefits: loose coupling , because callers depend on the contract and not on a specific class. Dynamic method resolution : at run time Java runs the method of the actual object behind the interface. It also lets unrelated classes share a capability outside one inheritance tree, since a Java class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. Give two differences between an abstract class and an interface (as defined in this course).
Further reading

Further reading on when to choose an interface or an abstract class in Java. Further reading on UML relationships. The #4 anchor jumps to the section on generalization and realization, the two arrows used on slides 10–12.
Refresh your memory … OOP concepts (Interface)

The code, line by line: Code What it does public interface AnimalInterface { Declares a contract named AnimalInterface. public void sound(); A required method: signature only, ending in ; , with no body. public void drawe (); A second required method (spelled “drawe” on the slide). } End of the contract. public class Cat implements AnimalInterface{ implements promises that Cat supplies a body for every method in the interface. public void sound(){ System.out.println("Miaw"); } Cat’s own version of sound(): prints Miaw. public void eat(){ System.out.println("Cat is eating fish!"); } Cat’s eat() body. Watch the mismatch: the interface asks for drawe() , but Cat provides eat() . As printed, Java would reject Cat (“does not override abstract method drawe()”). The UML on the right shows what was intended: the interface has sound() and eat() . Reading the UML: «interface» Animal The stereotype in guillemets marks the box as an interface. Horse, Cat Classes that each provide + sound() and + eat() . Dashed lines with a hollow triangle Realization : the triangle points at the interface each class implements. Which UML notation shows that class Cat implements interface Animal?
Refresh your memory … OOP concepts (Abstract Classes)

The code, line by line: Code What it does public abstract class Animal { An abstract class: it can’t be instantiated. public abstract void sound(); Abstract method: no body, and every concrete subclass must implement it. public void eat() { System.out.println("Animal is eating.."); } Concrete method: inherited as-is unless a subclass overrides it. public class Cat extends Animal { extends = inherits from Animal (a Java class can extend only one class). public void sound(){ System.out.println("Miaw"); } Required: fills in the abstract sound(). public void eat(){ System.out.println("Cat is eating fish!"); } Optional: overrides the inherited eat() with Cat’s version. In UML, italics carry meaning: the class name Animal in italics means abstract class, and sound() in italics means abstract operation. eat() is upright because it has a body. Notation trap: the slide calls the dashed arrows “Realization”. Standard UML uses realization (dashed line, hollow triangle) for implementing an interface , and generalization (solid line, hollow triangle) for extending a class , abstract or not. In an exam, draw extends with a solid line and say why. A class Dog extends an abstract class Animal. Which UML line connects them, and how is Animal’s name written?
Refresh your memory … OOP concepts (Inheritance)

Here Animal is an ordinary (concrete) class, so every method already has a body: Code What it does public class Animal { A normal class: it can be instantiated. public void sound(){ ..."Animal is making a sound"... } Default sound(). public void eat(){ ..."Animal is eating.."... } Default eat(). public class Horse extends Animal{ Horse is-a Animal. @Override public void sound(){ ..."Neigh"... } @Override asks the compiler to check that a matching parent method exists, which catches typos. @Override public void eat(){ ..."Horse is eating hay!"... } Horse’s own eat(). public class Cat extends Animal{ ...sound "Miaw", eat "Cat is eating fish!" } Cat overrides both methods the same way. Unlike slide 11, nothing forces the subclasses to override: they could inherit Animal’s versions unchanged. Overriding is a choice here, not a requirement. The UML shows generalization : solid lines meeting at one hollow triangle that points at the parent, Animal. Read it as “Horse is an Animal” and “Cat is an Animal”.
Refresh your memory … OOP concepts (Inheritance)

The demo creates one object of each class and calls both methods: Code What it does Animal a = new Animal(); a.sound(); a.eat(); Prints “Animal is making a sound” then “Animal is eating..”. Horse h = new Horse(); h.sound(); h.eat(); Prints “Neigh” then “Horse is eating hay!”. Cat c = new Cat(); c.sound(); c.eat(); Prints “Miaw” then “Cat is eating fish!”. The output panel on the right confirms each object runs the version defined in its own class. Every variable here has the same type as its object, so this is plain inheritance. Slide 14 shows what changes when the types differ.
Refresh your memory … OOP concepts (Polymorphism )

The variables are declared as Animal but hold a Horse and a Cat: Code What it does Animal ah = new Horse(); Declared type Animal, actual object Horse. This is allowed because a Horse is an Animal. ah.sound(); ah.eat(); Prints “Neigh” and “Horse is eating hay!”: the HORSE’s versions, not Animal’s. Animal ac = new Cat(); Same idea with a Cat. ac.sound(); ac.eat(); Prints “Miaw” and “Cat is eating fish!”. This is polymorphism (dynamic binding) . The declared type (Animal) decides which methods you are allowed to call; the actual object (Horse or Cat) decides which code runs. The choice happens at run time. Why it matters for this lecture: OCP (slides 22–31) works because a GameEngine holding a Character reference can call move() and get each character’s own movement without knowing its class. Animal x = new Cat(); x.sound(); What is printed, and what is this mechanism called?
Design Principles of Internal Component Design
SOLID is the acronym for the five principles: S ingle Responsibility, O pen-Closed, L iskov Substitution, I nterface Segregation, D ependency Inversion. S, O and L are covered in this lecture.
1- Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

The common misreading: “every module should do just one thing.” That is good advice for small functions, but it is not what SRP says. SRP is about who causes change. A module should answer to one actor (a user group, stakeholder or policy). Equivalently, a class has one reason to change. If the accountants and the IT team could each force edits to the same class, it has two responsibilities. State the Single Responsibility Principle and explain what “reason to change” means.
SRP - example

The code (TypeScript-style), line by line: Code What it does class Person { Represents a person. public name : string; public surname : string; public email : string; Person data: three text fields. constructor(name, surname, email){ Runs when a Person is created. this.surname = surname; this.name = name; Stores the names. if(this.validateEmail(email)) { this.email = email; } Checks the address format before storing it. else { throw new Error("Invalid email!"); } Rejects a bad address by throwing an error. validateEmail(email : string) { Email-format rule, living inside Person (the boxed part on the slide). var re = /^([\w-]+(?:\.[\w-]+)*)@(...)/; A regular expression describing a valid address. return re.test(email); } True if the address matches the pattern. greet() { alert("Hi!"); } Genuine person behavior. The boxed lines show the violation: Person now has two reasons to change. Its fields change when what a person is changes; validateEmail changes when the email rules change (new domains, longer TLDs). You also can’t test the email rule without building a Person.
SRP - example

The refactoring moves validation into its own class: Code What it does class Email { New class that owns everything about an email address. constructor(email){ if(this.validateEmail(email)) {...} else { throw ... } } An Email object can only exist if the address is valid. validateEmail(email){ ... return re.test(email); } The same rule, now in its only home. class Person { Back to pure person data and behavior. public email : Email; The field’s type is now Email, not string. constructor(name, surname, email : Email){ this.email = email; ... } Person receives an already-validated Email, so no check is needed. greet() { alert("Hi!"); } Unchanged. Each class now has one reason to change: email-rule changes touch only Email, and person changes touch only Person. A class with one responsibility (one actor) is also easier to read, test and extend.
SRP: does every function need its own class?

The violating Employee class stores data, calculates taxes and prints pay stubs. Three different things can force edits: the data structure, the tax laws and the print format. The SRP version keeps only the employee data in Employee. Tax calculation and pay-stub printing move to their own classes, so Employee changes only when the data changes. The slide’s question has a clear answer, given on slide 20: no . SRP does not mean one class per function.
SRP Applies to Responsibilities, Not Methods

A responsibility is usually carried out by several related methods working together. SRP limits the number of responsibilities, not the number of methods. TaxCalculator has three methods but one responsibility, tax calculation. The table adds two more good examples: UserAuthentication (login state, four methods) and ProductValidator (product data correctness, three methods). The test for splitting: if you change method A, would you also have to change method B? If yes, they belong together (both tax methods change with tax law). If no, they belong in separate classes ( calculateTax and printToPDF ).
In Class Exercises

Three requirements means three potential reasons to change: pay rules, storage technology and report format. Question 1, a design that violates SRP (one class does everything): Employee - id, name, baseSalary + calculateSalary(): double + saveToDatabase(): void + generateReport(): String Question 2, the SRP redesign. Employee keeps the data; each job gets its own class, and each one depends on (uses) Employee: Employee - id, name, baseSalary (data only) SalaryCalculator + calculateSalary(e: Employee): double EmployeeRepository + save(e: Employee): void EmployeeReportGenerator + generate(e: Employee): String all three - - -> Employee (dependency) NextGen Library: a junior developer put fee calculation, book data and report formatting into one BookManager class. Which detailed-design principle is violated? Draw a class diagram that fixes it.
2- The Open-Closed Principle (OCP)

OCP is what lets a system keep growing for years without every new feature breaking old ones. “Open to extension” means you can add new behavior. “Closed for modification” means code that already works and is tested stays as it is. There is no contradiction: the system still changes, but by adding classes (a new subclass, a new implementation) that plug into existing abstractions. No working code has to be edited for that. Explain how a design can be both “open for extension” and “closed for modification”.
The Open-Close Principle

The scenario matters: several kinds of characters exist, and more will be added . A change is expected, so the design must be ready for it. Reading the diagram: GameEngine Has one operation, add(pCharacter: TerrestrialCharacter*) . The * is a C++ pointer. Dashed arrow A dependency: GameEngine uses TerrestrialCharacter directly. TerrestrialCharacter A concrete class with draw() and run() . Why it violates OCP: GameEngine names a concrete class. Every new kind of character (one that flies, one that swims) forces a change to GameEngine, the code that already works.
The Open-Close Principle: the add() code

The C++ code, line by line: Code What it does class TerrestrialCharacter { A character that moves over land. virtual void draw() { ... } virtual = subclasses may override it, and the call is resolved at run time. virtual void run() { ... } Land movement. class GameEngine { Manages the game. void add(TerrestrialCharacter* pCharacter) { Accepts only terrestrial characters. pCharacter->draw(); -> calls a method through a pointer: show the character. pCharacter->run(); Make it move by running. add(...) is hard-wired to one concrete type and one way of moving ( run ). An AerialCharacter that flies doesn’t fit: it isn’t a TerrestrialCharacter and has no run() . Supporting it means editing add(...) , which is working code. That edit is the OCP violation.
The Open-Close Principle (OCP)

The fix students should propose: introduce an abstraction (an interface or abstract class) named Character with the operations every character has, and make GameEngine depend on Character instead of on a concrete class. Slides 26–29 show how a first attempt still goes wrong, and then the correct version.
The Open-Closed Principle (OCP): first attempt

Joe’s first attempt (C++): Code What it does class Character { virtual string getType() = 0; virtual void draw() = 0; }; = 0 makes a method pure virtual (abstract). A class with only pure virtual methods acts as an interface. class AerialCharacter : public Character { : public Character = inherits from (realizes) Character. getType() { return "aerial"; } draw() {...} fly() {...} Reports its type, draws itself, and has its own fly() . class TerrestrialCharacter : public Character { Same shape: getType() { return "terrestrial"; } draw() {...} run() {...} its own run() . Joe abstracted the drawing, but movement was left to each subtype under different names ( fly , run ). Character itself has no movement operation. The getType() method is the warning sign: a caller that has to ask “what type are you?” is about to branch on the answer. Slide 27 shows that branch.
The Open-Closed Principle (OCP): GameEngine with type checks

GameEngine.add with Joe’s design: Code What it does void add( Character* pCharacter ) { Now takes any Character, which is better. pCharacter->draw(); Drawing works for every character. if( pCharacter->getType().compare("aerial") == 0 ) { Asks for the type string. AerialCharacter* pAerial = dynamic_cast<AerialCharacter*>(pCharacter); dynamic_cast = a checked downcast to the concrete type. pAerial->fly(); } Only then can it call fly(). else { TerrestrialCharacter* pTerrestrial = dynamic_cast<...>(pCharacter); Otherwise assume terrestrial… pTerrestrial->run(); } …and run. test driver: TerrestrialCharacter madRabbit; AerialCharacter killerBee; engine.add(&madRabbit); engine.add(&killerBee); Prints: drawing terrestrial / running / drawing aerial / flying. Encapsulate variation: the part that changes (how each character moves) should be hidden behind one stable operation. Here it leaks into GameEngine as an if/else that “will always vary” with the set of characters. It runs correctly, but it still violates OCP: adding an AquaticCharacter means editing add() again with another branch and another cast.
The Open-Closed Principle (OCP): one move() for all

The fix: put one movement operation, move() , into Character itself ( virtual void move() = 0 ). “How it moves” becomes each subtype’s private business. Each subtype implements the full contract: AerialCharacter draw() draws it, move() makes it fly. TerrestialCharacter (sic) draw() draws it, move() makes it run.
The Open-Closed Principle (OCP): the redesign

Reading the new diagram (left) against the old one (right): GameEngine - - -> «interface» Character GameEngine depends only on the interface. The italic +draw() and +move() are abstract operations. Aerial / Terrestrial / AquaticCharacter Each realizes Character (dashed line, hollow triangle) and implements both operations. Old design GameEngine depended on the concrete TerrestrialCharacter. AquaticCharacter is added by writing one new class . GameEngine, Character and the existing characters are not touched. That is OCP. add() now just calls draw() and move() ; polymorphism (slide 14) runs the right movement. The same design in Java: interface Character { void draw(); void move(); } class AquaticCharacter implements Character { public void draw() { /* draw a fish */ } public void move() { /* swim */ } } class GameEngine { // never changes void add(Character c) { c.draw(); c.move(); } }
The Open-Closed Principle (OCP)

OCP is a direction, not an absolute. Something always has to be edited: a factory, a configuration or a list of characters. The skill is to predict where change is likely (new character types, new salary types, new payment methods), hide that variation behind an abstraction, and let polymorphism pick the implementation.
Exercise

Model answer: make the varying part (how a salary is computed) an interface, so a new salary type is a new class. «interface» SalaryPolicy + calculate(e: Employee): double MonthlySalary, HourlySalary, WeeklySalary - - -|> SalaryPolicy (realization) SalaryCalculator (never edited) + calculateSalary(e: Employee, p: SalaryPolicy): double New CommissionSalary = one new class that implements SalaryPolicy. NextGen Library (physical books now, E-books soon): by applying the Open/Closed Principle for E-books, draw the class diagram.
3- The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

The “implied contract” is everything callers rely on: the method names and types, but also the behavior (what the method promises to do and what it requires before it is called). If code works with a parent object, it must keep working when you hand it a child object instead. The slide calls this the “treat alike” rule. Two requirements: the method signatures stay compatible, and anything you could conclude from the parent’s specification must still hold for the subtype. State the Liskov Substitution Principle in one sentence.
The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

Signature rule: if a program type-checks against the parent’s methods, it type-checks with the child too (same methods with compatible parameters and return types). The compiler mostly enforces this. Methods rule: reasoning about a call stays valid even though the child’s code runs. If move() promises “moves over land”, every override must still move over land. The compiler can’t check this, so the designer must. The plain-language version: a child class must work anywhere the parent works, without anything breaking. Which LSP rule does the compiler NOT check for you, and why?
The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) - example

The code and its contract: Code What it does class TerrestrialCharacter : public Character { The parent. // Pre-Condition: Character is drawn on screen. What must be true before calling move() . // Post-Condition: Character roams around randomly over land... What move() promises: it stays on land, walking or running. virtual void move() { //code to make the character walk or run } Honors the promise. class EntryLevelTerrestrialCharacter : public TerrestrialCharacter { A “kind of” terrestrial character. virtual void move() { // code to make the character fly. } Overrides move() to FLY. Answer: no, it violates LSP. It compiles (signature rule OK) but breaks the postcondition “roams over land”. Code that relies on terrestrial characters staying on the ground, such as collision with water or bridges, misbehaves when given this subclass. The lesson in red: OCP alone isn’t enough. The class was added by extension (OCP satisfied), yet the design is wrong because the subtype isn’t substitutable. A similar trap is a subclass whose move() throws an exception (“Ghosts don’t move!”): that also breaks the contract. A subclass compiles and overrides every method, but one override throws UnsupportedOperationException. Does it satisfy LSP?
The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) – example 2

The classic LSP violation. Mathematically every square is a rectangle, but in software Square should not inherit from Rectangle. Rectangle’s implied contract: setH and setW change only their own dimension. A user that sets width 5 and height 2 expects an area of 10. A Square has to keep its sides equal, so its setters change both. After setW(5); setH(2) the area is 4, not 10. Diagram and fix: User → Rectangle Solid arrow: User is associated with and uses Rectangle ( +setH , +setW ). Square → Rectangle (hollow triangle) Generalization: Square inherits from Rectangle and adds +setSide . Fix Don’t inherit. Make Square and Rectangle siblings under a Shape abstraction that offers only what both can honor, e.g. area() . Why does Square extends Rectangle violate LSP? Use a short example.
The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) – example 3

Reading the diagram: Billing → License Billing uses License and calls calcFee() . <I> License An interface with one operation, + calcFee() . PersonalLicense, BusinessLicense Implement License. BusinessLicense also keeps - users (a private field) because its fee depends on the number of users. Each subtype computes the fee differently (a flat personal fee; a fee per business user), but both honor the contract “return this license’s fee”. Billing’s behavior never depends on which subtype it receives, so both are substitutable: LSP holds. It is also OCP-compliant, because a new license type is a new class. In Java: interface License { double calcFee(); } class PersonalLicense implements License { public double calcFee() { return 100.0; } } class BusinessLicense implements License { private int users; public double calcFee() { return users * 50.0; } } class Billing { void printBill(License l) { System.out.println(l.calcFee()); } }
LSP: a sanity check

Use LSP to sanity-check every inheritance arrow you draw: ask whether the child can stand in for the parent everywhere. Inheritance is about keeping expected behavior , not just reusing code. If the honest answer is “only sometimes”, use composition or a different abstraction instead.
Exercise

Fruit promises two operations every fruit can do: Peel() and MakeSmoothie() . Orange: peeling and blending both work exactly as Fruit promises. LSP holds. Coconut: you don’t peel a coconut like other fruit; you crack it open. If Coconut.Peel() throws an error or does something callers don’t expect, a program that peels any Fruit breaks. LSP is violated. Model drawing and fix: Violation Fruit (+Peel(), +MakeSmoothie()) ^ Orange both work ^ Coconut Peel() fails Fix «interface» Peelable (+Peel()) «interface» Blendable (+MakeSmoothie()) Orange implements Peelable, Blendable Coconut implements Blendable and adds its own +Crack() Does Coconut violate LSP if Fruit declares Peel()? How would you fix the design?
Lecture Outlines
Covered so far: component design, the OO refresher, and S, O and L. The Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion principles come in the next lecture.

decks.t: Principles of Detailed Design III: ISP, DIP, Internal Behaviour and Rules of Design
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 3: Principles of Detailed Design III: ISP, DIP, Internal Behaviour and Rules of Design
n: Slide 1

Third detailed-design lecture: the last two SOLID principles (I and D), then how to model a component’s behaviour and general rules of good design. Software Design and Architecture [Principles of Detailed Design] – Chapter 05, L03
Lecture Outlines

Already covered in Lecture 2: S RP, O CP and L SP. Lecture Outlines ➢Previously we covered the following design principles for internal component design ✓Single Responsibility Principle ✓Open-Closed Principle ✓Liskov Substitution Principle ➢This lecture we will cover the following topics: ✓Continue with Component Design Principles: −Interface-Segregation Principle −Dependency-Inversion Principle ✓Designing Internal Behavior of Components ✓Rules of Design Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

The starting point is SRP: a well-designed class has one reason to change. The example: a game with enemy characters that roam over land, fly or swim, plus a super enemy that can do all three. The tempting design: one EnemyCharacter with fly() , run() and swim() , inherited by Aerial, Terrestrial, Aquatic and SuperCharacter. The slide labels it a bloated interface . “Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use” states the: Interface Segregation Principle Dependency Inversion Principle Open-Closed Principle Liskov Substitution Principle Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) ➢Well-designed classes should have one (and only one) reason to change. ➢When this concept is violated, there is a strong indication that the interfaces provided by these classes are providing more information than they should ➔ makes designs harder to maintain and reuse. ➢ The interface segregation principle (ISP) states that classes/methods should not be forced to depend on methods that they do not use. ➢ Consider a gaming system that have different types of enemy character that is able to either roam over land, fly, or swim. The game also have a super enemy characters that can do all (roam over land, fly, or swim). ✓ Some would be tempted to design the system as seen in the figure. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
ISP: one general interface vs. many specific ones

Aerial, Terrestrial and Aquatic characters are polluted with methods they can’t perform: an aerial character inherits run() and swim() , a terrestrial one fly() . The design also violates LSP (Lecture 2): code holding an EnemyCharacter may call fly() , but a TerrestrialCharacter put in its place can’t fly, so it can’t safely substitute for its parent. Only SuperCharacter conforms to the base type syntactically and semantically. It is the only class that really needs (and honours) all three methods, so it is the only one that satisfies LSP. In the enemy-character design where every character extends EnemyCharacter with fly(), run() and swim(), which principles are violated and why? The ISP implies that many client-specific interfaces are better than one general purpose interface. ISP the SuperCharacter class requires behaviour from all other enemy characters These classes are polluted with unnecessary methods. Only the SuperCharacter conforms The design violates the LSP, why? both syntactically and semantically to the base type. It is the only class that maintain LSK 4
Extra: ISP and LSP explained

In short: ISP → interfaces should be specific; LSP → subclasses must behave consistently with their base class. Fixing the interfaces (next slide) fixes both. Extra Explanation: 1. ISP (Interface Segregation Principle) What it means: Use small, specific interfaces instead of one big interface with many unused methods. Problem: Classes (e.g., AerialCharacter, AquaticCharacter) are Why it’s bad: forced to implement methods they don’t need (like run() ). Interfaces get “polluted” with unnecessary methods →2. LviSoPla (tLeiss IkSoPv Substitution Principle) What it means: Subclasses should replace their parent class without breaking program correctness. Problem: A TerrestrialCharacter cannot replace an EnemyCharacter if code expects fly(). Why it’s bad: SuperCharacter correctly follows LSP. Subclasses don’t fully match parent behavior. Only In short: ISP → Interfaces should be specific. 5 LSP → Subclasses must behave consistently as their base class.
ISP: the segregated design

The ISP fix: three small interfaces, «interface» AerialCharacter ( fly() ), TerrestrialCharacter ( run() ) and AquaticCharacter ( swim() ). Each client class (dashed realization arrows) implements only the one it can honour. «interface» SuperCharacter declares all three operations and is implemented by SuperCharacterClient. In the slide’s version the three small interfaces extend SuperCharacter (hollow triangles pointing down to it); conceptually it is the combination of the three capabilities. The Extra box: Java rules about overriding when types are combined: Abstract class implements an interface No override needed: it can leave the methods abstract. Abstract class extended by a concrete class Yes: the concrete subclass must override every abstract method. Normal class implements an interface It must override all the interface’s abstract methods. Interface extends interface No override: interfaces only add declarations. ISP Extra: (NO override) If Abstract class extends Concrete subclass → YES, must override IIff aA bnsotrrmacatl ccllaassss iimmpplelemmenentitnsg a innt ienrtfaecrefa →ce , it MUST override ALL abstract methods If interface extends interface, (NO override) → 6
ISP: the segregated design in Java

The code, top to bottom: Code What it does interface SuperCharacter { void fly(); void run(); void swim(); } The full contract: all three capabilities. interface AerialCharacter extends SuperCharacter { void fly(); } A specialised interface that names the capability its clients use. (Because it extends SuperCharacter, a class implementing it must still provide all three methods; to apply ISP strictly, the small interfaces should not extend the big one.) interface TerrestrialCharacter extends SuperCharacter { void run(); } The same for running. interface AquaticCharacter extends SuperCharacter { void swim(); } The same for swimming. class SuperCharacterClient implements SuperCharacter { fly(){…} run(){…} swim(){…} } The only class that really supports all three; each prints what it is doing. class AerialCharacterClient implements AerialCharacter { public void fly(){ … "is flying" } } Implements only fly() . As printed it would not compile, because the inherited run() and swim() are missing; with stand-alone small interfaces it would. class TerrestrialCharacterClient implements TerrestrialCharacter { run() } Runs only. class AquaticCharacterClient implements AquaticCharacter { swim() } Swims only. AerialCharacterClient arialObject = new AerialCharacterClient(); arialObject.fly(); In main , each object is used through the capability it supports. SuperCharacterClient superCharacter = new SuperCharacterClient(); superCharacter.fly(); …swim(); …run(); The super character can be asked for all three. The intent: a reference of a narrow type can only request what that character can do, so unsupported calls become impossible. Exam answers should draw the small interfaces as independent, each implemented by the classes that need it. 7
ISP: Worker violation vs. applied

Violation : one Worker interface with work() and eat() . Code What it does interface Worker { void work(); void eat(); } One fat interface for two unrelated capabilities. class Robot implements Worker { A robot can work but cannot eat… public void work() { System.out.println("Robot working"); } …so work() is meaningful, public void eat() { } // Robot does not eat but eat() is forced on it and left empty: a lie in the type. Applied : split the interface by capability. Code What it does interface Workable { void work(); } The working capability. interface Eatable { void eat(); } The eating capability. class Robot implements Workable { work() } The robot implements only what it can do. class Human implements Workable, Eatable { work() … eat() } A human implements both: a class may implement several small interfaces. A Robot class implements a Worker interface that declares work() and eat(), and leaves eat() empty. Which principle is violated, and how do you fix it? 8
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

In particular, avoid depending on modules that are actively being developed and change frequently: every change there would ripple into your code. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) ➢The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) tells us that the most flexible systems are those in which source code dependencies refer only to abstractions, not to concretions. ➢In a statically typed language, like Java, this means that the use, import, and include statements should refer only to source modules containing interfaces, abstract classes, or some other kind of abstract declaration. Nothing concrete should be depended on. ➢We need to avoid depending on modules that are actively developing, and that are undergoing frequent change. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

The two rules. (1) High-level modules (policy, e.g. a Manager) must not depend on low-level modules (details, e.g. a Worker). Both depend on an abstraction (an interface). The diagram: without inversion, Object A in Package A references Object B in Package B directly. With inversion, Object A references Interface A, and Object B implements (inherits) Interface A. The arrow from B now points toward the abstraction, the opposite (“inverted”) direction of the original dependency. According to DIP, a high-level module should depend on: Abstractions (interfaces) Low-level modules Concrete classes Global variables Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) 1- What is the Dependency Inversion Principle ? • High-level modules should NOT depend on low- level modules. • Both should depend on abstractions (interfaces). Also: • Abstractions should NOT depend on details. • Details should depend on abstractions. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
Extra: DIP – charger and switch (bad)

The same mistake in code, the charger that only fits one phone : Switch without dependency inversion: Code What it does class Fan { void turnOn() { System.out.println("Fan is ON"); } } A concrete low-level device. class Switch { The high-level module. Fan fan = new Fan(); // directly depends on Fan The switch creates and holds a concrete Fan. void press() { fan.turnOn(); } } Pressing can only ever turn on a fan. Extra: Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
Extra: DIP – switch with an interface (good)

The fix in three steps: Code What it does interface Device { void turnOn(); } Step 1: the abstraction (the “USB port”). class Fan implements Device { public void turnOn() { …"Fan is ON"… } } Step 2: the details implement the abstraction. class Light implements Device { public void turnOn() { …"Light is ON"… } } A second device, added without touching Switch. class Switch { Device device; Switch(Device device) { this.device = device; } void press() { device.turnOn(); } } Step 3: Switch knows only Device; the concrete device is passed in through the constructor. Switch s1 = new Switch(new Fan()); s1.press(); Wiring a fan: prints “Fan is ON”. Switch s2 = new Switch(new Light()); s2.press(); Wiring a light: prints “Light is ON”. Same Switch class. Passing the dependency in from outside (instead of new Fan() inside) is called dependency injection; it is the usual way to apply DIP. Extra: Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
Dependency Inversion

The textbook bad example, line by line: Code What it does class Worker { public void work() { // ....working } } A concrete worker. class Manager { The high-level module (the boss). Worker worker; The manager is fixed to one concrete type. public void setWorker(Worker w) { worker = w; } It can only be given a Worker (the circled parameter type). public void manage() { worker.work(); } } It tells that worker to work. Manager is the high-level module and depends directly on the low-level Worker. Problem : the boss only understands Worker. A Robot or an Intern can’t be managed without changing Manager, and tests can’t substitute a fake worker. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) •Extra: violates DIP •class Worker → A worker who can do work. •public void work() → The worker does the job (prints "working"). • class Manager → The boss who manages workers. • Worker worker; → The boss is fixed to only one type: Worker. •setWorker → Assigns a worker to the boss. •manage() → Boss tells the worker to work. •Problem → Boss only understands Worker, can’t manage other worker types (like Robot). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

The good example: Code What it does interface IWorker { public void work(); } The contract: any worker must know how to work. class Worker implements IWorker { public void work() { // ....working } } The original worker now follows the contract. class RobotWorker implements IWorker { public void work() { …"Robot is working..."… } } A new kind of worker, added without touching Manager. Manager now depends only on the abstraction: Code What it does class Manager { IWorker worker; The boss only cares about the interface, not the exact type. public void setWorker(IWorker w) { worker = w; } Any worker (human, robot, AI, intern) can be assigned. public void manage() { worker.work(); } } At run time the actual object’s work() runs. Bad code: Manager → Worker (tightly coupled). Good code: Manager → IWorker ← Worker, RobotWorker (loosely coupled and flexible). New workers such as RobotWorker , AIWorker or InternWorker need no change to Manager, which also makes Manager open for extension (OCP). A Manager class holds a field of the concrete type Worker and calls worker.work(). Which principle does this violate? Draw or describe the fix. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) Good Example • Manager depends on IWorker (interface), not on Worker. • You can add new workers (e.g., RobotWorker, AIWorker, InternWorker) without changing Manager. • High-level module (Manager) depends on abstraction, not low-level implementation. • interface IWorker → A contract: any worker must know how to work. • class Worker implements IWorker → Worker follows the contract and knows how to work. • Manager → The boss. • IWorker worker; → Boss only cares about the interface, not the exact type. • setWorker → Assign any worker (human, robot, etc.) to the boss. manage() → Boss tells the worker (whatever type) to work. • Good → Now Manager can handle any worker type that implements IWorker. So: •Bad code: Manager depends on Worker → tightly coupled. •Good code: Manager depends on IWorker → loosely coupled, flexible. 14
Modeling Internal Behavior of

Reading the “Activate Sensors” example: 1: timer expires An outside event reaches the ScheduleManager ( sm ). 2: getMsg() / 4: interpretMsg() It fetches the scheduled message from s : Schedule and interprets it (a self-call). alt frame A choice: if msgId == HEAT_MSG_ID it sends 5: activate() to the HeatSensor; if msgId == VIBRATE_MSG_ID it sends 6: activate() to the VibrationSensor. Only one branch runs. Which UML diagrams model a component’s internal structure and its internal behaviour? Class diagram for structure, sequence diagram for behaviour Deployment diagram for structure, use case diagram for behaviour Package diagram for both Sequence diagram for structure, class diagram for behaviour Modeling Internal Behavior of a Component ➢The component design considers modeling the internal structure and the behavior of the component ➢As discussed in earlier slides, the internal structure of a component is modeled using a class diagram ➢We model the internal behavior of a component using a sequence diagram Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
Rules of Design

Separate orthogonal concerns : don’t connect what is independent (orthogonal = unrelated, changing for different reasons). Rules of Design ➢Make sure that the problem is well-defined ✓All design criteria, requirements, and constraints, should be known before a design is started. ➢What comes before how ✓i.e. Define the functionalities to be performed at every level of abstraction before deciding which structures should be implementing these functionalities. ➢ Separate orthogonal concerns ✓Do not connect what is independent. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 16
Rules of Design

External before internal : first treat the solution as a black box and decide how it interacts with its environment; then decide how the box is organised inside, usually as smaller black boxes refined the same way. Keep it simple : fancy designs are buggier, harder to implement and verify, and often slower. Problems that look complex are often simple problems huddled together; the designer’s job is to separate them and solve each one. Rules of Design ➢Design external functionality before internal functionality. ✓First consider the solution as a black-box and decide how it should interact with its environment. ✓Then decide how the black-box can be internally organized. Likely it consists of smaller black- boxes that can be refined in a similar fashion. ➢ Keep it simple. ✓Fancy designs are buggier than simple ones; they are harder to implement, harder to verify, and often less efficient. ✓Problems that appear complex are often just simple problems huddled together. ✓Our job as designers is to identify the simpler problems, separate them, and then solve them individually. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Rules of Design

Work at multiple levels of abstraction : good designers move quickly between the big picture and the details. Design for extensibility : a good design is “open-ended”, easy to extend. Don’t introduce what is immaterial (unimportant) and don’t restrict what is irrelevant (unrelated): both make later extension harder. Rules of Design ➢Work at multiple levels of abstraction ✓Good designers must be able to move between various levels of abstraction quickly and easily. ✓ Design for extensibility ➢Design for extensibility ✓A good design is “open-ended,” i.e., easily extendible. ✓Do not introduce what is immaterial (not important). ✓Do not restrict what is irrelevant (not related). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 18
Rules of Design

Details depend on abstractions; abstractions don’t depend on details : the DIP stated as a rule of design. Common closure : classes in a released component should change together; if one needs to change, they all probably do (“what affects one, affects all”). Group classes by the reasons they change. Rules of Design ➢Use rapid prototyping when applicable ✓Before implementing a design, build a high-level prototype and verify that the design criteria are met. ➢Details should depend upon abstractions ✓Abstractions should not depend upon details ➢ Classes within a released component should share common closure ✓That is, if one needs to be changed, they all are likely need to be changed ✓i.e., what affects one, affects all Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 19
Rules of Design

Common reuse : classes in a released component are reused together; you can’t take part of a component. Stable abstractions : the more stable a component is, the more it should consist of abstract classes; a completely stable component contains nothing but abstractions. That is why interfaces sit at the stable end of DIP diagrams. State the stable-dependencies rule and explain why stable components should be abstract. Rules of Design ➢Classes within a released component should be reused together ✓That is, it is impossible to separate the components from each other in order to reuse less than the total ➢Dependencies between released components must run in the direction of stability ✓The dependee must be more stable than the depender ➢The more stable a released component is, the more it must consist of abstract classes ✓A completely stable component consist of nothing but abstract classes Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
Common Design Mistakes

Depth-first design : perfecting one part early and only partially satisfying the requirements overall. Experience is the best cure. Directly refining the requirements specification into a design: produces overly constrained, inefficient designs, because the structure copies the document instead of the problem. Failing to consider potential changes : always design for extension and contraction (adding and removing features). Making the design too detailed : over-constrains the implementation and leaves programmers no sensible choices. Name two common design mistakes and their consequences. Common Design Mistakes ➢Depth-first design ✓Only partially satisfy the requirements (Experience is best cure for this problem) ➢ Directly refining requirements specification ✓Leads to overly constrained, inefficient designs ➢ Failure to consider potential changes ✓Always design for extension and contraction ➢ Making the design too detailed ✓This over-constrains the implementation Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 21
Summary

Recap: the internal-component design principles (the slide lists SRP and DIP; this lecture added ISP and DIP to Lecture 2’s SRP, OCP and LSP). Internal behaviour is modelled with sequence diagrams, and the rules of design guide every decision. Summary ➢Design Principles for Internal Component Design (Continue) ✓Single Responsibility Principle, ✓Dependency Inversion principle, ➢Designing Internal Behavior of Components ➢Rules of Design ➢ Next … − We will start the following chapter →Creational Design Patterns Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 22
Extra: The rules of design in one list

The rules from slides 16–20 in one list. Problem and requirements first; what before how ; separate independent concerns; design external behaviour first. 1. Extra: 2. Define the problem first Understand what you are solving before designing. 3. Know requirements and constraints early Don’t start design without clear requirements. 4. What before how Define what the system should do before how it will do it. 5. Separate independent concerns Don’t connect things that are unrelated. 6. Design external behavior first Treat the system as a black box → then design its inside. 7. Keep it simple Simple designs are easier, safer, and more reliable. 8. Work at multiple abstraction levels Move easily between high-level view and low-level details. 9. Design for extensibility Allow easy future changes and additions. 10.Avoid the unnecessary Don’t add what is unimportant or unrelated. 11.Use rapid prototyping when possible Build a quick model to validate the design early. 12.Depend on abstractions, not details Details should depend on interfaces, not the opposite. 13.Classes in one component change together If one changes, related ones likely change too. 14.Classes in one component are reused together You reuse the component as a whole, not partially. 15.Dependencies go toward stability Less stable components depend on more stable ones. 16.Stable components should be abstract The most stable components contain mostly abstractions. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 23
Analysis Models to Design Models

How analysis (requirements) models turn into design models. Left: the analysis models describe the problem. The domain model class diagram (Customer, Order) becomes the design class diagrams (with attributes and operations such as changeName() , shipOrder() ); use case diagrams and activity diagrams feed the component and interaction (sequence) diagrams. System sequence diagrams become detailed interaction diagrams ; requirements state machines (Ready → Shipped) become design state machines; and package diagrams organise the result into layers. Each design model traces back to an analysis model. Analysis Models to Design Models

decks.t: Design Patterns and the Abstract Factory
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 6 · Lecture 1: Design Patterns and the Abstract Factory
n: Slide 1

Chapter 6 starts design patterns , the detailed-design counterpart of Chapter 4’s architectural patterns. This lecture: what design patterns are, how they are classified, and the first creational pattern, Abstract Factory . Software Design and Architecture [Creational Design Patterns] Chapter 06, L01 –
Lecture Outlines

Lecture Outlines Patterns in Detailed Design Architectural vs. Design Patterns. Classification of Design Patterns Purpose Scope Documenting Design Patterns Creational Design Patterns Abstract Factory Computer Store Example What’s next… Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Patterns in Detailed Design

They are different from architectural patterns (Chapter 4, slide 11 of Lecture 1): architectural patterns fix the system-wide structure; design patterns work at the level of classes and objects inside a subsystem and don’t change the overall structure. Patterns in Detailed Design Design patterns are recurring solutions to object-oriented design problems in a particular context. They are different than architectural patterns/styles! Extra: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common problems They provide templates for how to solve problems efficiently and consistently, helping developers avoid reinventing the wheel. In which way they are different?!! Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Classifications of Design Patterns

Patterns are classified by purpose (what kind of problem they solve) and scope (next slide). Structural : deal with composing objects and classes into larger structures (Chapter 7: Adapter, Composite…). Behavioural : deal with how classes interact, how behaviour varies, and how responsibilities are assigned between objects (Chapter 7: Observer…). Patterns that deal with how classes interact and how responsibilities are assigned between objects are: Behavioral Creational Structural Architectural Classifications of Design Patterns  Design patterns can be classified based on:  Purpose  Scope  The purpose of a design pattern identifies the essence of the pattern. The three types of purposes used for classification are: 1. Creational: Patterns that deal with creation of objects. 2. Structural: Patterns that deal with creation of structures to form the existing objects. 3. Behavioral: Patterns that deal with how classes interact, the variation of behavior, and the assignment of responsibility between objects. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Classifications of Design Patterns

Class-level patterns deal with relationships between classes, fixed at design time through inheritance. Examples in the table: Factory Method (creational), Adapter (structural), Interpreter and Template Method (behavioural). Object-level patterns deal with relationships between objects, set up at run time through composition. Most patterns are here: Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton (creational); Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Façade, Proxy (structural); Chain of Responsibility, Command, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Flyweight, Observer, State, Strategy, Visitor (behavioural). Classify Abstract Factory, Composite and Observer by purpose and scope. Classifications of Design Patterns  The scope criterion captures whether a design pattern primarily applies to classes (during design time) or objects (during run-time). http://www.cs.unc.edu/~stotts/GOF/hires/chap1fso.htm Extra: 1. Class-level patterns: Patterns that apply at the class level, focusing on relationships between classes during design time. 2. Object-level patterns: Patterns that apply at the object level, focusing on relationships between objects at runtime. In short, class-level patterns deal with class structures, while object-level patterns focus on interactions during execution. 6
Patterns

Each pattern is documented with the same categories, so patterns can be compared and looked up. The categories : name and classification, intent (what problem it solves), also known as, motivation (an example scenario), applicability (when to use it), structure (UML class diagram), participants, collaborations, consequences (good and bad effects), implementation, sample code, known uses, related patterns. Documenting Design Patterns Extra: • This slide explains how design patterns are documented. • Each pattern is described using several key categories such as intent, motivation, applicability, structure, participants, and more. • These categories help provide a clear understanding of what the pattern does, when to use it, how it works, and its effects on the system. • you don't need to focus on presenting this extensive documentation for each pattern. Note: In this course, we’re not concerned with presenting this extensive documentation for each pattern Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 7
Creational Design Patterns

Creational patterns abstract and control how objects are created, by giving clients a common creational interface instead of scattered new ConcreteClass() calls. The five: Abstract Factory , Factory Method , Builder , Prototype , Singleton . This chapter covers Abstract Factory, Factory Method, Builder and Singleton. Which of these is NOT a creational pattern? Composite Builder Singleton Prototype Creational Design Patterns Creational design patterns abstract and control the way objects are created in software applications.  They do so by specifying a common creational interface.  Examples of creational patterns include:  The AbstractFactory  The Factory Method  The Builder  The Prototype  The Singleton Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
The Abstract Factory Pattern

What is the intent of the Abstract Factory pattern? Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes Ensure a class has exactly one instance Construct a complex object step by step Create objects by copying a prototype The Abstract Factory Pattern  The Abstract Factory is an object-creational design pattern intended to manage and encapsulate the creation of a set of objects that conceptually belong together and that represent a specific family of products.  The intent of the Abstract Factory is to:  Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes.  Like all creational patterns, Abstract Factory is composed of creator classes and product classes.  As it will be seen, some creational patterns fuse the creator and product into one class. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
The Abstract Factory Pattern

The same definition, plus the two benefits. Encapsulation : the client knows the abstract product names (Button, Textbox) but not the concrete classes (DarkButton, LightTextbox). Abstract Factory Step by Step Summary –  As seen, the Abstract Factory pattern can be used over and over tosupport new family of products or to add new products to existing ones. When designing with the Abstract Factory, execute the followingsteps: 1. Design the product interfaces (e.g., Cpu, Monitor, and Keyboard) 2. Identify the different families or groups required for the problem (e.g., standard vs. advanced computers) 3. For each product group identified in step 2, design concrete products that realize the respective product interfaces identified in step 1. 4. Create the factory interface (e.g., ComputerPartsFactory). The factory n interface contains interface methods, one for each product interface identified in step 1. 5. For each family or group identified in step 2, create concrete factories that realize the factory interface created in step 4. 6. Associate each concrete factory from step 5 with their respective products from step 3. 7. Create the Client (e.g., Computer) which is associated with both product and factory interfaces created in steps 1 and 4, respectively. Cons & Pros of Abstract Factory

Con : a large number of classes (an interface per product, a class per product per family, a factory per family). Pros : concrete product classes are isolated, so they are easier to reuse; products within a family are guaranteed consistent ; adding a new family needs no change to existing code, because additions are made by extension ( OCP ); modifiability increases. (The hidden con from slide 17: adding a new product type changes every factory.) Give one disadvantage and two advantages of the Abstract Factory pattern. Cons & Pros of Abstract Factory  Cons  Large number of classes are required  Pros  Isolates concrete product classes so that reusing them becomes easier  Promotes consistency within specific product families.  Adding new families of products require no modification to existing code.  Additions are made through extension, therefore, obeying the OCP.  Increases modifiability Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 34

Factory Method Design Pattern

Factory Method is a class creational pattern (it works through inheritance, so its relationships are fixed at design time) that encapsulates object creation and defers instantiation to derived classes . Structure : (1) Creator , an abstract class or interface that declares the factory method; (2) ConcreteCreator , which overrides it; (3) Product , the interface every product implements; (4) ConcreteProduct . Which pattern lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate through one overridable creation method? Factory Method Abstract Factory Singleton Builder State the intent of the Factory Method and name its four participants. Factory Method Design Pattern The Factory Method design pattern is a class creational pattern used to encapsulate and defer object instantiation to derived classes. The intent of the factory method is to: Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses. Purpose ✅ Defines one method for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Key Idea 🔹 “Defer instantiation to subclasses.” Creates: 🔹 One product at a time ➡ Structure: 🔹 1. Creator (abstract class or interface) 2. Concrete Creator 3. Product (interface) 3 4. Concrete Product
Factory Method Example

Like Abstract Factory it has creator and product classes, but the creator needs only one creational method, for products that share the same interface. Rule of thumb: Factory Method for one product type with several implementations ; Abstract Factory for several product types , each with several implementations. Reading the generic diagram: Creator createProduct() in italics: abstract, the factory method. someOperator() is a normal method that calls createProduct() and uses the result. ConcreteCreator Inherits from Creator (solid line, hollow triangle) and implements createProduct(). «interface» Product / ConcreteProduct ConcreteProduct realises Product (dashed line). The arrow from ConcreteCreator to ConcreteProduct shows which product it creates. Factory Method Example Structure The generic and applied structure of the factory method design pattern is presented below. As seen, the pattern requires both creational and product classes, similar to the abstract factory design pattern. However, unlike the abstract factory design pattern, creator classes in the factory method design pattern require only one creational interface method for creating products that share the same interface. Therefore, for each product in the system, the design incorporates concrete product and concrete creator classes. Extra: The Factory Method is simpler and is used when there is one product type with multiple implementations, while the Abstract Factory is used when there are multiple product types and multiple implementations of these product types. 4

Steps for designing with the Factory Method

Apply the Factory Method to a logistics app where RoadLogistics creates Trucks and SeaLogistics creates Ships. Name the classes and the factory method. Steps for designing with the Factory Method 1. Identify and design the product interface (e.g., Computer) 2. Identify and design the concrete products that realize the interface from step 1 (e.g., StandardComputer, AdvancedComputer, etc.) 3. Design the factory interface (e.g., ComputerStore), which contains one abstract factory interface method for delegating product creation to derived classes. 4. Benefits of the Factory Method Pattern

It separates code from product-specific classes , so the same code works with existing and newly created products. New product = new creator subclass, no edits elsewhere (OCP). Testability improves: a test can subclass the creator to return a fake product. True or false: the Factory Method helps follow the Open-Closed Principle when new product types are added. Benefits of the Factory Method Pattern Separates code from product-specific classes; therefore, the same code can work with various existing or newly created product classes. The development becomes efficient, since different developers can work on the different parts of the project at the same time. Easier to reuse specific parts of the code Easier to maintain specific parts of the code. Improve Testability. The Builder Pattern

… so that the same construction process can create different representations . The steps (the algorithm) stay fixed; what each step produces varies with the builder. Builder Design Pattern Example

Step 3 : from steps 1–2, design the builder interface : abstract methods for every part that must be created for the whole product to exist; concrete builders implement them. Builder Design Pattern Example Steps for designing using the Builder pattern: Identify and design the product class (e.g., GeneratedProduct) Identify the product’s creational process and algorithm, and design a class for its execution (e.g., CodeGenerator). Using the knowledge acquired from steps 1 and 2, design the builder interface, which specifies the parts that need to be created for the whole product to exist. These are captured as abstract interface methods that need to be implemented by derived concrete builders. Identify and design classes for the different representations of the product (e.g., CppMessageBuilder, JavaMessageBuilder, etc.) prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
Extra: Builder pattern in one slide

Contrast the Builder and Abstract Factory patterns. Extra: Builder pattern • Intent: separate how we build a complex object (steps) from what the final object looks like (representation). • When useful: same construction steps, but you want different outputs (e.g., generate Java vs. C# code; make small vs. large burger). • Key roles: • Director — orchestrates steps in order (doesn’t know details). • Builder (interface) — declares multistep methods (buildPartA/B/C…, getProduct()). • Concrete Builders — implement those steps to produce different representations. • Product — the thing being built. • Flow (always the same): • Client chooses a ConcreteBuilder and gives it to the Director • Director runs the steps in sequence • Client asks builder for the final Product • Builder vs Abstract Factory : • Builder builds one complex object step-by-step. • Abstract Factory creates a family of related objects all at once. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
Builder Design Pattern Example

The code-generator example as a picture. In : a messaging-specification document (message names, attributes, operations). The code generator runs the same construction process for every language: open and read the file, find message names, attributes and operations, generate language-specific code, close the file. Out : Java, C++ or C# code, i.e. different representations of the same messages. That combination (fixed process, varying output) is exactly the Builder’s use case. Builder Design Pattern Example prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
The Builder Pattern

Director with construct() : “this guy orchestrates the creational process”. It holds an AbstractBuilder and calls its steps in order. Product : the class being built; the ConcreteBuilder creates and assembles it. Creator classes = Director, AbstractBuilder, ConcreteBuilder; product class = Product. In the Builder pattern, which participant calls the construction steps in the right order? Director ConcreteBuilder Product Client The Builder Pattern These interface methods specify the multistep creational process for the Builder Structure  Product! This guy orchestratesthe Concrete Builders must provide creational process! implementation for creational interface functions! Extra: Builder Pattern – how to solve

6) Verify extensibility : a new variant needs only a new ConcreteBuilder; client and director stay unchanged.  2) Declare the Builder interface (steps) Extra:  Write the multistep API that builds parts of the Product. Typical methods: Builder Pattern — How to Solve (General buildPartA(...) Steps) buildPartB(...) buildPart…… 0) Recognize it’s a Builder problem getResult() (returns the Product) what to build Steps should describe , not how.  Same sequence of steps, different final 3) Implement Concrete Builders (variants) representations (outputs).  One class per variant (e.g., PdfReportBuilder,  Need to construct a complex object step-by- HtmlReportBuilder). step.  Each implements the steps its own way and stores intermediate state.  You want to hide construction from the client  getResult() returns the fully built Product. and make adding new variants easy. 4) Create the Director (optional but recommended)  Orchestrates order of steps. 1) Define the Product  Has a method like construct() that calls the steps in sequence.  Name the final thing being built (e.g., Report,  Keeps the construction process reusable and consistent. Burger, Form, Query, House). 5) Client wiring  List its parts/fields (what varies between variants).  Client picks the ConcreteBuilder (the variant desired).  Pass it to the Director, call construct().  Get the Product via builder.getResult() (or director.construct() returns it). 6) Verify extensibility  To add a new variant, create a new ConcreteBuilder 12 only—client and director stay the same.
Extra: Builder code skeleton

The skeleton in Java: Code What it does class Product { /* the final object being built */ } 1. The product. interface Builder { void buildPartA(); void buildPartB(); Product getResult(); } 2. The builder interface. class JavaBuilder implements Builder { buildPartA() { /* step A for Java */ } … getResult() { return new Product(); } } 3. Concrete builders (CSharpBuilder the same, with C# steps). class Director { private Builder builder; Director(Builder builder) { this.builder = builder; } 4. The director receives a builder… Product construct() { builder.buildPartA(); builder.buildPartB(); return builder.getResult(); } } …and runs the steps in a fixed order. Builder javaBuilder = new JavaBuilder(); Director director = new Director(javaBuilder); Product javaProduct = director.construct(); 5. The client chooses the builder; C# is the same three lines with CSharpBuilder. •Points to Remember •Product = the final object. •Builder interface = declares building steps. •Concrete Builders = implement steps differently (Java vs. C#). •Director = controls the order of building steps. •Client = chooses which builder to use. Same construction steps, but different final 👉 representations. 13
Builder Design Pattern Example: class diagram

The Builder provides the following benefits

It gives finer control over construction: parts of an object are created at discrete points in time , unlike Abstract Factory, which creates each product in one call. Give two benefits of the Builder pattern. The Builder provides the following benefits Separates an object’s construction process from its representation; therefore future representations can be added easily to the software. Changes to existing representations can be made without modifying the code for the creational process. Provides finer control over the construction process so that parts of objects can be created at discrete points in time (which differs from the Abstract Factory pattern) Improves maintainability, testability, and reusability. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15

Burger builder: solution code

The solution: Code What it does class Burger { String bun; String patty; String sauce; public String toString() { return bun + " + " + patty + " + " + sauce; } } 1. The product. interface BurgerBuilder { void addBun(); void addPatty(); void addSauce(); Burger getBurger(); } 2. The three steps plus the result. class BeefBurgerBuilder implements BurgerBuilder { Burger burger = new Burger(); 3. The beef recipe keeps its burger under construction… public void addBun() { burger.bun = "Sesame Bun"; } … addPatty → "Beef Patty" … addSauce → "BBQ Sauce" …and fills each part its own way. class ChickenBurgerBuilder implements BurgerBuilder { … "Whole Wheat Bun" … "Chicken Patty" … "Mayo Sauce" } The chicken recipe: same steps, other ingredients. class Chef { private BurgerBuilder builder; Chef(BurgerBuilder builder) { this.builder = builder; } 4. Builder Design Pattern

Builder Design Pattern The Builder Design pattern is an object creational pattern that encapsulates both the creational process and the representation of product objects. In the Abstract Factory Pattern, various product objects are created all at once, The Builder Pattern allows clients to control the (multistep) creational process of a single product object. The Builder dictates the creation of individual parts of the object at discrete points throughout software operations. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 21

The ICD is complex, and customers now want Java and C# as well: the same generation process, new representations, so Builder.
