Singleton Design Pattern

Which pattern guarantees exactly one instance of a class with a global access point? Singleton Prototype Factory Method Builder Singleton Design Pattern The Singleton design pattern is an object creational design pattern used to prevent objects from being instantiated more than once in a running program. The intent of the Singleton is to Ensure a class only has one instance, and provide a global point of access to it. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 26
Singleton Design Pattern

The UML, member by member. -Singleton() : a private constructor (minus sign) restricts instantiation, so no other class can call new Singleton() . -instance : Singleton (underlined): a private static attribute that holds the one instance. Underlined members are static in UML. +getInstance() : Singleton (underlined): a public static method that creates the instance if needed and gives everyone access to the one and only object. +operation() stands for the class’s ordinary behaviour. Draw the standard class diagram of the Singleton pattern and convert it into code (any language). Singleton Design Pattern prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 27
Singleton Design Pattern Example

The design: one central event manager that every object uses. It creates an event list on instantiation, adds events as they are logged, and writes them to a file at specific points. Singleton Design Pattern Example Problem: Consider an application that requires event logging capabilities. The application consists of many different objects that generate events to keep track of their actions, status of operations, errors, or any other information of interest. A decision is made to create an event manage that can be accessed by all objects and used to manage all events in the system. Upon instantiation, the event manager creates an event list that gets updated as events are logged. At specific points during the software system’s operation, these events are written to a file. To prevent conflicts, it is desirable that at any given time, there is only one instance of the event manager executing. Extra: The application needs event logging (recording actions, statuses, and errors). 🔹 Many objects in the system generate events, but instead of each one handling logging separately, a central 🔹 Event Manager is created. This Event Manager keeps an event list, updates it when events happen, and later writes the events to a file. 🔹 To avoid problems (like multiple versions writing at the same time), the design ensures there is only one 🔹 Event Manager instance in the whole system. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 28
Extra: Why Singleton?

Extra: Why Is There a Problem? In many software systems: •Multiple parts of the application (e.g. login system, payment system, notification system) need to log events — such as user actions, errors, system updates. •If each part creates its own logger, this leads to: • Multiple log files or conflicting writes. ❌ • Confusing or inconsistent data. ❌ • Harder to debug or audit the system. ❌ The real problem: If every part creates a new logger (event manager), it causes conflicts, redundancy, 🔴 and loss of control. Why Singleton Fixes This? •Singleton ensures that only one instance of the EventManager (Logger) exists. •All parts of the system share the same logger. •You maintain one log file, centralized control, and avoid conflicts. One object → One responsibility → No conflict. ✅ prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 29
Singleton Design Pattern Example: class diagrams

The example mapped onto the generic structure: EventManager has -instance_ : EventManager* (static), a private constructor -EventManager() , +getInstance(): EventManager* (static) and +logEvent(eventDescription: string) . Compared with the generic Singleton box, only the names changed: logEvent is the class’s real operation() . Singleton Design Pattern Example prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 30
Java Code for the Singleton Pattern: the class

The Java class: Code What it does public class Singleton { private static Singleton singleton = new Singleton(); The one instance, created when the class loads (eager initialisation). private Singleton() { } A private constructor prevents any other class from instantiating it. public static Singleton getInstance() { return singleton; } The static “instance” method: always returns the same object. protected static void demoMethod() { System.out.println("demoMethod for singleton"); } } Other methods, reached through the instance. A static variable is allocated statically: it lives for the entire run of the program, which is why it can hold the single instance. Compare with the exam version (slide 27), which creates the instance lazily inside getInstance(). The Singleton class Java Code for the Singleton Pattern A static variable is a variable that has been allocated "statically", meaning that its lifetime (or "extent") is the entire run of the program. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 31
Java Code for the Singleton Pattern

Using it: Code What it does public class SingletonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { The main program. Singleton tmp = Singleton.getInstance(); Not new Singleton() (that would not compile): ask the class for its instance. tmp.demoMethod(); } } Use it like any object. Java Code for the Singleton Pattern The main program file where we will create a singleton object prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 32
Singleton Design Pattern Example

3. Create a public static getInstance() method that uses the private constructor to create one object (if it doesn’t exist yet) and returns it to clients. These three steps are the whole answer to “write the Singleton code”. List the three steps to design a class with the Singleton pattern. Singleton Design Pattern Example  Steps to design using the Singleton design pattern: 1. Set the visibility of the constructor to private 2. Define a private static member attribute that can store a reference (i.e., a pointer) to the one instance of the singleton. 3. Create a public static getInstance() method that can access the private constructor to instantiate one object of the singleton type and return it to clients. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 33
Benefits of the Singleton Design Pattern

Benefit : it can be customised to allow a variable number of instances (e.g. a pool of at most N), since creation goes through one method. Drawback : it doesn’t work well in multithreaded environments: two threads calling getInstance() at the same moment can both see instance == null and create two objects, unless the method is synchronised. True or false: a Singleton’s constructor should be public so the instance can be created when needed. Why can the lazy Singleton fail in a multithreaded program, and how is it fixed? Benefits of the Singleton Design Pattern Benefits: It provides controlled access to a single instance of a given type. It can be customized to permit a variable number of instances. Drawback: It does not work well in multithreading environments prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 34
Extra: Real-World Scenario – banking logger

Step 1, the Singleton class: Code What it does public class EventLogger { private static EventLogger instance; The one instance. private EventLogger() {} Prevents outside creation. public static EventLogger getInstance() { if (instance == null) { instance = new EventLogger(); } return instance; } The global access point, created on first use. public void log(String message) { System.out.println("Log: " + message); } } In real use this would write to a file. Step 2, the login system: EventLogger.getInstance().log("User " + username + " logged in."); . Why not instance.log() ? Because instance is private and static inside the class; from outside, getInstance() is the public way to reach the one object, and then you call .log() on it. Extra: Real-World Scenario Let’s say you’re building a Banking App: Login System logs when a user logs in. Transaction System logs when money is transferred. N otification System logs when a message is sent. You want all events to go to the same log, 👉 in the correct order. Why don’t we write instance.log() directly? Because instance is private and static inside the class, and we’re outside the class when we want to use it. •getInstance() is a public static method → you can access it from anywhere. •It returns the instance (the one and only object). •Then you can call .log() on that object. 35
Extra: Transaction and notification systems

The transaction system logs "Transferred $" + amount + " from " + from + " to " + to through EventLogger.getInstance().log(...) . The notification system logs "Notification sent to " + user + ": " + message the same way. The main class runs login, a transfer and a notification, then prints EventLogger.getInstance() == EventLogger.getInstance() , which is true : proof that all three systems used the same logger object. Extra: Transaction System Step 3: Main Class to Run the App Notification System prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 36
Singleton Design Pattern Example: C++ EventManager

The textbook EventManager in C++: Code What it does EventManager* EventManager::_instance = 0; Initialise the static member: no instance yet. EventManager::EventManager(void) { /* Intentionally left blank. */ } The private constructor. EventManager* EventManager::getInstance(void) { The global point of access. if (_instance == 0) { _instance = new EventManager; } Create the one and only instance the first time. return _instance; } Every call returns the same pointer. void EventManager::logEvent(string eventDescription) { cout << eventDescription << endl; } The method that logs events. Singleton Design Pattern Example prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 37

An extra exercise on the fifth creational pattern, Prototype : a drawing app needs many copies of Circle (radius) and Square (side). Which pattern creates new objects by copying an existing instance? Prototype Builder Singleton Composite Extra: Example A drawing application needs to create many copies of two types of shapes: Circle and Square. radius side Each shape has one attribute (Circle → , Square → ). The system should allow creating new shapes by copying existing ones instead of creating them from scratch every time. Tasks: 1.Draw a class diagram that solves this problem. 2.Write Java code that: 1. Defines a common interface for all shapes. 2. Allows each shape to make a copy of itself. main 3. Demonstrates copying a Circle and a Square in the method. (Hint for students: Think of a design pattern where objects can create duplicates of themselves.) How Students Should See It Step 1 → Prototype interface with clone(). Step 2 → Concrete Prototype A (Circle). Step 3 → Concrete Prototype B (Square). Step 4 → Client (PrototypeDemo) that uses cloning instead of new. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 40

Step 1: Code What it does interface Shape { Shape clone(); } Every shape can duplicate itself; the copy is returned as a Shape. prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 41
Prototype step 2: Circle

Step 2: Code What it does class Circle implements Shape { int radius; Circle(int r) { this.radius = r; } A concrete prototype with its state. @Override public Shape clone() { return new Circle(this.radius); } Makes a copy with the same radius. public void show() { System.out.println("Circle with radius " + radius); } } 42

Step 3: Code What it does class Square implements Shape { int side; Square(int s) { this.side = s; } The second concrete prototype. @Override public Shape clone() { return new Square(this.side); } Copies the side length. public void show() { System.out.println("Square with side " + side); } } prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 43

Step 4, the client: Code What it does Shape c1 = new Circle(10); Shape c2 = c1.clone(); Create an original circle, then clone it. Shape s1 = new Square(5); Shape s2 = s1.clone(); The same for a square. ((Circle)c1).show(); ((Circle)c2).show(); ((Square)s1).show(); ((Square)s2).show(); Prints “Circle with radius 10” twice and “Square with side 5” twice. decks.t: Structural Design Patterns: Adapter, Composite and Facade
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 7 · Lecture 1: Structural Design Patterns: Adapter, Composite and Facade
n: Slide 1

Chapter 7 moves from creating objects to structuring them. Lecture 1: three structural patterns. Lecture 2: behavioural patterns. Software Design and Architecture [Structural Design Patterns] – Chapter 07, L01
Lecture Outlines

Previously: the creational patterns (Abstract Factory, Factory Method, Builder, Singleton). Lecture Outlines ➢Previously (Creational Design Patterns) ➢Structural Patterns in Detailed Design ✓Adaptor ✓Composite ✓Facade ➢What’s next… Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Structural Patterns in Detailed Design

Structural patterns deal with designing the structure of existing classes or objects : how they are connected and combined, so parts fit together or present a simpler boundary. The three here: Adapter (make incompatible interfaces fit), Facade (simplify a subsystem) and Composite (build part–whole trees). Structural Patterns in Detailed Design ➢Structural design patterns are patterns that deal with designing the structure of existing classes or objects at run . ➢Popular structural design patterns include: ✓Adaptor ✓Facade ✓Composite Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
Adapter Design Pattern

Adapter is a class or object structural pattern (it has both variants) used to adapt an existing interface to the one a system expects. Its intent : convert the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect . Adapter lets classes work together that otherwise couldn’t because their interfaces are incompatible. Think of a travel plug converter: the device and the socket don’t change; the converter between them does the fitting. Making an existing class with an incompatible interface usable by a client, without changing either, is the: Adapter pattern Facade pattern Composite pattern Observer pattern Adapter Design Pattern ➢The Adapter design pattern is a class/object structural design pattern used to adapt an exiting interface that is expected in a software system. ➢The intent of the Adapter is to: ✓Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn’t otherwise because of incompatible interfaces. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Adapter Design Pattern – a real-life example

The real-life version: your existing system (the client) has an Ethernet cable and sends its request() . The adapter (an Ethernet-to-USB dongle) offers the target interface the cable expects, and passes on a translated request() . The vendor class (adaptee) only understands its own adaptee interface (USB). Neither the cable nor the USB port changed; the adapter did the translation. Adapter Design Pattern- A real-life example for the use of adapters Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Adapter: the problems it solves
Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
Adapter: object and class adapters

Object adapter (left): implements Target by delegating to an Adaptee object held in a field, at run time ( adaptee.specificOperation() ). Class adapter (right): implements Target by inheriting from the Adaptee class, at compile time ( specificOperation() is called on itself). What is the difference between an object adapter and a class adapter? • In the above UML class diagram, the Client class that requires (depends on) a Target Interface cannot reuse the Adaptee class directly because its interface doesn't conform to the Target Interface. Instead, the Client works through an Adapter class that implements the Target Interface in terms of Adaptee: The Object Adapter implements the Target Interface by delegating to an Adaptee object at run-time (adaptee.specificOperation()). The Class Adapter implements the Target Interface by inheriting from an Adaptee class at compile-time (specificOperation()). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 7
Adapter Design Pattern - Structure

Class version (left): Adapter inherits from both Target and Adaptee (two hollow triangles) and its request() calls the inherited specificRequest() . Object version (right): Adapter realises Target and has an association arrow to an Adaptee object; its request() calls adaptee.specificRequest() . To use an adapter: (1) the client calls a method on the adapter through the target interface; (2) the adapter translates it into calls on the adaptee interface; (3) the client gets the results, never knowing an adaptee was involved. In the Adapter pattern, the existing class with the incompatible interface is called the: Adaptee Target Client Composite Adapter Design Pattern - Structure To use an adapter: 1.The client makes a request to the adapter by calling a method on it using the target interface. 2.The adapter translates that request on the adaptee using the adaptee interface. 3.Client receive the results of the call Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
Adapter Design Pattern Example*

Adapter Design Pattern – Example* Example: ‾ Suppose you have a Bird class with fly() , and makeSound() methods. ‾ Also a ToyDuck class with squeak() method. ‾ Let’s assume that you are short on ToyDuck objects and you would like to use Bird objects in their place. ‾ Birds have some similar functionality but implement a different interface, so we can’t use them directly. ‾ So we will use adapter pattern. Here our target would be ToyDuck and adaptee would be Bird. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9 * Source: http://www.geeksforgeeks.org/adapter-pattern/
Adapter Example: ToyDuck and Bird code

The existing code: Code What it does interface ToyDuck { public void squeak(); } The target interface: toy ducks don’t fly, they just squeak. class PlasticToyDuck implements ToyDuck { public void squeak() { System.out.println("Squeak"); } } A normal toy duck. interface Bird { public void fly(); public void makeSound(); } The adaptee interface: birds fly and make sounds. class Sparrow implements Bird { fly() { …"Flying"… } makeSound() { …"Chirp Chirp"… } } A concrete bird. Adapter Design Pattern – Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
Adapter Example: BirdAdapter

The adapter: Code What it does class BirdAdapter implements ToyDuck { Implements the interface the client expects (ToyDuck). Bird bird; Holds a reference to the object being adapted (object adapter). public BirdAdapter(Bird bird) { this.bird = bird; } The bird to adapt is passed in. public void squeak() { bird.makeSound(); } } Translates the target call into the adaptee call. The UML on the right: Client → «ToyDuck» ← BirdAdapter (realization) → Bird ← Sparrow: the object structural version of the pattern. Adapter Design Pattern – Example Bird ToyDuck +makeSound() +squeak() Sparrow BirdAdapter +makeSound() +squeak() Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
Adapter Example: the client

The client: Code What it does Sparrow sparrow = new Sparrow(); PlasticToyDuck toyDuck = new PlasticToyDuck(); A real bird and a real toy duck. ToyDuck birdAdapter = new BirdAdapter(sparrow); Wrap the bird so it behaves like a toy duck. sparrow.fly(); sparrow.makeSound(); toyDuck.squeak(); Prints “Flying”, “Chirp Chirp”, “Squeak”. birdAdapter.squeak(); A ToyDuck call that prints “Chirp Chirp”: the toy duck is behaving like a bird. Adapter Design Pattern – Example Bird ToyDuck +makeSound() +squeak() BirdAdapter Sparrow +squeak() +makeSound() Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
Adapter Design Pattern Example

The version just built is the object adapter , because the adapter holds an instance of the adaptee. The alternative, the class adapter , uses inheritance instead of composition, which requires multiple inheritance : BirdAdapter would extend Sparrow and implement ToyDuck (the diagram on the right). Adapter Design Pattern – Example Bird +makeSound() ➢Object Adapter Vs Class Adapter ✓The adapter pattern we have implemented ToyDuck Sparrow above is called Object Adapter Pattern +squeak() +makeSound() because the adapter holds an instance of adaptee. There is also another type called Class Adapter Pattern which use inheritance instead of composition but you BirdAdapter require multiple inheritance to implement it. +squeak() Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
Adapter Design Pattern Example

Because many languages don’t support multiple inheritance of classes (and it causes problems where they do), the object adapter is preferred . In Java this one case works only because ToyDuck is an interface. Adapter Design Pattern – Example Bird +makeSound() ➢Object Adapter Vs Class Adapter ✓Here instead of having an adaptee object ToyDuck Sparrow inside adapter (composition) to make use of +squeak() +makeSound() its functionality the adapter (BirdAdapter) class inherits the adaptee (Sparrow) class. ✓Since multiple inheritance is not supported BirdAdapter by many languages and is associated with +squeak() many problems object adapter pattern is preferred Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
Adapter Example: client code and explanation

The client again: create a Sparrow, wrap it in a BirdAdapter, and call birdAdapter.squeak() , which outputs “Chirp chirp”: the client expects a ToyDuck but actually uses a Bird. In the ToyDuck/Bird example, name the target, adaptee and adapter, and say which method call is translated. ➢Explanation ➢ToyDuck is the expected interface (Target). ➢Bird/Sparrow is the legacy interface (Adaptee). ➢BirdAdapter converts squeak() into makeSound(). ➢The Client works with ToyDuck but internally a Bird is used. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Adapter Design Pattern

Advantage : reusability and flexibility: existing classes are reused without modification. Disadvantage : sometimes a chain of adapters is needed to reach the required type (like the stacked plug adapters in the photo). Adapter Design Pattern ➢Advantages: ✓Helps achieve reusability and flexibility. ✓Client class is not complicated by having to use a different interface and can use polymorphism to swap between different implementations of adapters. ➢Disadvantages: ✓All requests are forwarded, so there is a slight increase in the overhead. ✓Sometimes many adaptations are required along an adapter chain to reach the type which is required. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 18
The Composite Design Pattern

Intent (2): let clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly : the same call works on one item or a whole group. File explorer: Files (leaf, with a size) and Directories (contain files and other folders, nested to any depth). Calculate a folder’s total size. Which pattern? Draw its class diagram. The Composite Design Pattern ➢The Composite design pattern is an object structural pattern that allows designers to compose tree-like design by strategically structuring objects that share a whole-part relationship. ➢The intent of the Composite is to: ✓Compose objects into tree structures to represent whole-part hierarchies. ✓Composite pattern lets clients treat individual objects and composites of objects uniformly. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 19
The Composite Design Pattern Structure

«interface» Component declares the common operation ( doOperation() ). The Client depends only on Component. Leaf realises Component and does the operation itself; it has no children. Composite realises Component too, and holds 0..\ * child Components (the filled diamond with multiplicity 1 to 0..\* is composition). It adds addComponent() , removeComponent() and getChild(index) , and its doOperation() calls doOperation() on each child. In the Composite pattern, what does the Composite class do when its operation is called? The Composite Design Pattern – Structure Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
The Composite Design Pattern Example

The example: «interface» Component with sayHello() and sayGoodbye() ; Leaf and Composite both realise it; Composite holds 0..\* Components; CompositeDemo is the client. The highlighted methods are the ones each class implements. The Composite Design Pattern – Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 21
Composite Example: Component.java

Component.java: Code What it does public interface Component { public void sayHello(); public void sayGoodbye(); } The operations every node, leaf or composite, supports. The Composite Design Pattern – Example* ➢The following slides have the Java code the represents the implementation of the classes in the Composite Design Pattern File: Component.java Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 22 *source: https://www.avajava.com/tutorials/lessons/composite-pattern.html?page=1
The Composite Design Pattern Example

The diagram with Leaf outlined: it has a String name and implements sayHello() and sayGoodbye() . The Composite Design Pattern – Example String name Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 23
Composite Example: Leaf.java

Leaf.java: Code What it does public class Leaf implements Component { String name; A leaf has its own data and no children. public Leaf(String name) { this.name = name; } @Override public void sayHello() { System.out.println(name + " leaf says hello"); } Does the work itself. @Override public void sayGoodbye() { System.out.println(name + " leaf says goodbye"); } } File: Leaf.java The Composite Design Pattern Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 24
The Composite Design Pattern Example

The diagram with Composite outlined: it implements sayHello() and sayGoodbye() plus the child-management methods addComponent() , removeComponent() and getChild() . The Composite Design Pattern – Example String name Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 25
Composite Example: Composite.java

Composite.java: Code What it does public class Composite implements Component { A composite is also a Component, so it can be nested. List<Component> components = new ArrayList<Component>(); Its children: leaves or other composites. @Override public void sayHello() { for (Component component : components) { component.sayHello(); } } Forward the call to every child: this loop is the recursion. @Override public void sayGoodbye() { for (…) { component.sayGoodbye(); } } public void add(Component component) { components.add(component); } Child management. public void remove(Component component) { … } getComponents() { … } getComponent(int index) { … } } The Composite Design Pattern Example File: Composite.java Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 26
The Composite Design Pattern Example

The diagram with the client CompositeDemo outlined: it depends only on Component, though it builds the tree from Leaf and Composite objects. The Composite Design Pattern – Example String name Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 27
Composite Example: CompositeDemo.java

CompositeDemo.java: Code What it does Leaf leaf1 = new Leaf("Bob"); … leaf5 = new Leaf("Joe"); Five leaves: Bob, Fred, Sue, Ellen, Joe. Composite composite1 = new Composite(); composite1.add(leaf1); composite1.add(leaf2); composite1 = {Bob, Fred}. Composite composite2 = new Composite(); composite2.add(leaf3); composite2.add(leaf4); composite2 = {Sue, Ellen}. Composite composite3 = new Composite(); composite3.add(composite1); composite3.add(composite2); composite3.add(leaf5); composite3 = {composite1, composite2, Joe}: a tree two levels deep. leaf1.sayHello(); composite1.sayHello(); composite2.sayHello(); composite3.sayGoodbye(); The same calls on a leaf and on composites. The Composite Design Pattern – Example File: CompositeDemo.java Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 28
Composite Example: output

sayGoodbye on composite3 prints goodbye from all five leaves (Bob, Fred, Sue, Ellen, Joe): one call at the root reached every nested leaf, because each composite forwarded it to its children. The Composite Design Pattern – Example Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 29
The Composite Design Pattern

3. Design the Composite class: it overrides the common methods, keeps an internal data structure for its child nodes, and adds methods to add and remove children. The Composite Design Pattern ➢The steps required to apply the composite design pattern include: 1. Identify, understand, and plan the tree-like structure required for the system. 2. Identify and design the Component base class: ✓ Includes overridable methods common to both Leaf and Composite objects. 3. Identify and design the Composite class, which will: ✓ Overrides common methods in the component interface. ✓ Requires an internal data structure to store objects (nodes) added to the hierarchy. ✓ Includes methods specific for Composite objects, which provide capability for adding and removing objects to the internal data structure (i.e. add objects to hierarchy). 4. Identify and design the Leaf classes, which overrides methods in the component class 5. Identify and design the client that uses both composite and leaf objects. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 30
The Composite Design Pattern

It gives one structure that supports both composite and primitive (leaf) objects. It minimises complexity for clients : they don’t need to know whether they hold a primitive or a composite, because operations are called the same way on both. A client written for a single object also works with a whole group. New component types are easy to add without changing client code. (The trade-off: a general Component interface can make it hard to restrict which children a composite may hold.) Give two benefits of the Composite pattern. The Composite Design Pattern ➢Benefits of the Composite design pattern: ✓Provides a design structure that supports both composite and primitive objects. ✓Minimizes complexity on clients by shielding them from knowing the operational differences between primitive and composite objects. −Clients that expect a primitive object will also work with a composite object, since operations are called uniformly on both primitive and composite objects. ✓Easy to create and add new components objects to applications. https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials/composite-design-pattern-in-java Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 31
Extra: Explanation of the Composite pattern

Extra: ➢Explanation of the Composite Design Pattern ➢The Composite design pattern is used when we want to treat individual objects (primitives) and groups of objects (composites) in the same way. ➢It provides a tree-like structure, where leaf nodes are simple objects and composite nodes are collections of objects. ➢Clients (the user or program that uses the objects) don’t need to know whether they’re dealing with a single object or a group — they can call the same operations uniformly. ➢This reduces complexity because the same interface is used for both simple and complex objects. ➢It also makes it easier to add new objects (either simple or composite) without changing the client code. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 32
Extra: Composite in real life

File system : a file is primitive (contains nothing), a folder is composite (contains files and other folders). The same “open” operation shows a file’s content or expands a folder: the file explorer treats both the same way. This is exactly the Final 252 question. Extra: Real-Life Example File System (Folders and Files): •A file is a primitive object — it doesn’t contain other objects. •A folder is a composite object — it can contain both files and other folders. •Whether you open a file or a folder, you’re using the same operation (open). If it’s a file, the content shows directly. If it’s a folder, it expands to show its contents. The file explorer treats both files (primitives) and folders (composites) the same way. Another Simple Example for Students Think about a university course structure: •A single course (like “Math 101”) is a primitive. •A program (like “Computer Science degree”) is a composite — it contains many courses. •Whether you check the details of one course or the whole program, you interact with them in a similar way. 33
Facade Design Pattern

Intent: provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem; the facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use. Like a hotel reception desk: one place to ask, many departments behind it. Providing one simple interface to a set of complex subsystem classes is the: Facade pattern Adapter pattern Composite pattern Singleton pattern Facade Design Pattern ➢The Facade design pattern is an object structural pattern that provides a simplified interface to complex subsystems. ➢The intent of the Facade is to: ✓Provide a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. ✓Facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 34
Facade Design Pattern - Structure

The structure: the Client depends only on the Facade , whose methods ( operation2() , operation41() ) are implemented by calling ClassA and ClassB in the subsystem ( operation1() … operation4() ). The client never touches ClassA or ClassB directly. Facade Design Pattern - Structure Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 35
Facade Design Pattern Example*

The example (from javatpoint): a mobile subsystem with «interface» MobileShop ( modelNo() , price() ) implemented by Iphone, Samsung and Blackberry. The client (FacadePatternClient) shouldn’t deal with those details, so a facade class, ShopKeeper , keeps one of each phone and offers simple methods: iphoneSale() , samsungSale() , blackberrySale() . Facade Design Pattern – Example* ➢Consider the following UML mobile sub-system example. The client class requires to <<interface>> MobileShop use the mobile sub-system without the need to deal with details of the sub-systems. ➢This can be achieved by using a Facade Pattern class (ShopKeeper) to allow to client class to use the mobile sub-system easily. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 36 *source: https://www.javatpoint.com/facade-pattern
Facade Example: MobileShop and Iphone

The subsystem: Code What it does public interface MobileShop { public void modelNo(); public void price(); } The subsystem interface. public class Iphone implements MobileShop { modelNo() { …" Iphone 6 "… } price() { …" Rs 65000.00 "… } } One subsystem class. Facade Design Pattern – Example (implementation) ➢The following Java code represent the implementation of the classes in the mobile sub-system: Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 37
Facade Example: Samsung and Blackberry

Samsung prints “Samsung galaxy tab 3” and “Rs 45000.00”; Blackberry prints “Blackberry Z10” and “Rs 55000.00”. Same interface, three classes the client would otherwise have to know. Facade Design Pattern – Example (implementation) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 38
Facade Example: ShopKeeper

The facade: Code What it does public class ShopKeeper { private MobileShop iphone; private MobileShop samsung; private MobileShop blackberry; It holds the subsystem objects. public ShopKeeper() { iphone = new Iphone(); samsung = new Samsung(); blackberry = new Blackberry(); } And creates them, so the client doesn’t have to. public void iphoneSale() { iphone.modelNo(); iphone.price(); } One task-level method = the right sequence of subsystem calls. public void samsungSale() { … } public void blackberrySale() { … } } Facade Design Pattern – Example (implementation) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 40
Facade Example: client and output

The client: Code What it does ShopKeeper sk = new ShopKeeper(); The only subsystem-related class it knows. switch (choice) { case 1: sk.iphoneSale(); break; case 2: sk.samsungSale(); break; case 3: sk.blackberrySale(); break; … } A menu: 1 iPhone, 2 Samsung, 3 Blackberry, 4 Exit. Facade Design Pattern – Example (implementation) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 42
Facade Design Pattern Example*

ShopKeeper lets the client use the mobile subsystem without knowing anything about it : which classes exist, how they are created, or which methods to call in which order. Facade Design Pattern – Example* ➢As noted from the example, the mobile sub-system Façade Pattern provided us with a <<interface>> MobileShop simplified interface to a complex subsystems. ➢The Facade Pattern class (ShopKeeper) to allow client class to use the mobile sub-system without knowing anything about the sub- system. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 43 *source: https://www.javatpoint.com/facade-pattern
Facade Design Pattern

True or false: Adapter changes an interface to match what a client expects, while Facade simplifies access to a whole subsystem. How do Adapter and Facade differ? Facade Design Pattern ➢The step-by-step procedure for applying the Facade design pattern include: 1. Identify all components involved in carrying out a subsystem operation 2. Create a list of the operations required to execute the subsystem operation. 3. Design a Facade class that includes an interface method to carry out the subsystem operation. 4. Implement the Facade interface method by calling operations on one or more subsystem components, in the list identified in step 2. 5. Allow one ore more clients to access the objects of the Facade type so that they can gain access to the subsystem operation. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 44
Facade Design Pattern

It promotes weak coupling : clients depend on one interface instead of many. (Keep facades focused on related tasks so they don’t become “god objects”.) Facade Design Pattern ➢Benefits of the Facade design pattern include ✓Shields clients from knowing the internals of complex subsystem, therefore minimizing complexity in clients. ✓The facade provides a stable interface that hides changes to internal subsystems; therefore, client code is more stable. ✓ Promotes weak coupling on clients; with facade, clients depend only on one interface instead of multiple interfaces Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 45

Summary ➢In this session, we presented structural design patterns, including: ✓Adapter ✓Facade ✓Composite ➢Next … we will present behavioral design patterns in detailed design. decks.t: Behavioral Design Patterns: Iterator and Observer
decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 7 · Lecture 2: Behavioral Design Patterns: Iterator and Observer
n: Slide 1

The last design-pattern lecture: behavioural patterns, which are about how objects interact and share work. Two are covered: Iterator and Observer . Software Design and Architecture [Behavioral Design Patterns] – Chapter 07, L02
Lecture Outlines

Lecture Outlines ⮚Previously- Structural Design Patterns ✔Adapter ✔Composite ✔Facade ⮚Behavioral Design Patterns ✔Iterator ✔Observer | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Behavioral Design Patterns

Behavioral Design Patterns ⮚Behavioral patterns are responsible for the efficient and safe distribution of behaviors among the program's objects. ⮚Popular behavioral design patterns include: ✔Iterator ✔Observer ✔Others not covered: − Memento −Command − State −Chain of responsibility − Strategy −Interpreter − Template Method −Mediator − Visitor | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3
1- Iterator Design Pattern

Its intent : provide a way to access the elements of a collection sequentially without knowing its underlying representation . The client asks “is there another one?” and “give me the next one”, and never sees whether the data is an array, a linked list or a tree. Traversing a collection without exposing whether it is stored as an array, a list or a tree is the: Iterator pattern Observer pattern Composite pattern Facade pattern 1- Iterator Design Pattern ⮚The Iterator design pattern is an object behavioral pattern that provides a standardized way for accessing and traversing objects in a collection data structure. ⮚The intent of the Iterators to: ✔Provide a way to access the elements of a collection object sequentially without any need to know its underlying representation. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Iterator: class and sequence diagrams

Iterator1 implements Iterator by accessing Aggregate1 , which creates it. The sequence diagram (right) shows the run: the client calls createIterator() , Aggregate1 creates an Iterator1 and returns it, then the client loops [while hasNext()] next() and gets one element each time. In the above UML class diagram, the Client class refers (1) to the Aggregate interface for creating an Iterator object (createIterator()) and (2) to the Iterator interface for traversing an Aggregate object (next(),hasNext()). The Iterator1 class implements the Iterator interface by accessing the Aggregate1 class. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Iterator: generic structure

The generic structure: an Aggregate with iterator() and an Iterator with next() and hasNext() (italic = abstract), linked by «create». ConcreteAggregate implements iterator() to create a ConcreteIterator , which implements next() and hasNext() and keeps a reference to its aggregate (the diamond) so it can read the elements. See example on https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/iterator-pattern/ | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
Iterator Design Pattern –

The example’s structure: «Interface» Container ( getIterator(): Iterator ) plays the aggregate; «Interface» Iterator has hasNext(): boolean and next(): Object . Iterator Design Pattern – Structure client | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 7
Iterator Example: Iterator.java and Container.java

The two interfaces: Code What it does public interface Iterator { public boolean hasNext(); public Object next(); } The traversal contract: is there another element, and give me it. public interface Container { public Iterator getIterator(); } The aggregate contract: hand out an iterator. Iterator Design Pattern – Example* | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8 *Source: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/design_pattern/iterator_pattern.htm
Iterator Design Pattern –

The diagram with the two concrete classes outlined: NameRepository (the concrete collection) and NameIterator (the concrete iterator). They are written next. Iterator Design Pattern – Structure client | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
Iterator Example: NameRepository.java

It has an inner class NameIterator implementing Iterator: Code What it does public class NameRepository implements Container { public String names[] = {"Robert", "John", "Julie", "Lora"}; The data, stored as an array. @Override public Iterator getIterator() { return new NameIterator(); } Hands out a fresh iterator each time. private class NameIterator implements Iterator { int index; An inner class, so it can read names directly; index is its own cursor. public boolean hasNext() { if (index < names.length) { return true; } return false; } Another element exists while the cursor is inside the array. public Object next() { if (this.hasNext()) { return names[index++]; } return null; } } } Return the current name and advance; null past the end. Iterator Design Pattern – Example ⮚ Create concrete class implementing the Container interface. ⮚ This class has inner class NameIterator implementing the Iterator interface. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
Iterator Example: the code together

All the code on one slide: the interfaces on the left and NameRepository with its inner NameIterator on the right. The client only ever sees Container and Iterator, so the names could move into a list or a database without changing it. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
Iterator Design Pattern –

The diagram with the client IteratorPatternDemo outlined: next, the code that uses the repository. Iterator Design Pattern – Structure client | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
Iterator Example: the client and output

The client: Code What it does NameRepository namesRepository = new NameRepository(); The collection. for (Iterator iter = namesRepository.getIterator(); iter.hasNext();) { Get an iterator and loop while there is a next element. String name = (String) iter.next(); System.out.println("Name : " + name); } Read and print each one. Iterator Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
Iterator Design Pattern

Iterator Design Pattern ⮚The step-by-step approach for designing the Iterator design pattern is presented as follows: 1. Identify and design the Iterator interface. 2. For each class representing a collection data structure in the software system, design a concrete Iterator and associate it with it. Implement the concrete iterator’s methods in terms of the collection data structure. 3. Create the Collection interface, which includes the interface method to create Iterators. 4. For each class representing a collection data structure, implement the Aggregate interface to instantiate and return a concrete Iterator. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
Iterator Design Pattern

Client code is easy to extend: many iterators can support different traversals (forward, reverse, filtered) over the same or different collections. Give two benefits of the Iterator pattern. Iterator Design Pattern ⮚Benefits of the Iterator design pattern include: ✔The Iterator provides a consistent way for clients to iterate through the objects in a collection. ✔It abstracts the internals of the collection objects so that if they change, clients do not have to change. ✔Allows client code to be extended easily; numerous iterators can be created to support different traversals from the same or different collection structure. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
In class exercise: the company directory

The exercise: a company directory stores employee records in two different internal data structures (an array and a list) but lets clients traverse both the same way . Answer: Iterator . A DirectoryIterator interface ( hasNext() , next() ); ArrayDirectory and ListDirectory each implement a Directory interface with createIterator() and createReverseIterator() , returning concrete iterators that know their structure. The client loops with hasNext() / next() whichever directory and direction it uses. A company directory stores employees in an array in one version and a linked list in another, and clients need forward and reverse traversal of both. Which pattern, and what classes? In class exercise ⮚ The Company Directory: This exercise involves creating a corporate directory that can store employee records using two different internal data structures (e.g., a simple array and a list) but allows a client to traverse them in a uniform way. Furthermore, the client needs two specific traversal methods: standard and reverse. ⮚ Which pattern to use based on the above scenarios ⮚ Draw class ⮚ Generate code 16
Observer Design Pattern

Its intent : define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state , all its dependents are notified and updated automatically . Like a newsletter: subscribe once, and every new issue is pushed to you. Global Weather Sync: when the primary weather station’s temperature changes, all registered city dashboards update instantly, in Celsius and Fahrenheit. Which pattern? Draw its class diagram. Observer Design Pattern ⮚The Observer design pattern is an object behavioral pattern that standardizes the operations between objects that interoperate using a one-to-many relationship. ⮚The intent of the Observer is to ✔Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Observer Design Pattern - Structure

Subject : attach(in Observer) to register observers, setState() to change, getState() to read. It keeps its observers (the “views”, multiplicity \*). «interface» Observer : update() . Each observer holds a reference back to its subject (the “model” arrow) so it can read the new state. ViewOne and ViewTwo realise Observer, each with its own update() . This is the same mechanism MVC uses to refresh views when the model changes. In the Observer pattern, what happens when the subject’s state changes? Observer Design Pattern - Structure | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 18
Observer Design Pattern – Example: class diagram

ObserverPatternDemo is the client. Whenever the number changes, each observer prints it in its own base. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 19 *Source: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/design_pattern/observer_pattern.htm
Observer Example: Subject.java

Subject.java: Code What it does private List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<Observer>(); private int state; The registered observers and the state they care about. public int getState() { return state; } Observers read the state through this. public void setState(int state) { this.state = state; notifyAllObservers(); } Changing the state triggers notification: the heart of the pattern. public void attach(Observer observer) { observers.add(observer); } Registration. public void notifyAllObservers() { for (Observer observer : observers) { observer.update(); } } Tell every observer, without knowing their concrete classes. Observer Design Pattern Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
Observer Example: the Observer class

The diagram with the abstract Observer outlined: it holds +subject: Subject and declares +update() . Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 21 *Source: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/design_pattern/observer_pattern.htm
Observer Example: Observer.java

Observer.java: Code What it does public abstract class Observer { protected Subject subject; An abstract class here (an interface works too); every observer knows its subject. public abstract void update(); } Called by the subject on every change. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 22
Observer Example: concrete observers

The diagram with the three concrete observers outlined: BinaryObserver , OctalObserver and HexaObserver , each implementing update() its own way. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 23 *Source: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/design_pattern/observer_pattern.htm
Observer Example: BinaryObserver.java

BinaryObserver.java: Code What it does public BinaryObserver(Subject subject) { this.subject = subject; this.subject.attach(this); } The observer registers itself with the subject when created. @Override public void update() { System.out.println("Binary String: " + Integer.toBinaryString(subject.getState())); } On notification it pulls the new state and prints it in binary. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 24
Observer Example: OctalObserver.java
Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 25
Observer Example: HexaObserver.java

HexaObserver prints Integer.toHexString(subject.getState()).toUpperCase() . Adding a fourth observer (say, Roman numerals) would need no change to Subject. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 26
Observer Example: the client

The diagram with the client ObserverPatternDemo outlined: it creates the subject and the observers, then changes the state. Observer Design Pattern – Example* | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 27 *Source: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/design_pattern/observer_pattern.htm
Observer Example: ObserverPatternDemo.java

The client: Code What it does Subject subject = new Subject(); One subject. new HexaObserver(subject); new OctalObserver(subject); new BinaryObserver(subject); Three observers; each attaches itself in its constructor. System.out.println("First state change: 15"); subject.setState(15); One state change… System.out.println("Second state change: 10"); subject.setState(10); …and another. Output: for 15, “Hex String: F”, “Octal String: 17”, “Binary String: 1111”; for 10, “A”, “12”, “1010”. Each setState call reached all three observers automatically, in the order they attached. Observer Design Pattern – Example | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 28
Observer Design Pattern

True or false: in the Observer pattern the subject must know the concrete classes of its observers. Observer Design Pattern ⮚The steps required to apply the Observer design pattern include: 1. Design the Subject interface and implement code for attaching, detaching, and notifying observer objects. The code for keeping track of observers can be done using existing linked-lists data structures. 2. For classes that manage information of interests to observers, inherit from the subject class created in step 1. 3. Design the Observer interface, which includes the abstract update interface method. 4. For all observers in the system, implement the Observer interface, which requires implementing the update method. 5. At run-time, create each observer and attach them to the subject. When changes occur, the subject iterates through its list of registered objects, and calls their update method. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 29
Observer Design Pattern

Flexibility to add new services: a new observer is just a new class that attaches itself. Specific services are compartmentalised (each observer handles its own reaction), so maintaining and modifying them is easier. (Watch for: notification order, slow observers holding up the rest, and observers that are never detached.) Give one benefit and one drawback of the Observer pattern. Observer Design Pattern ⮚Benefits of the Observer design pattern: ✔Flexibility for adding new services to the system. ✔Since specific services are compartmentalized, maintain and modifying existing system services becomes easier. | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 30
In class activity: social-media followers

The tasks, as code: Code What it does interface Follower { void update(String post); } The observer interface. class Influencer { List<Follower> followers = new ArrayList<>(); void follow(Follower f) { followers.add(f); } void unfollow(Follower f) { followers.remove(f); } The subject keeps its followers… void post(String text) { notifyFollowers(text); } void notifyFollowers(String p) { for (Follower f : followers) f.update(p); } } …and notifies all of them on each post. class MobileAppUser implements Follower { public void update(String post) { System.out.println("Mobile User received notification: " + post); } } Concrete observers (WebBrowserUser is the same with “Web User”). In class activity ⮚ The Scenario: Social Media Follower System: Imagine you are building a simplified version of a social media platform like Instagram or X (Twitter). ⮚ The Components: The Subject (The Influencer): A high-profile user who posts updates. When they post a new "Status Update," they don't want to manually message every single follower. ⮚ The Observers (The Followers): Various users who have "Subscribed" or "Followed" the Influencer. They want to be notified automatically the moment a new post is live. ⮚ The Exercise Task: ✔ Define the Subject: Create an Influencer class that maintains a list of followers. It should have methods to follow(), unfollow(), and notifyFollowers(). ✔ Define the Observer: Create a Follower interface with an update(String post) method. ✔ Implement Concrete Observers: Create a MobileAppUser and a WebBrowserUser. When they receive an update, they should print a message like: "Mobile User received notification: [Post Content]". 31
Summary

Behavioural patterns covered: Iterator (hide how a collection is traversed) and Observer (broadcast state changes to registered objects). Summary ⮚In this session, we presented behavioral design patterns, including: ✔Iterator ✔Observer ⮚Next … we will present architecture and design evaluation | Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 32

decks.c: SE322 · Chapter 8: Architecture Evaluation and ATAM
n: Slide 1

Chapter 8 returns to the third key task of architectural design from Chapter 2: evaluating and validating the architecture before it is built. Software Design and Architecture [Architecture and Design Evaluation] Chapter 08, L01 –
Lecture Outlines

ATAM in detail, and its lightweight version. Lecture Outlines Previously- Design Patterns Architecture Evaluation  Benefits of Architecture Evaluation  Methods of Architecture Evaluation  ATAM Evaluation  Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 2
Software Architecture Evaluation*

It is shaped by three drivers : functional requirements , non-functional (quality) requirements and business constraints (budget, schedule, regulations). An evaluation checks the architecture against all three. Which of these is NOT one of the three drivers that shape a software architecture? The programming language’s syntax Functional requirements Non-functional requirements Business constraints Software Architecture Evaluation* The architecture design is the foundation of any software system. It defines the structure of the system through its underlying components and their relationship as well as the properties and behavior that are exposed to the external world. The software architecture is basically shaped by the following drivers: functional requirements, non-functional requirements and business constraints. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 3 *Source: https://johnolamendy.wordpress.com/2011/08/12/evaluate-the-software-architecture-using-atam/
Software Architecture Evaluation

The earlier a problem is found, the cheaper it is to fix: a wrong decision found on paper costs a meeting; found in code, it costs a rewrite. Software Architecture Evaluation In order to run a successful project with a high quality software product, it is important to validate the architectural design in advance The earlier we find a problem in the design phase, the better (less cost to fix an error) architectural decisions Software architecture ( ) should be evaluated before the construction phase begins . Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 4
Benefits of Architecture Evaluation

It results in prioritisation of conflicting goals : stakeholders must agree which qualities matter most when they clash. It forces a clear explanation of the architecture : the architect must be able to present and justify it. It improves the quality of the architecture documentation , because gaps show up during the review. It leads to improved architecture practices in the organisation over time. What are the benefits of architecture evaluation? State two only. Benefits of Architecture Evaluation Results in prioritization of conflicting goals Forces clear explanation of architecture Improves quality of architecture documentation Uncovers opportunities for cross-project reuse Results in improved architecture practices Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 5
Major Architectural Evaluation Methods

ATAM : the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (the main one in this chapter). What they all have in common : they evaluate the architecture using scenarios and quality attributes . They differ in depth and focus, not in the underlying idea. What is the shared, common point between all architecture evaluation methods? Major Architectural Evaluation Methods Today, we have several methods to evaluate the software architecture : ATAM: Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method SAAM: Software Architecture Analysis Method ARID: Active Reviews for Intermediate Designs These methods, have in common, the use of scenarios and quality attribute in the evaluation process Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 6
ATAM Evaluation Method

In practice that means discovering risks : places where an architectural decision affects a quality attribute of interest, often through a trade-off between qualities. What does ATAM stand for, and what is its purpose? ATAM Evaluation Method ATAM The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method ( ), is one of the most used architectural decision method. ATAM The purpose of is to assess the consequences of architectural decisions in light of quality attribute requirements and business goals. This means discovering risks where a quality attribute of interest is affected by architectural decisions (a trade-off between the quality attributes). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 7
Slide 8

The key concept in every evaluation method is the quality attribute (Chapter 3). In complex systems qualities can never be achieved in isolation : improving one affects others, sometimes negatively (encryption adds security but costs performance), sometimes positively (modularity helps both modifiability and testability). So architectural decisions are really trade-offs between qualities in support of the business goals, which is exactly what ATAM analyses. ATAM Evaluation Method – Quality attributes Re-visited One important concept related to any architecture evaluation method is the quality attribute. In complex systems, quality attributes can never be achieved in isolation. In order to achieve one quality, other quality is affected (sometimes negative and sometimes positive). So … the architectural decisions are really a trade-off between the quality attributes in order to support the business goals. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 8
ATAM Evaluation Method - Quality attributes Re-visited

ATAM Evaluation Method - Quality attributes Re-visited We can group the quality attributes into three main categories: End-user perspective: performance, availability, usability and security Technical perspective: modifiability, portability, reusability, testability, interoperability Business community perspective: time to market, cost and benefits, projected life time, project budget In order to evaluate the software architecture using quality attributes, we need to characterize them in a proper way using quality attribute scenario. (see Chapter 3 slides for details about attribute scenarios) Then, a quality attribute scenario can be used to prioritize the quality attributes. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 9
Slide 10

Name the three groups that take part in an ATAM evaluation. ATAM Evaluation Method Participants – In order to execute the ATAM process correctly, we need three groups cooperating each other: Evaluation team: A group of experienced architects (three to five people) Project decision makers: People with the authority to make changes in the project (project manager, customer, manager) Architecture stakeholders: People interested in a good architecture for doing correctly there job (developers, testers, integrators, maintainers, performance engineering and users) Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 10
ATAM Evaluation - Team Roles

Team leader : sets up the evaluation contract with the client, forms the team, and makes sure the final report is produced and delivered. (The garbled text on the slide is overlapping lines in the PDF.) Scenario scribe writes scenarios on the board and captures their agreed wording, stopping discussion until it is exact; the proceedings scribe records everything electronically (scenarios, the issues behind them, how each was resolved) and prints the adopted scenarios. ATAM Evaluation - Team Roles Role Responsibilities Team leader establishes evaluation contract; forms evaluation team; sees that final report is Sperotsd uupce tdh ea nedva dluelaitvieorne;d c o(aolrtdhionuagthes t hwei twh rciltiienngt ,m maayk bine gd seulergea ctleiden)t’s needs are met; Runs evaluation; facilitates elicitation of scenarios; administers scenario Evaluation selection/prioritization process; facilitates evaluation of scenarios against architecture; leader facilitates on-site analysis Writes scenarios on flipchart or whiteboard during scenario elicitation; captures Scenario agreed-on wording of each scenario, halting discussion until exact wording is captured scribe Captures proceedings in electronic form on laptop or workstation: raw scenarios, Proceedings issue(s) that motivate each scenario (often lost in the wording of the scenario itself), scribe and resolution of each scenario when applied to architecture(s); also generates a printed list of adopted scenarios for handout to all participants Raises issues of architectural interest, usually related to the quality attributes in which Questioner he or she has expertise Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 11
ATAM Evaluation Method Steps

Steps 4–6 do the first analysis: identify architectural approaches, generate the quality-attribute utility tree , analyse the approaches against its top scenarios. List the nine steps of ATAM in order. In which ATAM step is the quality attribute utility tree generated? Step 5 Step 2 Step 7 Step 9 ATAM Evaluation Method Steps – The ATAM evaluation process consist of 9 steps: 1. Present the ATAM method 2. Present the business drivers 3. Present the architecture 4. Identify architectural approaches 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree 6. Analyze architectural approaches Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 12
ATAM Evaluation Method Steps

Steps 7–8 widen the view: all stakeholders brainstorm and prioritise scenarios, and the approaches are analysed again against them. ATAM Evaluation Method Steps – (cont.) The rest of the ATAM evaluation process steps: 7. Brainstorm and prioritize scenarios 8. Analyze architectural approaches 9. Present results Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 13
ATAM Evaluation – Phases
ATAM Evaluation Phases – Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 14
ATAM Evaluation Method Output

ATAM must produce at least the documentation of the selected architecture , whose key artefact is the SAD (Software Architecture Document) (Chapter 9). And an evaluation report that recaps the ATAM process, captures the scenario analysis (quality requirements written as scenarios), and explains the candidate architectures and the rationale for choosing one, with a summary of the work done. ATAM Evaluation Method Output – The output of the ATAM method must include at least the following artifacts: The documentation of the selected architecture: the key artifact to specify the architecture is the SAD (Software Architecture Document) An evaluation report that: −Recaps the ATAM process −Captures the scenario analysis (quality requirements captured in the form of scenarios). −Explains the candidate architectures and the underlying rationale in the architectural decision process to select the right architecture and a summary of all the work done. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 15
ATAM Steps in more detail

Section divider: slides 17–28 go through the nine steps one by one. ATAM Steps .. In more details … Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 16
Step 1. Present the ATAM method

Step 1. Present the ATAM method The evaluation team presents an overview of the ATAM process such as: The key steps, techniques (e.g. utility tree generation, architecture elicitation and analysis, scenario brainstorming). The expected output (architectural approaches, utility tree, scenarios, risks, sensitivity points). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 17
Step 2. Present the business drivers

Step 2. Present the business drivers The project decision maker presents the system from the business point of view including the following information: Business goals and context Major stakeholders High-level functional requirements (described as use cases or user stories) that impact on the system architecture Most important quality attributes (described as quality scenarios) that impact on the system architecture Constraints such as technical, managerial, economic and political Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 18
Step 3. Present architecture

The 4+1 view model (Chapter 2, Lecture 3) is a good way to structure the presentation. It covers the contextual view (relationships with people and other systems), the logical view (modules, layers), the process view (processes, threads, data flow, events) and the deployment view (CPUs, storage, devices, network). Step 3. Present architecture The lead architect makes a presentation describing the architectural approach used to meet the requirements and the constraints. In order to describe the architecture, it’s very useful to use the 4+1 architectural view model (see Chapter 02, L03) This view model describes the contextual view (e.g. relationship with humans and , the logical view , process view other systems) (module, layers, relationship) (e.g. and deployment view . process, threads, data flow, events) (CPU, storage, devices, network) And finally, describe risks associated in order to meet the architectural requirements. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 19
Step 4. Identify architectural approaches

The team analyses the architecture from step 3 in depth until it knows which patterns and approaches the architect used. These approaches are what the later analysis tests. Step 4. Identify architectural approaches The evaluation team tries to identify what key architectural approaches (patterns) are used for realizing the requirements and constraints. Possible architectural approaches like: client-server, multi-layer application, pipes-filters, etc. In this step, the evaluation team analyzes deeply the architecture presented in the step 3, and then it has a good idea of what patterns and approaches the architect used at designing the system. Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 20
Step 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree

A utility tree is a top-down way of characterising the quality requirements: the root is “utility”, the next level the most important qualities (performance, security, availability, modifiability, maintainability), and the leaves are concrete quality scenarios. Each leaf is rated for importance to the system’s success and difficulty to achieve (the architect’s assessment), usually H/M/L. High-importance, high-difficulty (H,H) scenarios are analysed first. What is a quality attribute utility tree, and how are its leaves rated? Step 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree In this step, the evaluation team (along with the project decision maker) identifies, prioritizes and refines the most important quality attribute goals (expressed by quality scenario) by building a utility tree. A utility tree is top-down approach for characterizing the quality attribute requirements, selecting the most important quality goals to be the high- level nodes (performance, security, availability, modifiability, maintainability) and the leaves of the tree are quality scenarios evaluated by important (success of the system) and difficulty (architect’s assessment). Prince Sultan University | Slides prepared from "Software Engineering Design: Theory and Practice" book and slides 21
Step 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree

A utility tree for a car’s anti-lock braking system (ABS), with three columns: quality attribute → requirement → scenario. Performance → R1 latency < 50 ms → “the ABS should respond in less than 50 ms after the driver hits the brake”. Reliability → R2 system reliability > 95% → “fault tolerance of at least 94%” (note the slide’s numbers don’t quite match). Resource consumption → R3 CPU utilisation < 80% → “CPU use of the ABS software below 80%”. Step 5. Generate quality attribute utility tree (cont.) Step 7 Brainstorm and prioritize scenarios

Step 7 : the wider group of stakeholders brainstorms scenarios that matter for their own roles. If new driving scenarios appear (they usually do), that may itself be a risk when the gap is large: the architect and stakeholders disagree about the system’s important goals. Step 7 Brainstorm and prioritize scenarios – In this step, the stakeholders brainstorm scenarios that are operationally meaningful with respect to the stakeholders’ individual roles.  The purpose of scenario brainstorming is to take the pulse of the larger stakeholder community: to understand what system success means for them. Once the scenarios have been collected, they are prioritized by voting. The list of prioritized scenarios is compared with those from the utility tree exercise:  If they agree, it indicates good alignment between what the architect had in mind and what the stakeholders actually wanted.  If additional driving scenarios are discovered—and they usually are—this may itself be a risk, if the conflict is large. This would indicate that there was some disagreement in the system’s important goals between the stakeholders and the architect. A Lightweight ATAM

It may be run entirely by people internal to the organisation. Because participants are internal and fewer, giving everyone their say and reaching shared understanding is much faster, and the steps run more quickly. The cost: a lower level of scrutiny and objectivity , so it may not probe the architecture as deeply as a full ATAM with an external team. What is the main difference between ATAM and lightweight ATAM? A Lightweight ATAM A Lightweight Architecture Evaluation method have been developed which is based on the ATAM, for smaller, less risky projects. May take place in a single day, or even a half-day meeting. May be carried out entirely by members internal to the organization. However, this lower level of scrutiny and objectivity may not probe the architecture as deeply. Because the participants are all internal to the organization and fewer in number than for the ATAM, giving everyone their say and achieving a shared understanding takes much less time. The steps and phases of a Lightweight Architecture Evaluation can be carried out more quickly.
